> This page describes the DuckDB ODBC driver, which lets other applications connect _to DuckDB_. To connect _from DuckDB to other databases_ over ODBC, use the [`odbc` extension](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:odbc:overview).

The ODBC (Open Database Connectivity) is a C-style API that provides access to different flavors of Database Management Systems (DBMSs).
The ODBC API consists of the Driver Manager (DM) and the ODBC drivers.

The Driver Manager is part of the system library, e.g., unixODBC, which manages the communications between the user applications and the ODBC drivers.
Typically, applications are linked against the DM, which uses Data Source Name (DSN) to look up the correct ODBC driver.

The ODBC driver is a DBMS implementation of the ODBC API, which handles all the internals of that DBMS.

The DM maps user application calls of ODBC functions to the correct ODBC driver that performs the specified function and returns the proper values.

#### DuckDB ODBC Driver {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:overview::duckdb-odbc-driver}

DuckDB supports the ODBC version 3.0 according to the [Core Interface Conformance](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/develop-app/core-interface-conformance?view=sql-server-ver15).

The ODBC driver is available for all operating systems. Visit the [installation page](https://duckdb.org/install) for direct links.

### ODBC API on Linux {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:linux}

#### Driver Manager {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:linux::driver-manager}

A driver manager is required to manage communication between applications and the ODBC driver.
We tested and support `unixODBC` that is a complete ODBC driver manager for Linux.
Users can install it from the command line:

On Debian-based distributions (Ubuntu, Mint, etc.), run:

```batch
sudo apt-get install unixodbc odbcinst
```

On Fedora-based distributions (Amazon Linux, RHEL, CentOS, etc.), run:

```batch
sudo yum install unixODBC
```

#### Setting Up the Driver {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:linux::setting-up-the-driver}

1. Download the ODBC Linux Asset corresponding to your architecture:

   

   * [x86_64 (AMD64)](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-odbc/releases/download/v{{ latest_package }}/duckdb_odbc-linux-amd64.zip)
   * [arm64 (AArch64)](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-odbc/releases/download/v{{ latest_package }}/duckdb_odbc-linux-arm64.zip)

   

2. The package contains the following files:

   * `libduckdb_odbc.so`: the DuckDB driver.
   * `unixodbc_setup.sh`: a setup script to aid the configuration on Linux.

   To extract them, run:

   ```batch
   mkdir duckdb_odbc && unzip duckdb_odbc-linux-amd64.zip -d duckdb_odbc
   ```

3. The `unixodbc_setup.sh` script performs the configuration of the DuckDB ODBC Driver. It is based on the unixODBC package that provides some commands to handle the ODBC setup and test like `odbcinst` and `isql`.

   Run the following commands with either option `-u` or `-s` to configure DuckDB ODBC.

   The `-u` option based on the user home directory to setup the ODBC init files.

   ```batch
   ./unixodbc_setup.sh -u
   ```

   The `-s` option changes the system level files that will be visible for all users, because of that it requires root privileges.

   ```batch
   sudo ./unixodbc_setup.sh -s
   ```

   The option `--help` shows the usage of `unixodbc_setup.sh` prints the help.

   ```batch
   ./unixodbc_setup.sh --help
   ```

   ```text
   Usage: ./unixodbc_setup.sh <level> [options]

   Example: ./unixodbc_setup.sh -u -db ~/database_path -D ~/driver_path/libduckdb_odbc.so

   Level:
   -s: System-level, using 'sudo' to configure DuckDB ODBC at the system-level, changing the files: /etc/odbc[inst].ini
   -u: User-level, configuring the DuckDB ODBC at the user-level, changing the files: ~/.odbc[inst].ini.

   Options:
   -db database_path>: the DuckDB database file path, the default is ':memory:' if not provided.
   -D driver_path: the driver file path (i.e., the path for libduckdb_odbc.so), the default is using the base script directory
   ```

4. The ODBC setup on Linux is based on the `.odbc.ini` and `.odbcinst.ini` files.

   These files can be placed to the user home directory `/home/⟨username⟩`{:.language-sql .highlight} or in the system `/etc`{:.language-sql .highlight} directory.
   The Driver Manager prioritizes the user configuration files over the system files.

   For the details of the configuration parameters, see the [ODBC configuration page](#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:configuration).

### ODBC API on Windows {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:windows}

#### Setup {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:windows::setup}

Using the DuckDB ODBC API on Windows requires the following steps:

1. Microsoft Windows requires an ODBC Driver Manager to manage communication between applications and the ODBC drivers.
   The Driver Manager on Windows is provided in a DLL file `odbccp32.dll`, and other files and tools.
   For detailed information check out the [Common ODBC Component Files](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/desktop/odbc/dn170563(v=vs.85)).

2.  DuckDB releases the ODBC driver as an asset. For Windows, download it from the [Windows ODBC asset (x86_64/AMD64)](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-odbc/releases/download/v{{ latest_package }}/duckdb_odbc-windows-amd64.zip). 

3. The archive contains the following artifacts:

   * `duckdb_odbc.dll`: the DuckDB driver compiled for Windows.
   * `duckdb_odbc_setup.dll`: a setup DLL used by the Windows ODBC Data Source Administrator tool.
   * `odbc_install.exe`: an installation script to aid the configuration on Windows.

   Decompress the archive to a directory (e.g., `duckdb_odbc`).

4. The `odbc_install.exe` binary performs the configuration of the DuckDB ODBC Driver on Windows. It depends on the `Odbccp32.dll` that provides functions to configure the ODBC registry entries.

   Inside the permanent directory (e.g., `duckdb_odbc`), double-click on the `odbc_install.exe`.

   Windows administrator privileges are required. In case of a non-administrator, a User Account Control prompt will occur.

5. `odbc_install.exe` adds a default DSN configuration into the ODBC registries with a default database `:memory:`.

##### DSN Windows Setup {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:windows::dsn-windows-setup}

After the installation, it is possible to change the default DSN configuration or add a new one using the Windows ODBC Data Source Administrator tool `odbcad32.exe`.

It also can be launched through the Windows start:

![](../images/blog/odbc/launch_odbcad.png)


##### Default DuckDB DSN {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:windows::default-duckdb-dsn}

The newly installed DSN is visible on the ***System DSN*** in the Windows ODBC Data Source Administrator tool:

![Windows ODBC Config Tool](../images/blog/odbc/odbcad32_exe.png)

##### Changing DuckDB DSN {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:windows::changing-duckdb-dsn}

When selecting the default DSN (i.e., `DuckDB`) or adding a new configuration, the following setup window will display:

![DuckDB Windows DSN Setup](../images/blog/odbc/duckdb_DSN_setup.png)

This window allows you to set the DSN and the database file path associated with that DSN.

#### More Detailed Windows Setup {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:windows::more-detailed-windows-setup}

There are two ways to configure the ODBC driver, either by altering the registry keys as detailed below,
or by connecting with [`SQLDriverConnect`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/syntax/sqldriverconnect-function?view=sql-server-ver16).
A combination of the two is also possible.

Furthermore, the ODBC driver supports all the [configuration options](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview)
included in DuckDB.

> If a configuration is set in both the connection string passed to `SQLDriverConnect` and in the `odbc.ini` file,
> the one passed to `SQLDriverConnect` will take precedence.

For the details of the configuration parameters, see the [ODBC configuration page](#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:configuration).

##### Registry Keys {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:windows::registry-keys}

The ODBC setup on Windows is based on registry keys (see [Registry Entries for ODBC Components](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/install/registry-entries-for-odbc-components?view=sql-server-ver15)).
The ODBC entries can be placed at the current user registry key (` HKCU`) or the system registry key (` HKLM`).

We have tested and used the system entries based on `HKLM->SOFTWARE->ODBC`.
The `odbc_install.exe` changes this entry that has two subkeys: `ODBC.INI` and `ODBCINST.INI`.

The `ODBC.INI` is where users usually insert DSN registry entries for the drivers.

For example, the DSN registry for DuckDB would look like this:

![`HKLM->SOFTWARE->ODBC->ODBC.INI->DuckDB`](../images/blog/odbc/odbc_ini-registry-entry.png)

The `ODBCINST.INI` contains one entry for each ODBC driver and other keys predefined for [Windows ODBC configuration](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/install/registry-entries-for-odbc-components?view=sql-server-ver15).

##### Updating the ODBC Driver {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:windows::updating-the-odbc-driver}

When a new version of the ODBC driver is released, installing the new version will overwrite the existing one.
However, the installer doesn't always update the version number in the registry.
To ensure the correct version is used,
check that `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\ODBC\ODBCINST.INI\DuckDB Driver` has the most recent version,
and `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\ODBC\ODBC.INI\DuckDB\Driver` has the correct path to the new driver.

### ODBC API on macOS {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:macos}

1. A driver manager is required to manage communication between applications and the ODBC driver. DuckDB supports `unixODBC`, which is a complete ODBC driver manager for macOS and Linux. Users can install it from the command line via [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/):

   ```batch
   brew install unixodbc
   ```

2.  DuckDB releases ODBC drivers for macOS on [Apple Silicon (` arm64`)](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-odbc/releases/download/v{{ latest_package }}/duckdb_odbc-macos-arm64.zip) and [Intel (` x86_64`)](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-odbc/releases/download/v{{ latest_package }}/duckdb_odbc-macos-amd64.zip) CPUs. To download the driver for Apple Silicon, run:

   ```batch
   wget https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-odbc/releases/download/v{{ latest_package }}/duckdb_odbc-macos-arm64.zip
   ```

   To download the driver for Intel, run:

   ```batch
   wget https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-odbc/releases/download/v{{ latest_package }}/duckdb_odbc-macos-amd64.zip
   ```

   

3. The archive contains the `libduckdb_odbc.dylib` artifact. To extract it to a directory, run (on Intel, replace `arm64` with `amd64`):

   ```batch
   mkdir duckdb_odbc && unzip duckdb_odbc-macos-arm64.zip -d duckdb_odbc
   ```

4. There are two ways to configure the ODBC driver, either by initializing via the configuration files, or by connecting with [`SQLDriverConnect`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/syntax/sqldriverconnect-function?view=sql-server-ver16).
   A combination of the two is also possible.

   Furthermore, the ODBC driver supports all the [configuration options](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview) included in DuckDB.

   > If a configuration is set in both the connection string passed to `SQLDriverConnect` and in the `odbc.ini` file,
   > the one passed to `SQLDriverConnect` will take precedence.

   For the details of the configuration parameters, see the [ODBC configuration page](#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:configuration).

5. After the configuration, to validate the installation, it is possible to use an ODBC client. unixODBC uses a command line tool called `isql`.

   Use the DSN defined in `odbc.ini` as a parameter of `isql`.

   ```batch
   isql DuckDB
   ```

   ```text
   +---------------------------------------+
   | Connected!                            |
   |                                       |
   | sql-statement                         |
   | help [tablename]                      |
   | echo [string]                         |
   | quit                                  |
   |                                       |
   +---------------------------------------+
   ```

   ```sql
   SQL> SELECT 42;
   ```

   ```text
   +------------+
   | 42         |
   +------------+
   | 42         |
   +------------+

   SQLRowCount returns -1
   1 rows fetched
   ```

### ODBC Configuration {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:configuration}

This page documents the files using the ODBC configuration, [`odbc.ini`](#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:configuration::odbcini-and-odbcini) and [`odbcinst.ini`](#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:configuration::odbcinstini-and-odbcinstini).
These are either placed in the home directory as dotfiles (` .odbc.ini` and `.odbcinst.ini`, respectively) or in a system directory.
For platform-specific details, see the pages for [Linux](#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:linux), [macOS](#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:macos), and [Windows](#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:windows).

#### `odbc.ini` and `.odbc.ini` {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:configuration::odbcini-and-odbcini}

The `odbc.ini` file contains the DSNs for the drivers, which can have specific knobs.
An example of `odbc.ini` with DuckDB:

```ini
[DuckDB]
Driver = DuckDB Driver
Database = /path/to/database.duckdb
access_mode = read_only
```

The lines correspond to the following parameters:

* `[DuckDB]`: between the brackets is a DSN for the DuckDB.
* `Driver`: Describes the driver's name, as well as where to find the configurations in the `odbcinst.ini`.
* `Database`: Describes the database name used by DuckDB, can also be a file path to a `.db` in the system.
* `access_mode`: The mode in which to connect to the database.

#### `odbcinst.ini` and `.odbcinst.ini` {#docs:2.0:clients:odbc:configuration::odbcinstini-and-odbcinstini}

The `odbcinst.ini` file contains general configurations for the ODBC installed drivers in the system.
A driver section starts with the driver name between brackets, and then it follows specific configuration knobs belonging to that driver.

Example of `odbcinst.ini` with the DuckDB:

```ini
[ODBC]
Trace = yes
TraceFile = /tmp/odbctrace

[DuckDB Driver]
Driver = /path/to/libduckdb_odbc.dylib
```

The lines correspond to the following parameters:

* `[ODBC]`: The DM configuration section.
* `Trace`: Enables the ODBC trace file using the option `yes`.
* `TraceFile`: The absolute system file path for the ODBC trace file.
* `[DuckDB Driver]`: The section of the DuckDB installed driver.
* `Driver`: The absolute system file path of the DuckDB driver. Change to match your configuration.

## Python {#clients:python}

### Python API {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview}

> Installation To use the DuckDB Python client, visit the [Python installation page](https://duckdb.org/install/?environment=python).
>
> The latest stable version of the DuckDB Python client is 2.0.0.

#### Installation {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::installation}

The DuckDB Python API can be installed using [pip](https://pip.pypa.io): `pip install duckdb`. Please see the [installation page](https://duckdb.org/install): `conda install python-duckdb -c conda-forge`.

**Python version:**
DuckDB requires Python 3.11 or newer. Free-threaded builds of CPython are not supported.

If you are upgrading from DuckDB 1.x, see [Migrating Python Code to DuckDB 2.0](#docs:2.0:clients:python:migration).

#### Basic API Usage {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::basic-api-usage}

The most straight-forward manner of running SQL queries using DuckDB is using the `duckdb.sql` command.

```python
import duckdb

duckdb.sql("SELECT 42").show()
```

This runs the query on an **in-memory database** that is stored globally inside the Python module. The first call that needs this database creates it.

`duckdb.sql()` returns a **relation**: an object you can query further or convert to Python data. A query that only reads data runs when you fetch or display its result. Reading it again runs the query again. Use `duckdb.execute()` for statements such as `CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT`. See [Lazy Evaluation](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::lazy-evaluation) for details.

Relations can be referenced in subsequent queries by storing them inside variables, and using them as tables. This way queries can be constructed incrementally.

```python
import duckdb

r1 = duckdb.sql("SELECT 42 AS i")
duckdb.sql("SELECT i * 2 AS k FROM r1").show()
```

#### Data Input {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::data-input}

DuckDB can ingest data from a wide variety of formats – both on-disk and in-memory. See the [data ingestion page](#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion) for more information.

```python
import duckdb

duckdb.read_csv("example.csv")                # read a CSV file into a Relation
duckdb.read_parquet("example.parquet")        # read a Parquet file into a Relation
duckdb.read_json("example.json")              # read a JSON file into a Relation

duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM 'example.csv'")     # directly query a CSV file
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM 'example.parquet'") # directly query a Parquet file
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM 'example.json'")    # directly query a JSON file
```

##### DataFrames {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::dataframes}

DuckDB can directly query Pandas DataFrames, Polars DataFrames and Arrow tables.
Note that these are read-only, i.e., editing these tables via [`INSERT`](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:insert) or [`UPDATE` statements](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:update) is not possible.

###### Pandas {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::pandas}

To directly query a Pandas DataFrame, run:

```python
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

pandas_df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [42]})
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM pandas_df")
```

```text
┌───────┐
│   a   │
│ int64 │
├───────┤
│    42 │
└───────┘
```

###### Polars {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::polars}

To directly query a Polars DataFrame, run:

```python
import duckdb
import polars as pl

polars_df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [42]})
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM polars_df")
```

```text
┌───────┐
│   a   │
│ int64 │
├───────┤
│    42 │
└───────┘
```

###### PyArrow {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::pyarrow}

To directly query a PyArrow table, run:

```python
import duckdb
import pyarrow as pa

arrow_table = pa.Table.from_pydict({"a": [42]})
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM arrow_table")
```

```text
┌───────┐
│   a   │
│ int64 │
├───────┤
│    42 │
└───────┘
```

#### Result Conversion {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::result-conversion}

DuckDB supports converting query results efficiently to a variety of formats. See the [result conversion page](#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion) for more information.

```python
import duckdb

duckdb.sql("SELECT 42").fetchall()        # Python objects
duckdb.sql("SELECT 42").df()              # Pandas DataFrame
duckdb.sql("SELECT 42").pl()              # Polars DataFrame
duckdb.sql("SELECT 42").to_arrow_table()  # Arrow Table
duckdb.sql("SELECT 42").to_arrow_reader() # Arrow RecordBatchReader
duckdb.sql("SELECT 42").fetchnumpy()      # NumPy Arrays
```

#### Writing Data to Disk {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::writing-data-to-disk}

DuckDB supports writing Relation objects directly to disk in a variety of formats. The [`COPY` statement](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:copy) can be used to write data to disk using SQL as an alternative.

```python
import duckdb

duckdb.sql("SELECT 42").write_parquet("out.parquet")  # Write to a Parquet file
duckdb.sql("SELECT 42").write_csv("out.csv")          # Write to a CSV file
duckdb.execute("COPY (SELECT 42) TO 'out.parquet'")   # Copy to a Parquet file
```

#### Connection Options {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::connection-options}

Applications can open a new DuckDB connection via the `duckdb.connect()` method.

##### Using an In-Memory Database {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::using-an-in-memory-database}

When using DuckDB through `duckdb.sql()`, it operates on an **in-memory** database, i.e., no tables are persisted on disk.
Invoking the `duckdb.connect()` method without arguments returns a connection, which also uses an in-memory database:

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.sql("SELECT 42 AS x").show()
```

##### Persistent Storage {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::persistent-storage}

The `duckdb.connect(dbname)` creates a connection to a **persistent** database.
Any data written to that connection will be persisted, and can be reloaded by reconnecting to the same file, both from Python and from other DuckDB clients.

```python
import duckdb

# create a connection to a file called 'file.db'
con = duckdb.connect("file.db")
# create a table and load data into it
con.execute("CREATE TABLE test (i INTEGER)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO test VALUES (42)")
# query the table
con.table("test").show()
# explicitly close the connection
con.close()
# Note: connections also closed implicitly when they go out of scope
```

When you reconnect with a context manager, the connection is closed at the end of the `with` block:

```python
import duckdb

with duckdb.connect("file.db") as con:
    con.execute("INSERT INTO test VALUES (43)")
    con.table("test").show()
    # the context manager closes the connection automatically
```

##### Configuration {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::configuration}

The `duckdb.connect()` method takes three arguments: `database`, `read_only` and `config`. Settings go into the `config` dictionary, where [configuration options](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview::configuration-reference) can be specified. For example:

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect(config={"threads": 1})
```

Besides its worker threads, each database starts a pool of [asynchronous I/O threads](#docs:2.0:data:io::thread-pools): by default four times the number of CPU cores, at most 256. To start fewer, set `async_threads`:

```python
con = duckdb.connect(config={"threads": 4, "async_threads": 4})
```

To specify the [storage version](#docs:2.0:internals:storage), pass the `storage_compatibility_version` option. DuckDB 1.5 cannot open a database file that DuckDB 2.0 wrote in its default format. To keep a file readable by DuckDB 1.5, write it with `v1.5.0`:

```python
con = duckdb.connect("compatible.db", config={"storage_compatibility_version": "v1.5.0"})
```

##### Connection Object and Module {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::connection-object-and-module}

Nearly every method of a connection object is also a function of the `duckdb` module, which runs it on a global in-memory database. A few differ: `duckdb.df(frame)` builds a relation from a DataFrame, as `con.from_df(frame)` does, while `con.df()` fetches the result of `execute()`; `duckdb.arrow(obj)` builds a relation from an Arrow object; and `description` and `rowcount` are functions of the module but properties of a connection.

> If you are developing a package designed for others to use, and use DuckDB in the package, it is recommended that you create connection objects instead of using the methods on the `duckdb` module. That is because the `duckdb` module uses a shared global database, which can cause hard to debug issues if used from within multiple different packages.

##### Using Connections in Parallel Python Programs {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::using-connections-in-parallel-python-programs}

A connection runs one call at a time. A call from another thread while the connection is busy does not wait: it raises a `ResourceInUseException` saying `connection is busy with another call; it refuses instead of waiting, so use a separate connection from cursor()`.

`duckdb.sql()`, the other functions of the `duckdb` module and `duckdb.connect(":default:")` all use one shared default connection, so the same holds for them. To run queries in parallel, give each thread its own cursor:

```python
import threading

import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("CREATE TABLE numbers AS SELECT range AS n FROM range(1000)")


def count_even(cursor, results):
    results.append(cursor.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM numbers WHERE n % 2 = 0").fetchall())


results = []
threads = [threading.Thread(target=count_even, args=(con.cursor(), results)) for _ in range(4)]
for thread in threads:
    thread.start()
for thread in threads:
    thread.join()
print(results)
```

```text
[[(500,)], [(500,)], [(500,)], [(500,)]]
```

###### About `cursor()` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::about-cursor}

The [`DuckDBPyConnection.cursor()` method](#docs:2.0:clients:python:reference:index::duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection.cursor) opens a new connection to the same database. A cursor has its own transaction and its own session settings, such as `search_path`, so cursors can run queries in parallel. A global setting, such as `threads` or `memory_limit`, applies to the whole database, also when a cursor sets it. Closing a connection closes its cursors.

Code that runs inside a query, such as a [Python function](#docs:2.0:clients:python:function) called from SQL, cannot use the connection that runs the query: the call raises an error saying `code running inside a query cannot use that query's connection; use a separate connection from cursor()`. Let the function use a cursor instead.

#### Loading and Installing Extensions {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::loading-and-installing-extensions}

The `install_extension()` and `load_extension()` methods install and load an [extension](#docs:2.0:extensions:overview), as the `INSTALL` and `LOAD` statements do. Many core extensions are [installed and loaded automatically](#docs:2.0:extensions:overview::autoloading-extensions) when a query uses them.

##### Community Extensions {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::community-extensions}

To load [community extensions](https://duckdb.org/community_extensions/), use the `repository="community"` argument with the `install_extension` method.

For example, install and load the `h3` community extension as follows:

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.install_extension("h3", repository="community")
con.load_extension("h3")
```

##### Unsigned Extensions {#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::unsigned-extensions}

To load [unsigned extensions](#docs:2.0:extensions:extension_distribution::unsigned-extensions), use:

```python
con = duckdb.connect(config={"allow_unsigned_extensions": "true"})
```

> **Warning.** Only load unsigned extensions from sources you trust.
> Avoid loading unsigned extensions over HTTP.
> Consult the [Securing DuckDB page](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:securing_extensions) for guidelines on how to set up DuckDB in a secure manner.

### Data Ingestion {#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion}

This page contains examples for data ingestion to Python using DuckDB. First, import the DuckDB package:

```python
import duckdb
```

Then, proceed with any of the following sections.

#### CSV Files {#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion::csv-files}

CSV files can be read using the `read_csv` function, called either from within Python or directly from within SQL. By default, the `read_csv` function attempts to auto-detect the CSV settings by sampling from the provided file.

Read from a file using fully auto-detected settings:

```python
duckdb.read_csv("example.csv")
```

Read multiple CSV files from a folder:

```python
duckdb.read_csv("folder/*.csv")
```

Specify options on how the CSV is formatted internally:

```python
duckdb.read_csv("example.csv", header = False, sep = ",")
```

Override types of the first two columns:

```python
duckdb.read_csv("example.csv", dtype = ["int", "varchar"])
```

Directly read a CSV file from within SQL:

```python
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM 'example.csv'")
```

Call `read_csv` from within SQL:

```python
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM read_csv('example.csv')")
```

Add a `filename` column that holds the file each row was read from:

```python
duckdb.read_csv("example.csv", filename=True)
```

Read a file-like object, such as an `io.BytesIO` or an open file; this needs the `fsspec` package:

```python
import io

duckdb.read_csv(io.BytesIO(b"a,b\n1,2\n"))
```

See the [CSV Import](#docs:2.0:data:csv:overview) page for more information. To write a relation to a CSV file, use [`write_csv`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::write_csv). If you pass `overwrite=False` then it refuses to replace a file that exists.

#### Parquet Files {#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion::parquet-files}

Parquet files can be read using the `read_parquet` function, called either from within Python or directly from within SQL.

Read from a single Parquet file:

```python
duckdb.read_parquet("example.parquet")
```

Read multiple Parquet files from a folder:

```python
duckdb.read_parquet("folder/*.parquet")
```

Read a Parquet file over [https](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:httpfs:overview):

```python
duckdb.read_parquet("https://some.url/some_file.parquet")
```

Read a list of Parquet files:

```python
duckdb.read_parquet(["file1.parquet", "file2.parquet", "file3.parquet"])
```

Directly read a Parquet file from within SQL:

```python
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM 'example.parquet'")
```

Call `read_parquet` from within SQL:

```python
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM read_parquet('example.parquet')")
```

See the [Parquet Loading](#docs:2.0:data:parquet:overview) page for more information. To write a relation to a Parquet file, use [`write_parquet`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::write_parquet); with `overwrite=False`, it refuses to replace a file that exists.

#### JSON Files {#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion::json-files}

JSON files can be read using the `read_json` function, called either from within Python or directly from within SQL. By default, the `read_json` function will automatically detect if a file contains newline-delimited JSON or regular JSON, and will detect the schema of the objects stored within the JSON file.

Read from a single JSON file:

```python
duckdb.read_json("example.json")
```

Read multiple JSON files from a folder:

```python
duckdb.read_json("folder/*.json")
```

Directly read a JSON file from within SQL:

```python
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM 'example.json'")
```

Call `read_json` from within SQL:

```python
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM read_json('example.json')")
```

#### Directly Accessing DataFrames and Arrow Objects {#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion::directly-accessing-dataframes-and-arrow-objects}

DuckDB can query a Pandas DataFrame by the name of its variable, as if it were a table:

```python
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

test_df = pd.DataFrame.from_dict({"i": [1, 2, 3, 4], "j": ["one", "two", "three", "four"]})
print(duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM test_df").fetchall())
```

```text
[(1, 'one'), (2, 'two'), (3, 'three'), (4, 'four')]
```

The same works for Pandas Series, Polars DataFrames, LazyFrames and Series, NumPy arrays, a `dict` of one-dimensional NumPy arrays, [relations](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api) and Arrow objects.

The masked elements in a NumPy masked array are `NULL`. In a `dict` of arrays, names that differ only in case get a suffix, so the keys `a` and `A` become the columns `a` and `A_1`.

Use `register()` to give a DataFrame or Arrow object a SQL name. This also works for objects stored in a dictionary or class attribute.

```python
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

my_dictionary = {}
my_dictionary["test_df"] = pd.DataFrame.from_dict({"i": [1, 2, 3, 4], "j": ["one", "two", "three", "four"]})
duckdb.register("test_df_view", my_dictionary["test_df"])
print(duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM test_df_view").fetchall())
```

```text
[(1, 'one'), (2, 'two'), (3, 'three'), (4, 'four')]
```

You can also create a table in DuckDB from the contents of the DataFrame (or the view):

```python
# create a new table from the contents of a DataFrame
duckdb.execute("CREATE TABLE test_df_table AS SELECT * FROM test_df")
# insert into an existing table from the contents of the registered view
duckdb.execute("INSERT INTO test_df_table SELECT * FROM test_df_view")
```

A relation's [`create`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::create) method also makes a table. A name with a catalog, such as `other_db.main.test_df_table`, creates the table in that attached database.

Only variables that are visible to Python code at the location of the `sql()` or `execute()` call can be queried by name. To also look in the functions that called it, set `python_scan_all_frames` to `true`.
Accessing these variables is made possible by [replacement scans](#docs:2.0:clients:c:replacement_scans). To disable replacement scans entirely, use:

```sql
SET python_enable_replacements = false;
```

The precedence of objects with the same name is as follows:

* Objects explicitly registered via `register()`
* Native DuckDB tables and views
* [Replacement scans](#docs:2.0:clients:c:replacement_scans)

DuckDB supports querying multiple types of Apache Arrow objects including [tables](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.Table.html), record batches, arrays and chunked arrays, [datasets](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.dataset.Dataset.html), [RecordBatchReaders](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.RecordBatchReader.html) and [scanners](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.dataset.Scanner.html). See the Python [guides](#docs:2.0:guides:overview::python-client) for more examples.

* The filters of a query are pushed into Arrow datasets and Polars LazyFrames. Tables, record batches, readers, scanners and Polars DataFrames are read whole, and the filter applies to what they return.
* A `RecordBatchReader` can be read once. A second scan raises `InvalidInputException: This RecordBatchReader has already been consumed and cannot be scanned again.` To scan its data more than once, read it into a table first, for example with `read_all()`.
* Arrow tables and Polars DataFrames are scanned on all threads, even when they hold a single chunk. A query that depends on the order of rows without an `ORDER BY`, such as one using `first()`, can return different rows between runs.

##### Custom Arrow Objects {#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion::custom-arrow-objects}

DuckDB can also consume any object that implements the [Arrow PyCapsule interface](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/CDataInterface/PyCapsuleInterface.html) through an `__arrow_c_stream__` method. Such objects can be queried directly through replacement scans and passed to `duckdb.from_arrow()`:

```python
import duckdb
import pyarrow as pa

class MyArrowStream:
    def __init__(self, table):
        self._table = table

    def __arrow_c_stream__(self, requested_schema=None):
        return self._table.__arrow_c_stream__(requested_schema)

obj = MyArrowStream(pa.table({"i": [1, 2, 3]}))
print(duckdb.sql("SELECT sum(i) AS s FROM obj").fetchall())
print(duckdb.from_arrow(obj).fetchall())
```

```text
[(6,)]
[(1,), (2,), (3,)]
```

##### Pandas DataFrames – `object` Columns {#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion::pandas-dataframes--object-columns}

`pandas.DataFrame` columns of an `object` dtype require some special care, since this stores values of arbitrary type.
To convert these columns to DuckDB, we first go through an analyze phase before converting the values.
In this analyze phase a sample of all the rows of the column are analyzed to determine the target type.
This sample size is by default set to 1000.
If the type picked during the analyze step is incorrect, this will result in `Invalid Input Error: Failed to cast value`, in which case you will need to increase the sample size.
The sample size can be changed by setting the `pandas_analyze_sample` config option.

```python
# example setting the sample size to 100k
duckdb.execute("SET GLOBAL pandas_analyze_sample = 100_000")
```

#### Appending Rows {#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion::appending-rows}

Use the [appender](#docs:2.0:clients:python:appender) to insert rows produced by Python. The `with` block writes the rows to the table when it finishes without an exception:

```python
duckdb.execute("CREATE TABLE people (id INTEGER, name VARCHAR)")
with duckdb.appender("people") as appender:
    appender.append_row(1, "Mark")
```

### Appender {#docs:2.0:clients:python:appender}

Use an appender to insert rows that your Python code produces. It collects rows and writes them together in one SQL statement; this is called flushing. The `with` block below flushes on successful exit:

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("CREATE TABLE people (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR)")

with con.appender("people") as appender:
    appender.append_row(1, "Mark")
    appender.append_rows([(2, "Hannes"), (3, "Gabor")])

print(con.sql("SELECT * FROM people ORDER BY id").fetchall())
```

```text
[(1, 'Mark'), (2, 'Hannes'), (3, 'Gabor')]
```

For data already in a DataFrame or Arrow table, `INSERT INTO people SELECT * FROM df` is faster than the appender. For pandas DataFrames, `con.append("people", df)` is also faster. See [Directly Accessing DataFrames and Arrow Objects](#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion::directly-accessing-dataframes-and-arrow-objects).

Use `con.appender(table)` for table operations or `con.query_appender(statement, columns)` for custom SQL. For the appender in other clients, see the [Appender page](#docs:2.0:data:appender).

Both functions are also available on the `duckdb` module. They use the default connection unless you supply the `connection` argument.

#### Appending to a Table {#docs:2.0:clients:python:appender::appending-to-a-table}

`con.appender(table)` resolves the table once, when the appender is created, the way SQL resolves a table name. It appends to the table's columns in declared order and skips generated columns. `append_row` takes one value per column, and `append_rows` takes any iterable of rows. Values are converted exactly as [`executemany` parameters](#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::query-parameters) are.

To append to some of the columns, list them in `columns`. The other columns take their default value, per row:

```python
con.execute("CREATE SEQUENCE event_ids")
con.execute(
    "CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER DEFAULT nextval('event_ids'), kind VARCHAR, note VARCHAR DEFAULT 'none')"
)

appender = con.appender("events", columns=["kind"])
appender.append_row("login")
appender.append_row("logout")
appender.flush()
```

#### Updates, Upserts and Deletes {#docs:2.0:clients:python:appender::updates-upserts-and-deletes}

The `action` argument picks the statement: `"insert"` (the default), `"upsert"`, `"update"` or `"delete"`. An upsert inserts new rows and updates existing rows that have the same primary key or unique key.

```python
con.execute("CREATE TABLE stock (sku VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, qty INTEGER)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('widget', 3), ('gadget', 5)")

with con.appender("stock", action="upsert") as appender:
    appender.append_row("widget", 10)
    appender.append_row("gizmo", 1)

with con.appender("stock", action="update", key=["sku"]) as appender:
    appender.append_row("gadget", 0)

with con.appender("stock", action="delete", key=["sku"]) as appender:
    appender.append_row("gizmo")

print(con.sql("SELECT * FROM stock ORDER BY sku").fetchall())
```

```text
[('gadget', 0), ('widget', 10)]
```

* `upsert` runs an [`INSERT OR REPLACE`](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:insert::insert-or-replace-into), so the table needs exactly one primary key or unique constraint. It takes `columns` like an insert; on a conflict, only the listed columns change.
* `update` matches rows on the `key` columns and sets every other appended column. Use `columns` to choose the appended columns.
* `delete` appends only the `key` columns, in the order of `key`, and deletes the rows that match.
* A `NULL` key matches nothing.
* A plain insert writes the rows in append order while [`preserve_insertion_order`](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview) is on, which is the default. An upsert does not keep append order.
* When a flush contains duplicate keys, an upsert keeps one row per key value, including `NULL`; an update applies one input row; and `MERGE INTO` raises an error.

#### Custom Statements {#docs:2.0:clients:python:appender::custom-statements}

`con.query_appender` runs your SQL statement when you flush. Declare the appended columns as a dictionary of names to types. Your statement reads the appended rows as `appender_data`.

To transform the rows first, supply a `source` query. This query reads the appended rows as `appender_buffer`, and your statement reads its result as `appender_data`. The example below uses `source` to look up the product ID for each product code (` sku`). The `source` can be any query that returns rows; DuckDB runs it as you wrote it.

```python
con.execute("CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER, sku VARCHAR)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO products VALUES (1, 'widget'), (2, 'gadget')")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (product_id INTEGER, qty INTEGER)")

appender = con.query_appender(
    "INSERT INTO orders FROM appender_data",
    {"sku": "VARCHAR", "qty": "INTEGER"},
    source="SELECT p.id AS product_id, b.qty FROM appender_buffer AS b JOIN products AS p USING (sku)",
)
appender.append_row("gadget", 4)
appender.append_row("widget", 2)
appender.flush()
```

* The statement is one `INSERT` (including `INSERT OR REPLACE` and `ON CONFLICT`), `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or [`MERGE INTO`](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:merge_into).
* A type is anything the [Types API](#docs:2.0:clients:python:types) accepts, such as `"INTEGER"`, `duckdb.sqltypes.INTEGER` or `int`.
* A declared column that the statement does not read is allowed.
* DataFrames and other Python objects named in `source` or in the statement are looked up once, where the appender is created, and reused at every flush. If you later create a DuckDB table with the same name, later flushes use that table instead.

#### Flushing {#docs:2.0:clients:python:appender::flushing}

Each `flush()` applies the rows collected since the previous flush. It runs in your transaction if you started one with `BEGIN` or `con.begin()`, and otherwise commits by itself. A flush with no rows does nothing.

A `with` block flushes on successful exit. When an exception leaves the block, the buffered rows are discarded and the exception propagates. Outside a `with` block, call `flush()` to write the rows and `clear()` to discard them. There is no `close()` method. The appender remains usable after `flush()`, `clear()` or leaving a `with` block.

> **Warning.** Garbage collection discards buffered rows and emits a `ResourceWarning`. Call `flush()` or use a `with` block to write the rows.

#### Errors and Retrying {#docs:2.0:clients:python:appender::errors-and-retrying}

* The appender checks its statement when you create it, without running it. Invalid SQL, incorrect column counts, unsupported statement types, `RETURNING` clauses and SQL parameter placeholders such as `?` raise an exception at creation. These errors leave the transaction usable. Cast errors and constraint violations raise an exception during `flush()`.
* A flush that raises because an earlier result is still open or another call is running on the connection keeps its buffered rows, and so does an interrupted flush. Finish the result or wait for the other call, then call `flush()` again. Other failures discard the rows and raise an exception.
* An interrupted flush inside your transaction keeps its buffered rows but aborts the transaction. Roll back before retrying. Start a new transaction if the retry must be part of one.
* If you press Ctrl-C while a Python function called from SQL is running during a flush, DuckDB treats it as an error in that function and discards the buffered rows.

#### Memory Use {#docs:2.0:clients:python:appender::memory-use}

The rows waiting to be flushed count toward DuckDB's `memory_limit`. When they no longer fit in memory, DuckDB can store them in temporary files. If DuckDB has no temporary directory, a full buffer makes every query on the connection raise an `OutOfMemoryException` until you call `flush()` or `clear()`. If a write into the buffer fails, `append_row`, `append_rows` and `flush()` raise an exception until you call `clear()`.

#### Connections and Threads {#docs:2.0:clients:python:appender::connections-and-threads}

Concurrent calls on the same appender raise an exception rather than wait. Calls from a callback during a flush also raise an exception. Use a separate appender for each thread. You can append rows or call `clear()` while an `execute()` result is open, but must finish that result before calling `flush()`: call `con.fetchall()`, call `con.fetchone()` repeatedly until it returns `None`, or call `con.complete()` or `con.abort()`.

### Conversion between DuckDB and Python {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion}

This page documents the rules for converting [DuckDB results to Python](#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::result-conversion-duckdb-results-to-python) and [Python objects to DuckDB](#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::object-conversion-python-object-to-duckdb).

#### Result Conversion: DuckDB Results to Python {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::result-conversion-duckdb-results-to-python}

A result is read from a [relation](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api) or, when using the [DB-API](#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi) / `con.execute()`, from the connection. `con.sql()`, `con.table()`, the readers and the other relational methods return relations. Each has its own methods:



| Result               | Relation                                             | DB-API 2.0 (` con.execute()`)                                  |
|:---------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Python tuples        | `fetchall()`, `iter_rows(batch_size=1024)`           | `fetchone()`, `fetchmany(size=1)`, `fetchall()`               |
| Python dicts         | `to_dicts()`                                         |                                                               |
| NumPy                | `fetchnumpy()`                                       | `fetchnumpy()`                                                |
| Pandas               | `df()`                                               | `df()`, `fetch_df_chunk()`                                    |
| Apache Arrow         | `to_arrow_table()`, `to_arrow_reader()`              | `to_arrow_table()`, `to_arrow_reader()`, both make a copy     |
| Polars               | `pl()`                                               |                                                               |
| PyTorch              | `torch()`                                            | `torch()`                                                     |
| TensorFlow           | `tf()`                                               | `tf()`                                                        |

Relations are recommended for most conversion, except when you want to do row-based work. A relation has no `fetchone()`, `fetchmany()` or `fetch_df_chunk()` because it is stateless, i.e. it does not hold a result itself. To get specific rows of a result with the relational API you would use `limit(n).fetchall()`, `iter_rows()` or `to_arrow_reader()` instead. Note that with the DB-API, after a partial read with `fetchone()` or `fetchmany()`, the `df()`, `fetchnumpy()` and Arrow methods of the connection return only the remaining rows.

##### Examples {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::examples}

Below are some examples. See the [Python guides](#docs:2.0:guides:overview::python-client) for more. To run the examples, use this table:

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("CREATE TABLE items (item VARCHAR, value DECIMAL(10, 2), count INTEGER)")
con.execute("""
    INSERT INTO items VALUES
        ('jeans', 20.0, 1),
        ('hammer', 42.2, 2),
        ('laptop', 2000.0, 1),
        ('chainsaw', 500.0, 10),
        ('iphone', 300.0, 2)
""")
```

Fetch as Pandas DataFrame:

```python
df = con.execute("SELECT * FROM items").df()
print(df)
```

```text
       item   value  count
0     jeans    20.0      1
1    hammer    42.2      2
2    laptop  2000.0      1
3  chainsaw   500.0     10
4    iphone   300.0      2
```

Fetch as dictionary of NumPy arrays:

```python
arr = con.execute("SELECT * FROM items").fetchnumpy()
print(arr)
```

```text
{'item': array(['jeans', 'hammer', 'laptop', 'chainsaw', 'iphone'], dtype=object), 'value': array([  20. ,   42.2, 2000. ,  500. ,  300. ]), 'count': array([ 1,  2,  1, 10,  2], dtype=int32)}
```

Fetch as an Arrow table. Converting to Pandas afterwards just for pretty printing:

```python
tbl = con.sql("SELECT * FROM items").to_arrow_table()
print(tbl.to_pandas())
```

```text
       item    value  count
0     jeans    20.00      1
1    hammer    42.20      2
2    laptop  2000.00      1
3  chainsaw   500.00     10
4    iphone   300.00      2
```

##### NumPy {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::numpy}

* `fetchnumpy()` fetches the data as a dictionary of NumPy arrays. A column without `NULL` values is a plain array. A column with `NULL` values is a masked array.

##### Pandas {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::pandas}

* `df()` fetches the data as a Pandas DataFrame
* `fetchdf()` and, on the connection, `fetch_df()` are older names of `df()`
* `fetch_df_chunk(vectors_per_chunk)` fetches the next portion of the results of `con.execute()` into a DataFrame. Each chunk has at most the vector size (2048 by default) times `vectors_per_chunk` (1 by default) rows.

##### Apache Arrow {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::apache-arrow}

* `to_arrow_table()` fetches the data as an [Arrow table](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.Table.html)
* `to_arrow_reader(batch_size)` returns an [Arrow record batch reader](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.RecordBatchReader.html) with _at most_ `batch_size` rows per batch (the default is 131072)
* `arrow()` is an older name of `to_arrow_reader()`, on relations only
* A relation is also an Arrow stream through the [Arrow PyCapsule Interface](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/CDataInterface/PyCapsuleInterface.html). `pyarrow.table(rel)` returns an Arrow table and `polars.DataFrame(rel)` a Polars DataFrame, which unlike `pl()` needs no pyarrow

After `con.execute()`, `to_arrow_table()` and `to_arrow_reader()` first fetch the rows and then convert them, so they make an extra copy of the result, and the reader returns its first batch only after the whole query ran. They warn: `UserWarning: Arrow output on a DB-API result makes an extra copy of the rows, use con.sql(query).to_arrow_table() instead.` The module functions `duckdb.to_arrow_table()` and `duckdb.to_arrow_reader()` read the result of `duckdb.execute()` and warn the same way. For Arrow output, run the query with `con.sql(query)`.

> **Deprecated.** on relations, `fetch_arrow_table()`, `fetch_record_batch()` and `fetch_arrow_reader()` are deprecated aliases of `to_arrow_table()` and `to_arrow_reader()`. After `con.execute()`, `fetch_arrow_table()`, `fetch_record_batch()`, `arrow()` and `pl()` no longer exist, and neither do the module functions `duckdb.fetch_arrow_table()`, `duckdb.fetch_record_batch()` and `duckdb.pl()`.

DuckDB has a single `INTERVAL` type that stores months, days and microseconds, so it maps onto Arrow's `month_day_nano_interval` type. On import, every Arrow interval and duration type, including `duration[s]`, `duration[ms]`, `duration[us]` and `duration[ns]`, is read into that one `INTERVAL` type. As a result, a `duration` column that is passed through DuckDB and read back as Arrow is returned as a `month_day_nano_interval` rather than as its original `duration` type. This is expected. The resolution and unit of the original Arrow type are not preserved.

##### Polars {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::polars}

* `pl()` fetches the data of a relation as a Polars DataFrame, and `pl(lazy=True)` returns a Polars LazyFrame

#### Object Conversion: Python Object to DuckDB {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::object-conversion-python-object-to-duckdb}

Python objects are converted when they are passed as query parameters (` execute()`, `executemany()` and `sql(..., params=...)`), as rows of `values()`, as constants in [expressions](#docs:2.0:clients:python:expression) and as the value of a `duckdb.Value`. The rules are the same on all of these paths, except where a section below says otherwise.

This is a mapping of Python object types to DuckDB [Logical Types](#docs:2.0:sql:data_types:overview):

* `None` → `NULL`
* `bool` → `BOOLEAN`
* `datetime.timedelta` → `INTERVAL`
* `str` → `VARCHAR`
* `bytearray` → `BLOB`
* `memoryview` → `BLOB`
* `decimal.Decimal` → `DECIMAL` / `DOUBLE` / `FLOAT`
* `uuid.UUID` → `UUID`

The rest of the conversion rules are as follows.

##### `str` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::str}

A `str` that UTF-8 cannot encode, such as one that holds a lone surrogate (` "\ud800"`), raises an `InvalidInputException` that says it `cannot encode str as UTF-8`. The connection stays usable.

##### `memoryview` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::memoryview}

A `memoryview` converts to a `BLOB` of the bytes it shows. As a query parameter, it must be contiguous: a strided view such as `memoryview(b"abcdef")[::2]` raises `BufferError: memoryview: underlying buffer is not C-contiguous`. `values()` and expressions accept it and read its bytes in order, here `b'ace'`.

##### `decimal.Decimal` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::decimaldecimal}

A `Decimal` becomes a `DECIMAL` whose width and scale follow from its digits and its exponent: `Decimal("12.5")` is a `DECIMAL(3,1)`, `Decimal("1E+2")` is a `DECIMAL(3,0)` that holds 100 and `Decimal("1E-7")` is a `DECIMAL(8,7)`. A value that needs more than 38 digits becomes a `DOUBLE`, such as `Decimal("1E+38")` or `Decimal(0.1)`, which holds the 55 decimal digits of the binary float 0.1. `NaN` and the infinities become `FLOAT`.

##### `int` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::int}

Since integers can be of arbitrary size in Python, there is not a one-to-one conversion possible for ints. An `int` becomes the first of these types that fits it:

* `INTEGER`
* `BIGINT`
* `UBIGINT`
* `HUGEINT`
* `UHUGEINT`

So `2**31` is a `BIGINT`, `2**63` a `UBIGINT`, `2**64` and `-(2**63) - 1` are `HUGEINT` and `2**127` is a `UHUGEINT`. An integer that does not fit in 128 bits raises `InvalidInputException: Python integer too large for 128-bit integer type`. A subclass of `int` converts by the value it stores.

When using the DuckDB Value class, it's possible to set a target type, which will influence the conversion:

```python
import duckdb
from duckdb.sqltypes import TINYINT

con = duckdb.connect()
print(con.execute("SELECT typeof(?), typeof(?), typeof(?)", [5, 2**64, duckdb.Value(5, TINYINT)]).fetchall())
```

```text
[('INTEGER', 'HUGEINT', 'TINYINT')]
```

##### `float` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::float}

A `float` is always a `DOUBLE`.

##### `datetime.datetime` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::datetimedatetime}

For `datetime` we will check `pandas.isnull` if it's available and return `NULL` if it returns `true`.

If the `datetime` has tzinfo, we will use `TIMESTAMPTZ`, otherwise it becomes `TIMESTAMP`. Fetching a `TIMESTAMPTZ` value into Python needs the `pytz` package, which is not installed with DuckDB; without it, the fetch raises `InvalidInputException: Required module 'pytz' failed to import`.

`datetime.datetime.max` and `datetime.datetime.min` convert to ordinary timestamps, not to infinity. In the other direction, the timestamp `infinity` is returned as `datetime.datetime.max` and `-infinity` as `datetime.datetime.min`.

##### `datetime.time` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::datetimetime}

If the `time` has tzinfo, we will use `TIMETZ`, otherwise it becomes `TIME`.

##### `datetime.date` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::datetimedate}

`date` converts to the `DATE` type. `datetime.date.max` and `datetime.date.min` convert to ordinary dates; the date `infinity` is returned as `datetime.date.max` and `-infinity` as `datetime.date.min`.

##### `bytes` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::bytes}

`bytes` converts to `BLOB` by default. When it's used to construct a Value object of type `BIT`, it maps to `BIT` instead, and its bytes are read as the characters `0` and `1`, as in `duckdb.Value(b"0101", duckdb.sqltypes.BIT)`.

##### `list` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::list}

`list` becomes a `LIST` type of the “most permissive” type of its children. For example, `[12345, "test"]` becomes `VARCHAR[]`, because 12345 can convert to `VARCHAR` but `test` can not convert to `INTEGER`:

```python
print(con.execute("SELECT ?", [[12345, "test"]]).fetchall())
```

```text
[(['12345', 'test'],)]
```

A `NaN` stays `NaN` inside a list, a struct, a map or a `duckdb.Value` of a nested type. A list that mixes `datetime` values with and without tzinfo becomes a `TIMESTAMPTZ` list as a query parameter and in `values()`, which read the values without tzinfo as UTC.

##### `dict` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::dict}

The `dict` object can convert to either `STRUCT(...)` or `MAP(..., ...)`, depending on its keys and on where it is used:

* A dict whose keys are all strings becomes a `STRUCT` with one field per key.
* A dict with exactly the two keys `key` and `value`, each holding a list and both lists of the same length, becomes a `MAP` of the two lists zipped together when passed as a query parameter and in `values()`. In an expression, it is a `STRUCT` like any other dict with string keys.
* A dict with a key that is not a string becomes a `MAP` in `values()` and in expressions, written as a SQL [`MAP` literal](#docs:2.0:sql:data_types:map). As a query parameter, it becomes a `STRUCT` whose field names are the keys converted to strings. Keys or values of types that SQL cannot combine raise an error.

A dict in the `key` and `value` form:

```python
my_map_dict = {
    "key": [
        1, 2, 3
    ],
    "value": [
        "one", "two", "three"
    ]
}

duckdb.values(my_map_dict).show()
```

becomes a `MAP(INTEGER, VARCHAR)`:

```text
┌─────────────────────────┐
│          col0           │
│  map(integer, varchar)  │
├─────────────────────────┤
│ {1=one, 2=two, 3=three} │
└─────────────────────────┘
```

A dict with string keys becomes a `STRUCT`:

```python
my_struct_dict = {
    "name": "duck",
    "count": 2,
    "tags": [1, 2, 3],
    "active": True
}

duckdb.values(my_struct_dict).show()
```

```text
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                 col0                                  │
│ struct("name" varchar, count integer, tags integer[], active boolean) │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ {'name': duck, 'count': 2, 'tags': [1, 2, 3], 'active': true}         │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

As a query parameter, a dict with other keys becomes a `STRUCT` with string field names:

```python
my_mixed_dict = {1: "one", "2": 2, "three": [1, 2, 3], False: True}
print(con.execute("SELECT typeof(?)", [my_mixed_dict]).fetchone()[0])
```

```text
STRUCT("1" VARCHAR, "2" INTEGER, three INTEGER[], "False" BOOLEAN)
```

A dict returned by a [function](#docs:2.0:clients:python:function) converts to the function's return type. For a `MAP` return type, a dict in the `key` and `value` form gives the entries of the map, so the return type has to describe those entries:

```python
duckdb_conn = duckdb.connect()

def get_map() -> dict[str, list[str] | list[int]]:
    return {
        "key": [
            1, 2, 3
        ],
        "value": [
            "one", "two", "three"
        ]
    }

duckdb_conn.create_function("get_map", get_map, return_type=dict[int, str])

duckdb_conn.sql("SELECT get_map()").show()
```

```text
┌─────────────────────────┐
│        get_map()        │
│  map(bigint, varchar)   │
├─────────────────────────┤
│ {1=one, 2=two, 3=three} │
└─────────────────────────┘
```

Without `return_type`, the annotation `dict[str, list[str] | list[int]]` is the return type, so each value, such as `"one"`, has to convert to a `UNION(u1 VARCHAR[], u2 BIGINT[])`, and the query fails:

```python
duckdb_conn.create_function("get_map_error", get_map)

duckdb_conn.sql("SELECT get_map_error()").show()
```

```console
_duckdb.ConversionException: Conversion Error: Could not convert value of type VARCHAR to UNION(u1 VARCHAR[], u2 BIGINT[])
```

A function annotated to return a `dict` returns a `MAP`, due to [automatic conversion](#docs:2.0:clients:python:types::dictkey_type-value_type). To return a `STRUCT`, the `return_type` has to be provided:

```python
from duckdb import list_type, struct_type
from duckdb.sqltypes import BOOLEAN, INTEGER, VARCHAR

def get_struct() -> dict[str, str | int | list[int] | bool]:
    return my_struct_dict

duckdb_conn.create_function("get_struct_as_map", get_struct)

duckdb_conn.sql("SELECT get_struct_as_map()").show()

duckdb_conn.create_function("get_struct", get_struct, return_type=struct_type({
    "name": VARCHAR,
    "count": INTEGER,
    "tags": list_type(INTEGER),
    "active": BOOLEAN
}))

duckdb_conn.sql("SELECT get_struct()").show()
```

```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         get_struct_as_map()                         │
│ map(varchar, union(u1 varchar, u2 bigint, u3 bigint[], u4 boolean)) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ {name=duck, count=2, tags=[1, 2, 3], active=true}                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                             get_struct()                              │
│ struct("name" varchar, count integer, tags integer[], active boolean) │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ {'name': duck, 'count': 2, 'tags': [1, 2, 3], 'active': true}         │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

A `STRUCT` type, as a return type or as the type of a `duckdb.Value`, takes each field from the dict key of the same name, ignoring case. A dict whose keys do not match the fields raises `InvalidInputException: We could not convert the object ... to the desired target type`.

##### `tuple` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::tuple}

`tuple` converts to `LIST` by default, when it's used to construct a Value object of type `STRUCT` it will convert to `STRUCT` instead.

##### NumPy Objects {#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::numpy-objects}

`numpy.ndarray` and `numpy.datetime64` are converted by calling `tolist()` and converting the result of that.

A NumPy integer scalar such as `numpy.int64(5)` is read by its value in `values()` and in expressions. As a query parameter, it raises `NotImplementedException: Unable to transform python value of type ...`; pass its Python value, `numpy.int64(5).item()`, instead.

### Python DB API {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi}

The standard DuckDB Python API provides a SQL interface compliant with the [DB-API 2.0 specification described by PEP 249](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0249/) similar to the [SQLite Python API](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html).

#### Connection {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::connection}

To use the module, you must first create a `DuckDBPyConnection` object that represents a connection to a database.
This is done through the [`duckdb.connect`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:reference:index::duckdb.connect) method, which takes three arguments: `database`, `read_only` and `config`.

The `config` keyword argument can be used to provide a `dict` that contains key-value pairs referencing [settings](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview::configuration-reference) understood by DuckDB.

##### In-Memory Connection {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::in-memory-connection}

The special value `:memory:` can be used to create an **in-memory database**. Note that for an in-memory database no data is persisted to disk (i.e., all data is lost when you exit the Python process).

###### Named In-memory Connections {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::named-in-memory-connections}

The special value `:memory:` can also be postfixed with a name, for example: `:memory:conn3`.
When a name is provided, subsequent `duckdb.connect` calls will create a new connection to the same database, sharing the catalogs (views, tables, macros etc.).

Using `:memory:` without a name will always create a new and separate database instance.

##### Default Connection {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::default-connection}

The `duckdb` module has a default connection to an unnamed **in-memory database**.
Functions such as `duckdb.sql()` and `duckdb.execute()` use the default connection; the first function that needs it creates it. Some module functions differ from connection methods; see [Connection Object and Module](#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::connection-object-and-module).

The special value `:default:` and the `duckdb.default_connection()` function return the default connection:

```python
import duckdb

duckdb.execute("CREATE TABLE tbl AS SELECT 42 AS a")
con = duckdb.connect(":default:")
con.sql("SELECT * FROM tbl")
# or
duckdb.default_connection().sql("SELECT * FROM tbl")
```

```text
┌───────┐
│   a   │
│ int32 │
├───────┤
│    42 │
└───────┘
```

To make another connection the default connection, pass it to `duckdb.set_default_connection()`:

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("CREATE TABLE answer AS SELECT 42 AS a")
duckdb.set_default_connection(con)
duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM answer").fetchall()
```

```text
[(42,)]
```

##### File-Based Connection {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::file-based-connection}

If the `database` is a file path, a connection to a persistent database is established.
If the file does not exist the file will be created (the extension of the file is irrelevant and can be `.db`, `.duckdb` or anything else).

###### `read_only` Connections {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::read_only-connections}

If you would like to connect in read-only mode, you can set the `read_only` flag to `True`. If the file does not exist, it is **not** created when connecting in read-only mode.
Read-only mode is required if multiple Python processes want to access the same database file at the same time.

Within one Python process, all connections to a database file must use the same configuration, `read_only` included.

```python
import duckdb

# to start an in-memory database
con = duckdb.connect(database=":memory:")
# to use a database file (not shared between processes)
con = duckdb.connect(database="my-db.duckdb", read_only=False)
con.close()
# to use a database file (shared between processes)
con = duckdb.connect(database="my-db.duckdb", read_only=True)
con.close()
# to explicitly get the default connection
con = duckdb.connect(database=":default:")
```

You can open another connection to the same database with the `cursor()` method. A cursor has its own transaction and its own session settings, and cursors can run queries at the same time. A single connection runs one call at a time: a call from another thread while it is busy raises a `ResourceInUseException` instead of waiting, so give each thread its own cursor. Closing a connection closes its cursors. See [About `cursor()`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview::about-cursor) for details.

Connections are closed implicitly when they go out of scope or if they are explicitly closed using `close()`. Once the last connection to a database instance is closed, the database instance is closed as well.

#### Querying {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::querying}

SQL queries can be sent to DuckDB using the `execute()` method of connections. Once a query has been executed, results can be retrieved using the `fetchone`, `fetchmany` and `fetchall` methods on the connection. `fetchone()` returns the next row, or `None` when no rows are left. `fetchmany(size)` returns a list of at most `size` rows, one by default. `fetchall()` returns all remaining rows. `df()` and `fetchnumpy()` return the remaining rows as a pandas DataFrame or as NumPy arrays. Below are some short examples:

```python
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()
# create a table
con.execute("CREATE TABLE items (item VARCHAR, value DECIMAL(10, 2), count INTEGER)")
# insert two items into the table
con.execute("INSERT INTO items VALUES ('jeans', 20.0, 1), ('hammer', 42.2, 2)")
print(con.rowcount)

# retrieve the items again
con.execute("SELECT * FROM items")
print(con.fetchall())

# retrieve the items one at a time
con.execute("SELECT * FROM items")
print(con.fetchone())
print(con.fetchmany(5))
print(con.fetchone())
```

```text
2
[('jeans', Decimal('20.00'), 1), ('hammer', Decimal('42.20'), 2)]
('jeans', Decimal('20.00'), 1)
[('hammer', Decimal('42.20'), 2)]
None
```

The `description` property of the connection object contains the column names as per the standard. The `rowcount` property holds the number of rows that the last `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` changed, counted over all parameter sets of an `executemany()` call. It is `-1` after a query and after a statement with a `RETURNING` clause.

##### Query Parameters {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::query-parameters}

Pass parameter values as the second argument to `execute()`. Use `?` with a list in placeholder order, `$1` to reuse a list value or `$name` with a dictionary. Pass values separately from the SQL text. The query then runs as a [prepared statement](#docs:2.0:sql:query_syntax:prepared_statements), and the values are converted according to the [conversion rules](#docs:2.0:clients:python:conversion::object-conversion-python-object-to-duckdb).

```python
rows = con.execute(
    "SELECT item FROM items WHERE value > $minimum",
    {"minimum": 40},
).fetchall()
print(rows)
```

```text
[('hammer',)]
```

Parameter names are not case sensitive: the key `"ABC"` binds `$abc`, so do not pass two keys that differ only in case.

Insert a row with `?` placeholders, and several rows with `executemany()`, which runs the statement once for each list of values:

```python
con.execute("INSERT INTO items VALUES (?, ?, ?)", ["laptop", 2000, 1])
con.executemany("INSERT INTO items VALUES (?, ?, ?)", [["chainsaw", 500, 10], ["iphone", 300, 2]])
```

```python
con.execute("SELECT item FROM items WHERE value > ?", [400])
print(con.fetchall())
```

```text
[('laptop',), ('chainsaw',)]
```

`$1` stands for the first value of the list, so a value can appear more than once:

```python
con.execute("SELECT $1, $1, $2", ["duck", "goose"])
print(con.fetchall())
```

```text
[('duck', 'duck', 'goose')]
```

> **Warning.** Do *not* use `executemany` to insert large amounts of data into DuckDB. For rows that Python code produces, use the [appender](#docs:2.0:clients:python:appender); see the [data ingestion page](#docs:2.0:clients:python:data_ingestion) for other options.

##### Open Results {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::open-results}

`execute()` starts the statement and returns the connection. A query runs until its first rows are ready, so an error up to that point raises from `execute()`, and an error further into the query raises from the fetch that reaches it. Any other statement, `INSERT ... RETURNING` included, runs to its end inside `execute()`.

The result of a query stays open until a fetch returns no rows, or until `fetchall()`, `df()` or `fetchnumpy()` reads the rest of it. After a partial read with `fetchone()` or `fetchmany()`, these methods return the rows not fetched yet. `con.complete()` runs an open result to its end without reading its rows, and `con.abort()` cancels it, which fails an open transaction when the statement may write. Both are also functions of the `duckdb` module. The next `execute()` replaces an open result. If the replaced result may have side effects then it runs to its end first.

While a result is open, everything that runs a query on the connection raises an error, including reading a relation, `register()` and `create_function()`. Building a relation, the `description` property and `cursor()` still work, so a cursor can run other queries in the meantime.

```python
con.execute("SELECT * FROM items")
con.sql("SELECT 42").fetchall()
```

```console
_duckdb.ResourceInUseException: Resource In Use Error: connection has an unfinished result from execute(); call complete() or abort(), or fetch until a fetch returns no rows, before other work on this connection, or use a separate connection from cursor()
```

```python
con.complete()
con.sql("SELECT 42").fetchall()
```

```text
[(42,)]
```

##### Arrow and Polars Output {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::arrow-and-polars-output}

A result of `execute()` has no `fetch_arrow_table()`, `fetch_record_batch()`, `arrow()` or `pl()` method. Its `to_arrow_table()` and `to_arrow_reader()` methods copy the rows and emit a `UserWarning`, and that reader does not stream: its first batch arrives after the whole query ran. For Arrow and Polars output, use a [relation](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api) instead: `con.sql(query).to_arrow_table()`, `con.sql(query).pl()` or `con.sql(query).to_arrow_reader()`, which streams.

##### Transactions {#docs:2.0:clients:python:dbapi::transactions}

`con.begin()`, `con.commit()` and `con.rollback()` start, commit and roll back a transaction, as the [`BEGIN`, `COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK` statements](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:transactions) do. Inside a transaction, any statement run with `execute()` that fails aborts the transaction, including one with a syntax error or one that names a missing table. After that, `commit()` rolls the transaction back without raising an error, and any other statement raises a `TransactionException` until you roll back:

```python
con.begin()
con.execute("INSERT INTO items VALUES ('drill', 80, 1)")
try:
    con.execute("SELECT * FROM missing_table")
except duckdb.CatalogException:
    pass
con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM items")
```

```console
_duckdb.TransactionException: TransactionContext Error: Current transaction is aborted (please ROLLBACK)
```

```python
con.rollback()
con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM items").fetchall()
```

```text
[(5,)]
```

### Relational API {#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api}







The Relational API builds a query one step at a time from Python.
A relation, a `DuckDBPyRelation`, is a piece of SQL text: the methods of the [Transformation](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::transformation) and [Functions](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::functions) sections return a new relation whose text extends the one they were called on.

#### Lazy Evaluation {#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::lazy-evaluation}

Building a relation runs nothing: DuckDB binds the text once to learn the columns and their types, and holds no data.
For example, a relation over a billion rows is built at once:

```python
import duckdb

duckdb_conn = duckdb.connect()

rel = duckdb_conn.sql("FROM range(1_000_000_000) t(id) SELECT id, id % 7 AS bucket")
print(rel.sql_query())
```

```text
FROM range(1_000_000_000) t(id) SELECT id, id % 7 AS bucket
```

[`sql_query()`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::sql_query) returns exactly the text that runs.
The query runs when a method of the [Output](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::output) section reads the relation, and it runs again on every read, so each read sees the current data.
Printing a relation, or calling [`show()`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::show), also runs it and displays the first rows:

```python
import duckdb

duckdb_conn = duckdb.connect()
rel = duckdb_conn.sql("FROM range(1_000_000_000) t(id) SELECT id, id % 7 AS bucket")
rel.filter("bucket = 3").order("id").limit(3).show()
```

```text
┌───────┬────────┐
│  id   │ bucket │
│ int64 │ int64  │
├───────┼────────┤
│     3 │      3 │
│    10 │      3 │
│    17 │      3 │
└───────┴────────┘
```

Only a statement that reads, such as a `SELECT`, gives a lazy relation.
Any other statement passed to [`sql()`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::sql), such as `CREATE TABLE` or `INSERT`, runs at the call, and the relation holds what it returned.
The `params` list or dict is copied when the relation is created, and its values are converted each time the relation runs.
A column is also an attribute of the relation, as in `rel.price`, unless a method has its name: a column called `offset` is reached as `rel["offset"]`, since `rel.offset` is the [`offset()`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::offset) method.

To run a query once and keep its rows, call [`materialize()`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::materialize):

```python
import duckdb

duckdb_conn = duckdb.connect()
duckdb_conn.sql("CREATE TABLE items (id INTEGER)")
counted = duckdb_conn.sql("SELECT count(*) AS n FROM items")
held = counted.materialize()
duckdb_conn.sql("INSERT INTO items VALUES (1), (2)")
print(counted.fetchall(), held.fetchall())
```

```text
[(2,)] [(0,)]
```



#### Relation Creation  {#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::relation-creation-}

This section contains the details on how a relation is created. A relation over a query that reads is [lazy evaluated](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::lazy-evaluation).

| Name | Description |
|:--|:-------|
| [`from_arrow`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::from_arrow) | Create a relation object from an Arrow object. |
| [`from_csv_auto`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::from_csv_auto) | Alias of [`read_csv()`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::read_csv). |
| [`from_df`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::from_df) | Create a relation object from the DataFrame in df. |
| [`from_parquet`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::from_parquet) | Alias of [`read_parquet()`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::read_parquet). |
| [`from_query`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::from_query) | Alias of [`sql()`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::sql). |
| [`query`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::query) | Alias of [`sql()`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::sql). |
| [`read_csv`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::read_csv) | Create a relation object from the CSV file in 'name'. |
| [`read_json`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::read_json) | Create a relation object from the JSON file in 'name'. |
| [`read_parquet`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::read_parquet) | Create a relation object from the Parquet path(s) or file-like object(s) in 'path_or_buffer'. |
| [`sql`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::sql) | Run a SQL query. A statement that only reads returns a relation that runs the query each time it is read, parameter values bound at every run. Any other statement runs once, now, and gives a relation over what it returned. Statements before the last one run immediately. |
| [`table`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::table) | Create a relation object for the named table. |
| [`table_function`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::table_function) | Create a relation object from the named table function with given parameters. |
| [`values`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::values) | Create a relation object from the passed values. |
| [`view`](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::view) | Create a relation object for the named view. |

##### `from_arrow` {#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api::from_arrow}

```python
from_arrow(self: _duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection, arrow_object: object) -> DuckDBPyRelation
```
