#### Backup Repository {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:overview::backup-repository}

The `core` repository is mirrored at `http://extensions.duckdb-backup.org`. If `extensions.duckdb.org` is unavailable, DuckDB automatically falls back to the backup server. To use the backup server manually, run:

```sql
SET custom_extension_repository = 'http://extensions.duckdb-backup.org';
```

For details, see [Backup Extension Repositories](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:backup_extension_repositories).

## AutoComplete Extension {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:autocomplete}

The `autocomplete` extension adds support for autocomplete in the [CLI client](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:overview).
The extension is shipped by default with the CLI client.

#### Behavior {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:autocomplete::behavior}

For the behavior of the `autocomplete` extension, see the [documentation of the CLI client](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:autocomplete).

#### Functions {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:autocomplete::functions}

| Function                          | Description                                          |
|:----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| `sql_auto_complete(query_string)` | Attempts autocompletion on the given `query_string`. |

#### Example {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:autocomplete::example}

```sql
SELECT *
FROM sql_auto_complete('SEL');
```

Returns:

| suggestion  | suggestion_start |
|-------------|------------------|
| SELECT      |                0 |
| DELETE      |                0 |
| INSERT      |                0 |
| CALL        |                0 |
| LOAD        |                0 |
| CALL        |                0 |
| ALTER       |                0 |
| BEGIN       |                0 |
| EXPORT      |                0 |
| CREATE      |                0 |
| PREPARE     |                0 |
| EXECUTE     |                0 |
| EXPLAIN     |                0 |
| ROLLBACK    |                0 |
| DESCRIBE    |                0 |
| SUMMARIZE   |                0 |
| CHECKPOINT  |                0 |
| DEALLOCATE  |                0 |
| UPDATE      |                0 |
| DROP        |                0 |

## Avro Extension {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:avro}

The `avro` extension enables DuckDB to read [Apache Avro](https://avro.apache.org) files.

> The `avro` extension was [released as a community extension in late 2024](https://duckdb.org/2024/12/09/duckdb-avro-extension) and became a core extension in early 2025.

#### The `read_avro` Function {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:avro::the-read_avro-function}

The extension adds a single DuckDB function, `read_avro`. This function can be used like so:

```sql
FROM read_avro('⟨some_file⟩.avro');
```

This function will expose the contents of the Avro file as a DuckDB table. You can then use any arbitrary SQL constructs to further transform this table.

#### File IO {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:avro::file-io}

The `read_avro` function is integrated into DuckDB's file system abstraction, meaning you can read Avro files directly from, e.g., HTTP or S3 sources. For example:

```sql
FROM read_avro('https://blobs.duckdb.org/data/userdata1.avro');
FROM read_avro('s3://⟨your-bucket⟩/⟨some_file⟩.avro');
```

should "just" work.

You can also *glob* multiple files in a single read call or pass a list of files to the functions:

```sql
FROM read_avro('some_file_*.avro');
FROM read_avro(['some_file_1.avro', 'some_file_2.avro']);
```

If the filenames somehow contain valuable information (as is unfortunately all-too-common), you can pass the `filename` argument to `read_avro`:

```sql
FROM read_avro('some_file_*.avro', filename=true);
```

This will result in an additional column in the result set that contains the actual filename of the Avro file. 

#### Schema Conversion {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:avro::schema-conversion}

This extension automatically translates the Avro Schema to the DuckDB schema. *All* Avro types can be translated, except for *recursive type definitions*, which DuckDB does not support.

The type mapping is very straightforward except for Avro's "unique" way of handling `NULL`. Unlike other systems, Avro does not treat `NULL` as a possible value in a range of e.g. `INTEGER` but instead represents `NULL` as a union of the actual type with a special `NULL` type. This is different to DuckDB, where any value can be `NULL`. Of course DuckDB also supports `UNION` types, but this would be quite cumbersome to work with.

This extension *simplifies* the Avro schema where possible: An Avro union of any type and the special null type is simplified to just the non-null type. For example, an Avro record of the union type `["int","null"]` becomes a DuckDB `INTEGER`, which just happens to be `NULL` sometimes. Similarly, an Avro union that contains only a single type is converted to the type it contains. For example, an Avro record of the union type `["int"]` also becomes a DuckDB `INTEGER`.

The extension also "flattens" the Avro schema. Avro defines tables as root-level "record" fields, which are the same as DuckDB `STRUCT` fields. For more convenient handling, this extension turns the entries of a single top-level record into top-level columns.

#### Implementation {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:avro::implementation}

Internally, this extension uses the "official" [Apache Avro C API](https://avro.apache.org/docs/++version++/api/c/), albeit with some minor patching to allow reading of Avro files from memory.

#### Limitations and Future Plans {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:avro::limitations-and-future-plans}

* This extension currently does not make use of **parallelism** when reading either a single (large) Avro file or when reading a list of files. Adding support for parallelism in the latter case is on the roadmap. 
* There is currently no support for either projection or filter **pushdown**, but this is also planned at a later stage.
* There is currently no support for the Wasm or the Windows-MinGW builds of DuckDB due to issues with the Avro library dependency (sigh again). We plan to fix this eventually.
* As mentioned above, DuckDB cannot express recursive type definitions that Avro has, this is unlikely to ever change.
* There is no support to allow users to provide a separate Avro schema file. This is unlikely to change, all Avro files we have seen so far had their schema embedded.
* There is currently no support for the `union_by_name` flag that other readers in DuckDB support. This is planned for the future.

## AWS Extension {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws}

The `aws` extension adds functionality, e.g., authentication, on top of the `httpfs` extension's [S3 capabilities](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:httpfs:overview::s3-api), using the AWS SDK.

#### Installing and Loading {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::installing-and-loading}

The `aws` extension will be transparently [autoloaded](#docs:2.0:extensions:overview::autoloading-extensions) on first use from the official extension repository.
If you would like to install and load it manually, run:

```sql
INSTALL AND LOAD aws;
```

> In most cases, the `aws` extension works in conjunction with the [`httpfs` extension](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:httpfs:overview).

#### Configuration and Authentication {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::configuration-and-authentication}

> **Tip.** For an overview of the available methods and guidance on which one to use, see the [S3 and AWS Authentication](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:httpfs:authentication) page.

The preferred way to configure and authenticate to AWS S3 endpoints is to use [secrets](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:create_secret).
There are two S3 secret providers:

* The `config` provider, where you supply the access key and secret manually. It is part of the `httpfs` extension and is documented in the [S3 API page](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:httpfs:s3api::config-provider). Use it when you already have static credentials.
* The `credential_chain` provider, described below, which fetches credentials automatically using the AWS SDK. It is provided by the `aws` extension and supports profiles, SSO, assumed roles, web identities (IRSA), and instance metadata.

The full list of S3 secret parameters that apply to *both* providers (` ENDPOINT`, `REGION`, `URL_STYLE`, `USE_SSL`, `KMS_KEY_ID`, `REQUESTER_PAYS`, …) is documented in the [S3 API page](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:httpfs:s3api::overview-of-s3-secret-parameters).

#### `credential_chain` Provider {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::credential_chain-provider}

The `credential_chain` provider allows automatically fetching credentials using mechanisms provided by the AWS SDK. For example, to use the AWS SDK default provider:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET secret (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain
);
```

To query a file using the above secret, simply query any `s3://` prefixed file.

DuckDB also allows specifying a specific chain using the `CHAIN` keyword. This takes a semicolon-separated list (` a;b;c`) of providers that will be tried in order. For example:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET secret (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    CHAIN 'env;config'
);
```

The possible values for `CHAIN` are the following:

* [`config`](https://sdk.amazonaws.com/cpp/api/LATEST/aws-cpp-sdk-core/html/class_aws_1_1_auth_1_1_profile_config_file_a_w_s_credentials_provider.html)
* [`sts`](https://sdk.amazonaws.com/cpp/api/LATEST/aws-cpp-sdk-core/html/class_aws_1_1_auth_1_1_s_t_s_assume_role_web_identity_credentials_provider.html)
* [`sso`](https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/sso/)
* [`env`](https://sdk.amazonaws.com/cpp/api/LATEST/aws-cpp-sdk-core/html/class_aws_1_1_auth_1_1_environment_a_w_s_credentials_provider.html)
* [`instance`](https://sdk.amazonaws.com/cpp/api/LATEST/aws-cpp-sdk-core/html/class_aws_1_1_auth_1_1_instance_profile_credentials_provider.html)
* [`process`](https://sdk.amazonaws.com/cpp/api/LATEST/aws-cpp-sdk-core/html/class_aws_1_1_auth_1_1_process_credentials_provider.html)
* `web_identity` (for [IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/iam-roles-for-service-accounts.html); see [Web Identity (IRSA)](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::web-identity-irsa))

The `credential_chain` provider also allows overriding the automatically fetched config. For example, to automatically load credentials, and then override the region, run:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET secret (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    CHAIN config,
    REGION '⟨eu-west-1⟩'
);
```

##### Selecting a Profile {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::selecting-a-profile}

To load credentials based on a named profile which is not the default (from the `AWS_PROFILE` environment variable or the default profile based on AWS SDK precedence), use the `PROFILE` parameter:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET secret (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    CHAIN config,
    PROFILE '⟨my_profile⟩'
);
```

This approach is equivalent to the [deprecated S3 API](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:httpfs:s3api_legacy_authentication)'s method `load_aws_credentials('⟨my_profile⟩')`.

##### Assuming a Role (STS) {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::assuming-a-role-sts}

To assume an IAM role, pass its ARN via `ASSUME_ROLE_ARN`. An `EXTERNAL_ID` can be supplied for the role's trust policy:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET secret (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    CHAIN 'sts',
    ASSUME_ROLE_ARN 'arn:aws:iam::⟨account_id⟩:role/⟨role⟩',
    EXTERNAL_ID '⟨external_id⟩',
    REGION '⟨us-east-1⟩'
);
```

> The `sts` chain value requires an `ASSUME_ROLE_ARN` value. If the selected profile itself uses STS, use `CHAIN 'config'` instead.

##### Web Identity (IRSA) {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::web-identity-irsa}

For [IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/iam-roles-for-service-accounts.html) — commonly used on Amazon EKS — use the `web_identity` chain together with a role ARN and a token file. A `SESSION_NAME` can optionally be set:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET secret (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    CHAIN 'web_identity',
    ASSUME_ROLE_ARN 'arn:aws:iam::⟨account_id⟩:role/⟨role⟩',
    WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE '⟨/var/run/secrets/eks.amazonaws.com/serviceaccount/token⟩'
);
```

##### Single Sign-On (SSO) {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::single-sign-on-sso}

DuckDB can use credentials obtained through [AWS IAM Identity Center](https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/sso/) (formerly AWS SSO). DuckDB does not perform the sign-in itself: it reads the short-lived token that the [AWS CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sso.html) caches after you sign in. The setup therefore has three steps.

First, configure an SSO-enabled profile in `~/.aws/config`, either by running `aws configure sso` or by adding an `sso_session` and `sso_account_id` to the profile manually.

Second, sign in from the command line, which opens a browser to complete authentication and caches a temporary token locally:

```batch
aws sso login --profile ⟨my-sso-profile⟩
```

Third, create a secret that uses the `sso` chain and points at that profile. DuckDB then picks up the cached token automatically:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET secret (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    CHAIN 'sso',
    PROFILE '⟨my-sso-profile⟩'
);
```

The token expires after the SSO session's configured lifetime. When it does, run `aws sso login` again. You do not need to recreate the secret.

##### HTTP Proxy {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::http-proxy}

When credentials must be fetched through an HTTP proxy, configure it on the secret:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET secret (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    HTTP_PROXY '⟨proxy.example.com:8080⟩',
    HTTP_PROXY_USERNAME '⟨username⟩',
    HTTP_PROXY_PASSWORD '⟨password⟩'
);
```

##### Region Resolution {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::region-resolution}

If no region is provided explicitly, DuckDB resolves it from the following sources, in order:

1. The `REGION` secret parameter.
2. The `s3_region` [setting](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview) (` SET s3_region = '⟨region⟩'`{:.language-sql .highlight}).
3. The `AWS_REGION` environment variable.
4. The `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` environment variable.
5. The `region` of the profile in `~/.aws/config`.

If none of these resolve, `CREATE SECRET` still succeeds, but DuckDB logs a warning:

```console
Set region explicitly using REGION 'us-east-1' in your CREATE SECRET statement, adding a region to your profile in ~/.aws/config or configure the AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION environment variables.
```

##### Validation {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::validation}

The AWS `credential_chain` provider will look for any required credentials during `CREATE SECRET` time, failing if absent/unavailable.

This behavior may be configured via the `VALIDATION` option as follows:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET secret (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    VALIDATION 'exists'
);
```

Two validation modes are supported:

* `exists` (default) requires present credentials.
* `none` allows `CREATE SECRET` to succeed for `credential_chain`s with no available credentials.

> `VALIDATION 'exists'` validates only the __presence__ of a credential, __not its operational readiness__. Thus, no attempt is made to
> convert into an access token, or perform a read, write, etc.

##### Auto-Refresh {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::auto-refresh}

Some AWS endpoints require periodic refreshing of the credentials.
This can be specified with the `REFRESH auto` option:

```sql
CREATE SECRET env_test (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    REFRESH auto
);
```

> When `CHAIN` is `sts` or `web_identity`, `REFRESH auto` is enabled automatically, since these credentials are short-lived.

#### Amazon RDS (IAM Authentication) {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::amazon-rds-iam-authentication}

The `aws` extension can generate short-lived [IAM authentication tokens](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/UsingWithRDS.IAMDBAuth.html) for connecting to Amazon RDS and Aurora databases, exposed through a secret of type `rds`. It accepts the same [`credential_chain`](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::credential_chain-provider) options as an `s3` secret, plus the required `RDS_USER`, `RDS_HOST`, `RDS_PORT`, and `REGION` parameters. Unlike an `s3` secret, an `rds` secret also requires an explicit `CHAIN`:

```sql
CREATE SECRET aws_rds_secret (
    TYPE rds,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    CHAIN 'env;sso',
    REGION '⟨eu-west-1⟩',
    RDS_USER '⟨db_user⟩',
    RDS_HOST '⟨instance⟩.⟨identifier⟩.⟨region⟩.rds.amazonaws.com',
    RDS_PORT '5432'
);
```

> The `rds` secret _type_ is registered by the [`postgres` extension](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:postgres:overview), not by `aws`, so the `postgres` extension must be installed and loaded before the statement above will run. For the complete end-to-end setup — passing the secret to a connection via `AWS_RDS_SECRET`, attaching, and querying — see the [Amazon RDS with IAM authentication guide](#docs:2.0:guides:database_integration:rds_iam) or the [Postgres secrets documentation](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:postgres:secrets::aws-rds-iam-authentication).

#### Legacy Features {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::legacy-features}

> **Deprecated.** The `load_aws_credentials` function is deprecated and is removed in later releases. Use a [secret](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:create_secret) with the [`credential_chain` provider](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::credential_chain-provider) instead.

Prior to version 0.10.0, DuckDB did not have a [Secrets manager](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:create_secret), to load the credentials automatically, the AWS extension provided
a special function to load the AWS credentials in the [legacy authentication method](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:httpfs:s3api_legacy_authentication).

| Function | Type | Description |
|---|---|-------|
| `load_aws_credentials` | `PRAGMA` function | Loads the AWS credentials through the [AWS Default Credentials Provider Chain](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-java/latest/developer-guide/credentials-chain.html) |

##### Load AWS Credentials (Legacy) {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:aws::load-aws-credentials-legacy}

To load the AWS credentials, run:

```sql
CALL load_aws_credentials();
```



| loaded_access_key_id | loaded_secret_access_key | loaded_session_token | loaded_region |
|----------------------|--------------------------|----------------------|---------------|
| AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE | `<redacted>`             | NULL                 | us-east-2     |

The function takes a string parameter to specify a specific profile:

```sql
CALL load_aws_credentials('minio-testing-2');
```



| loaded_access_key_id | loaded_secret_access_key | loaded_session_token | loaded_region |
|----------------------|--------------------------|----------------------|---------------|
| minio_duckdb_user_2  | `<redacted>`             | NULL                 | NULL          |

There are several parameters to tweak the behavior of the call:

```sql
CALL load_aws_credentials('minio-testing-2', set_region = false, redact_secret = false);
```



| loaded_access_key_id | loaded_secret_access_key     | loaded_session_token | loaded_region |
|----------------------|------------------------------|----------------------|---------------|
| minio_duckdb_user_2  | minio_duckdb_user_password_2 | NULL                 | NULL          |

## Azure Extension {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure}

The `azure` extension lets DuckDB read and write files in [Azure Blob Storage](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/storage/blobs) and Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2.

#### Installing and Loading {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::installing-and-loading}

The `azure` extension will be transparently [autoloaded](#docs:2.0:extensions:overview::autoloading-extensions) on first use from the official extension repository.
If you would like to install and load it manually, run:

```sql
INSTALL AND LOAD azure;
```

#### Usage {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::usage}

Queries need a [secret](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::authentication-with-secret); for a public container, a secret with the storage account name is enough (see the [`CONFIG` provider](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::config-provider)). Then you can query Azure storage as follows:

##### Azure Blob Storage {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::azure-blob-storage}

Allowed URI schemes: `az` or `azure`

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM 'az://⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩/⟨my_file⟩.⟨parquet_or_csv⟩';
```

Globs are also supported:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM 'az://⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩/*.csv';
```

```sql
SELECT *
FROM 'az://⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩/**';
```

Or with a fully qualified path syntax:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM 'az://⟨my_storage_account⟩.blob.core.windows.net/⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩/⟨my_file⟩.⟨parquet_or_csv⟩';
```

```sql
SELECT *
FROM 'az://⟨my_storage_account⟩.blob.core.windows.net/⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩/*.csv';
```

##### Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::azure-data-lake-storage-adls}

Allowed URI schemes: `abfss` or `abfs` (both connect over HTTPS)

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM 'abfss://⟨my_filesystem⟩/⟨path⟩/⟨my_file⟩.⟨parquet_or_csv⟩';
```

Globs are also supported:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM 'abfss://⟨my_filesystem⟩/⟨path⟩/*.csv';
```

```sql
SELECT *
FROM 'abfss://⟨my_filesystem⟩/⟨path⟩/**';
```

Or with a fully qualified path syntax:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM 'abfss://⟨my_storage_account⟩.dfs.core.windows.net/⟨my_filesystem⟩/⟨path⟩/⟨my_file⟩.⟨parquet_or_csv⟩';
```

```sql
SELECT *
FROM 'abfss://⟨my_storage_account⟩.dfs.core.windows.net/⟨my_filesystem⟩/⟨path⟩/*.csv';
```

The fully qualified path can also use the `⟨my_filesystem⟩@⟨my_storage_account⟩`{:.language-sql .highlight} form:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM 'abfss://⟨my_filesystem⟩@⟨my_storage_account⟩.dfs.core.windows.net/⟨path⟩/⟨my_file⟩.⟨parquet_or_csv⟩';
```

#### Writing to Azure Blob Storage {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::writing-to-azure-blob-storage}

You can write data directly to Azure Blob or ADLSv2 Storage using the [`COPY` statement](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:copy).

```sql
-- Write query results to a Parquet file on Blob Storage
COPY (SELECT * FROM my_table)
TO 'az://⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩/output.parquet';
```

```sql
-- Write a table to a CSV file on ADLSv2 Storage
COPY my_table
TO 'abfss://⟨my_filesystem⟩/⟨path⟩/output.csv';
```

You can also use fully qualified paths:

```sql
COPY my_table
TO 'az://⟨my_storage_account⟩.blob.core.windows.net/⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩/output.parquet';
```

Since v1.5.4, the extension buffers written data locally and uploads it in blocks of `azure_write_block_size` bytes (default: 8 MiB).
By default, the uploaded blocks are committed when the file is closed, so other readers see the new content only after the write completes.
To commit earlier, set `azure_write_staged_blocks_per_commit` to the number of blocks after which an intermediate commit happens.

> **Warning.** An intermediate commit makes an incomplete file visible to readers. A Parquet file cannot be read until its footer is written at the end, so keep the default `0` for Parquet files and for Delta, Iceberg or DuckLake tables.

##### Writing Large Files {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::writing-large-files}

Azure limits a blob to 50,000 blocks.
With the default block size of 8 MiB, the largest file you can write is about 390 GiB.
To write larger files, increase `azure_write_block_size` (maximum: 4000 MiB, about 3.9 GiB). For example, to write files up to about 3 TiB:

```sql
SET azure_write_block_size = 64 * 1024 * 1024;
```

#### Configuration {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::configuration}

Use the following [configuration options](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview) to control how the extension reads and writes remote files:

| Name | Description | Type | Default |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `azure_http_stats` | Include HTTP info from Azure Storage in the [`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` statement](#docs:2.0:dev:profiling). | `BOOLEAN` | `false` |
| `azure_http_logging` | Write Azure HTTP requests to the DuckDB `HTTP` log when it is enabled. See [Logging](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::logging). | `BOOLEAN` | `true` |
| `azure_http_logging_redact_query_params` | Semicolon-separated list of URL query parameter names (case-sensitive) whose values are redacted in the HTTP log. | `VARCHAR` | `sig` |
| `azure_http_logging_redact_headers` | Semicolon-separated list of header names (case-insensitive) whose values are redacted in the HTTP log, for both requests and responses. | `VARCHAR` | `Authorization` |
| `azure_read_transfer_concurrency` | Maximum number of threads the Azure client can use for a single parallel read. Values above 1 let the client fill one buffer with parallel requests, when the chunk size is smaller than the buffer. | `INTEGER` | `5` |
| `azure_read_transfer_chunk_size` | Maximum size in bytes that the Azure client will read in a single request. Should be a divisor of `azure_read_buffer_size`. | `BIGINT` | `8*1024*1024` |
| `azure_read_buffer_size` | Size of the read buffer. Should be a multiple of `azure_read_transfer_chunk_size`. | `UBIGINT` | `8*1024*1024` |
| `azure_write_block_size` | Size in bytes of each block for Blob and ADLS writes. Setting it to `0` restores the default. The maximum is 4000 MiB (about 3.9 GiB). See [Writing Large Files](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::writing-large-files). | `UBIGINT` | `8*1024*1024` |
| `azure_write_staged_blocks_per_commit` | Number of uploaded blocks after which an intermediate commit happens. With `0`, all blocks are committed when the file is closed. Non-zero values make partial writes visible sooner, at the cost of extra requests. This option does not change the 50,000-block limit. | `UBIGINT` | `0` |
| `azure_transport_option_type` | Underlying [adapter](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-cpp/blob/main/doc/HttpTransportAdapter.md) to use in the Azure SDK. Valid values are: `default` or `curl`. | `VARCHAR` | `default` |
| `azure_context_caching` | Enable/disable the caching of the underlying Azure SDK HTTP connection in the DuckDB connection context when performing queries. If you suspect that this is causing some side effect, you can try to disable it by setting it to false (not recommended). | `BOOLEAN` | `true` |

Since v1.5.4, `azure_read_transfer_chunk_size` and `azure_read_buffer_size` default to 8 MiB (previously 1 MiB).

> **Tip.** Setting `azure_transport_option_type` to `curl` has the following effects:
>
> * On Linux, it may fix certificate errors such as `Problem with the SSL CA cert (path? access rights?)`: the extension then looks for the CA bundle in the usual paths, which *curl* does not do by default and which static linking may get wrong.
> * On Windows, it replaces the default adapter (*WinHTTP*), so you can use all *curl* features, e.g., SOCKS proxies.
> * On all operating systems, it honors these environment variables:
>     * `CURL_CA_INFO`: path to a PEM encoded file with the certificate authorities for libcurl. It is known to work only on Linux and may fail on other platforms.
>     * `CURL_CA_PATH`: path to a directory of PEM encoded files with the certificate authorities for libcurl.

Example:

```sql
SET azure_http_stats = false;
SET azure_read_transfer_concurrency = 5;
SET azure_read_transfer_chunk_size = 8_388_608;
SET azure_read_buffer_size = 8_388_608;
```

#### Authentication {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::authentication}

Authenticate with a [secret](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::authentication-with-secret). The `SET` variables in [Authentication with Variables](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::authentication-with-variables) still work but are deprecated.

##### Authentication with Secret {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::authentication-with-secret}

Several [Secret Providers](#docs:2.0:configuration:secrets_manager::secret-providers) are available, described below. These rules apply to every provider:

* If you need to define different secrets for different storage accounts, use the [`SCOPE` configuration](#docs:2.0:configuration:secrets_manager::creating-multiple-secrets-for-the-same-service-type). Note that the `SCOPE` requires a trailing slash (` SCOPE 'az://⟨my_storage_account⟩.blob.core.windows.net/'`{:.language-sql .highlight}).
* With fully qualified paths, `ACCOUNT_NAME` is optional.
* For paths that are not fully qualified, the `ENDPOINT` attribute overrides the default endpoint (` blob.core.windows.net` for `az://` and `azure://`, `dfs.core.windows.net` for `abfss://` and `abfs://`).

###### `CONFIG` Provider {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::config-provider}

The default provider, `CONFIG` (i.e., user-configured), allows access to the storage account using a connection string or anonymously. For example:

```sql
CREATE SECRET secret1 (
    TYPE azure,
    CONNECTION_STRING '⟨connection_string⟩'
);
```

For anonymous access, give the storage account name:

```sql
CREATE SECRET secret2 (
    TYPE azure,
    PROVIDER config,
    ACCOUNT_NAME '⟨storage_account_name⟩'
);
```

###### `credential_chain` Provider {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::credential_chain-provider}

The `credential_chain` provider allows connecting using credentials automatically fetched by the Azure SDK via the Azure credential chain.
By default, the provider uses the Azure SDK's [`DefaultAzureCredential`](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-cpp/blob/azure-identity_1.6.0/sdk/identity/azure-identity/README.md#defaultazurecredential) chain. The token is fetched at query time, not when the secret is created. For example:

```sql
CREATE SECRET secret3 (
    TYPE azure,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    ACCOUNT_NAME '⟨storage_account_name⟩'
);
```

DuckDB also allows specifying a specific chain using the `CHAIN` keyword. This takes a semicolon-separated list (` a;b;c`) of providers that will be tried in order. For example:

```sql
CREATE SECRET secret4 (
    TYPE azure,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    CHAIN 'cli;env',
    ACCOUNT_NAME '⟨storage_account_name⟩'
);
```

The possible values are:

* [`cli`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/authenticate-azure-cli): the Azure CLI login
* [`managed_identity`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview)
* [`workload_identity`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/workload-id/workload-identities-overview), e.g., on AKS
* [`env`](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-cpp/blob/azure-identity_1.6.0/sdk/identity/azure-identity/README.md#environment-variables): environment variables
* [`default`](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-cpp/blob/azure-identity_1.6.0/sdk/identity/azure-identity/README.md#defaultazurecredential): the full default chain, used when no `CHAIN` is given

###### `MANAGED_IDENTITY` Provider {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::managed_identity-provider}

If the machine has one managed identity, the `credential_chain` provider uses it with no extra options. If it has several, use the `MANAGED_IDENTITY` provider and pick one with `CLIENT_ID`, `OBJECT_ID` or `RESOURCE_ID`:

```sql
CREATE SECRET azure_mi (
    TYPE azure,
    PROVIDER managed_identity,
    ACCOUNT_NAME '⟨storage_account_name⟩',
    CLIENT_ID '⟨client_id⟩'
);
```

Without an ID, the provider works like `credential_chain`. With several identities and no ID, the Azure SDK decides which one is used, so set an ID.

###### `SERVICE_PRINCIPAL` Provider {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::service_principal-provider}

The `SERVICE_PRINCIPAL` provider allows connecting using an [Azure Service Principal (SPN)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/architecture/service-accounts-principal).

With a client secret:

```sql
CREATE SECRET azure_spn (
    TYPE azure,
    PROVIDER service_principal,
    TENANT_ID '⟨tenant_id⟩',
    CLIENT_ID '⟨client_id⟩',
    CLIENT_SECRET '⟨client_secret⟩',
    ACCOUNT_NAME '⟨storage_account_name⟩'
);
```

Or with a certificate:

```sql
CREATE SECRET azure_spn_cert (
    TYPE azure,
    PROVIDER service_principal,
    TENANT_ID '⟨tenant_id⟩',
    CLIENT_ID '⟨client_id⟩',
    CLIENT_CERTIFICATE_PATH '⟨client_cert_path⟩',
    ACCOUNT_NAME '⟨storage_account_name⟩'
);
```

###### `ACCESS_TOKEN` Provider {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::access_token-provider}

The `ACCESS_TOKEN` provider allows connecting with an OAuth access token (bearer token) that you obtained outside of DuckDB:

```sql
CREATE SECRET azure_token (
    TYPE azure,
    PROVIDER access_token,
    ACCESS_TOKEN '⟨access_token⟩',
    ACCOUNT_NAME '⟨storage_account_name⟩'
);
```

> **Warning.** The extension does not refresh the token. When it expires, run `CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET` with a new token; it takes effect on the next query.

###### Configuring a Proxy {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::configuring-a-proxy}

To configure proxy information when using secrets, you can add `HTTP_PROXY`, `PROXY_USER_NAME` and `PROXY_PASSWORD` in the secret definition. For example:

```sql
CREATE SECRET secret5 (
    TYPE azure,
    CONNECTION_STRING '⟨connection_string⟩',
    HTTP_PROXY 'http://localhost:3128',
    PROXY_USER_NAME '⟨proxy_user_name⟩',
    PROXY_PASSWORD '⟨proxy_password⟩'
);
```

> **Note.** When you use secrets:
>
> * The `HTTP_PROXY` environment variable is still honored, unless the secret sets `HTTP_PROXY`.
> * The `SET` variables of [Authentication with Variables](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::authentication-with-variables) are ignored.

##### Authentication with Variables {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::authentication-with-variables}

> **Deprecated.** Use [secrets](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::authentication-with-secret) instead.

```sql
SET ⟨variable_name⟩ = ⟨value⟩;
```

Where `variable_name` can be one of the following:

| Name | Description | Type | Default |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `azure_storage_connection_string` | Azure connection string, used for authenticating and configuring Azure requests. | `VARCHAR` | - |
| `azure_account_name` | Azure account name, when set, the extension will attempt to automatically detect credentials (not used if you pass the connection string). | `VARCHAR` | - |
| `azure_endpoint` | Override the Azure endpoint for when the Azure credential providers are used. | `VARCHAR` | `blob.core.windows.net` |
| `azure_credential_chain`| Ordered list of Azure credential providers, in string format separated by `;`. For example: `'cli;managed_identity;env'`. See the list of possible values in the [`credential_chain` provider section](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::credential_chain-provider). Not used if you pass the connection string. | `VARCHAR` | - |
| `azure_http_proxy` | Proxy for login and for requests to Azure. | `VARCHAR` | `HTTP_PROXY` environment variable (if set). |
| `azure_proxy_user_name` | HTTP proxy username if needed. | `VARCHAR` | - |
| `azure_proxy_password` | HTTP proxy password if needed. | `VARCHAR` | - |

#### Additional Information {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::additional-information}

##### Logging {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::logging}

Since v1.5.2, the Azure extension writes its HTTP requests to the DuckDB [`HTTP` log](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview). To inspect them:

```sql
CALL enable_logging('HTTP');
SELECT * FROM 'az://⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩/⟨my_file⟩.parquet';
SELECT request.type, request.url, response.status FROM duckdb_logs_parsed('HTTP');
```

Logged requests show the DuckDB `User-Agent` header.
The values of the `sig` query parameter and the `Authorization` header are replaced by `REDACTED`.
To change what is redacted, set `azure_http_logging_redact_query_params` and `azure_http_logging_redact_headers`.
A new value replaces the default list, so include `sig` or `Authorization` if you still want them redacted:

```sql
SET azure_http_logging_redact_headers = 'Authorization;x-ms-date';
```

> **Warning.** The Azure extension applies only these settings, not DuckDB's `redact_http_logs` setting. To keep Azure requests out of the `HTTP` log, run `SET azure_http_logging = false;`.

The Azure extension relies on the Azure SDK to connect to Azure Blob storage and supports printing the SDK logs to the console.
To control the log level, set the [`AZURE_LOG_LEVEL`](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-cpp/blob/main/sdk/core/azure-core/README.md#sdk-log-messages) environment variable.

For instance, to start the DuckDB CLI with verbose logs:

```batch
AZURE_LOG_LEVEL=verbose duckdb
```

```sql
CREATE SECRET myaccount (
    TYPE azure,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    SCOPE 'az://⟨my_storage_account⟩.blob.core.windows.net/'
);
SELECT count(*) FROM 'az://⟨my_storage_account⟩.blob.core.windows.net/⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩/⟨my_file⟩.parquet';
```

##### Difference between ADLS and Blob Storage {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::difference-between-adls-and-blob-storage}

For glob patterns over many directories, prefer `abfss://`: the ADLS endpoint lists only the directories that match, while the Blob endpoint lists every file under the prefix and filters afterwards. The following example shows how a glob is performed through each endpoint.

Using the following filesystem:

```text
root
├── l_receiptmonth=1997-10
│   ├── l_shipmode=AIR
│   │   └── data_0.csv
│   ├── l_shipmode=SHIP
│   │   └── data_0.csv
│   └── l_shipmode=TRUCK
│       └── data_0.csv
├── l_receiptmonth=1997-11
│   ├── l_shipmode=AIR
│   │   └── data_0.csv
│   ├── l_shipmode=SHIP
│   │   └── data_0.csv
│   └── l_shipmode=TRUCK
│       └── data_0.csv
└── l_receiptmonth=1997-12
    ├── l_shipmode=AIR
    │   └── data_0.csv
    ├── l_shipmode=SHIP
    │   └── data_0.csv
    └── l_shipmode=TRUCK
        └── data_0.csv
```

The following query is performed through the Blob endpoint:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM 'az://root/l_receiptmonth=1997-*/l_shipmode=SHIP/*.csv';
```

It will perform the following steps:

* List all the files with the prefix `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10/l_shipmode=SHIP/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10/l_shipmode=AIR/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10/l_shipmode=TRUCK/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11/l_shipmode=SHIP/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11/l_shipmode=AIR/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11/l_shipmode=TRUCK/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12/l_shipmode=SHIP/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12/l_shipmode=AIR/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12/l_shipmode=TRUCK/data_0.csv`
* Filter the result with the requested pattern `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-*/l_shipmode=SHIP/*.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10/l_shipmode=SHIP/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11/l_shipmode=SHIP/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12/l_shipmode=SHIP/data_0.csv`

Meanwhile, the same query can be performed through the datalake endpoint as follows:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM 'abfss://root/l_receiptmonth=1997-*/l_shipmode=SHIP/*.csv';
```

This will perform the following steps:

* List all directories in `root/`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12`
* Filter and list subdirectories: `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10`, `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11`, `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10/l_shipmode=SHIP`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10/l_shipmode=AIR`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10/l_shipmode=TRUCK`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11/l_shipmode=SHIP`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11/l_shipmode=AIR`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11/l_shipmode=TRUCK`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12/l_shipmode=SHIP`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12/l_shipmode=AIR`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12/l_shipmode=TRUCK`
* Filter and list subdirectories: `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10/l_shipmode=SHIP`, `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11/l_shipmode=SHIP`, `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12/l_shipmode=SHIP`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-10/l_shipmode=SHIP/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-11/l_shipmode=SHIP/data_0.csv`
    * `root/l_receiptmonth=1997-12/l_shipmode=SHIP/data_0.csv`

Because the Blob endpoint does not support the notion of directories, the filter can only be performed after the listing, whereas the ADLS endpoint will list files recursively. Especially with higher partition/directory counts, the performance difference can be very significant.

## Delta Extension {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta}

The `delta` extension adds support for the [Delta Lake open-source storage format](https://delta.io/). It is built using the [Delta Kernel](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs). The extension reads Delta tables, local and remote, and writes them: it can create tables and append to them.

For implementation details, see the [“Native Delta Lake Support in DuckDB” blog post](https://duckdb.org/2024/06/10/delta).

> To connect to Unity Catalog, DuckDB has the [`unity_catalog` extension](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:unity_catalog).

#### Installing and Loading {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::installing-and-loading}

The `delta` extension will be transparently [autoloaded](#docs:2.0:extensions:overview::autoloading-extensions) on first use from the official extension repository.
If you would like to install and load it manually, run:

```sql
INSTALL AND LOAD delta;
```

#### Usage {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::usage}

To scan a local Delta table, run:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM delta_scan('file:///⟨path⟩');
```

##### Attaching Tables {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::attaching-tables}

A Delta table can also be attached as a database. The database holds exactly one table, with the same name as the database, so `my_table` and `my_table.my_table` refer to the same table:

```sql
ATTACH 'file:///⟨path⟩' AS my_table (TYPE delta);
SELECT * FROM my_table;
```

##### Reading from an S3 Bucket {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::reading-from-an-s3-bucket}

To scan a Delta table in an [S3 bucket](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:httpfs:s3api), run:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM delta_scan('s3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩');
```

To authenticate, create a [secret](#docs:2.0:configuration:secrets_manager):

```sql
CREATE SECRET (
    TYPE s3,
    PROVIDER credential_chain
);
SELECT *
FROM delta_scan('s3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩');
```

For a public bucket, you may need to set its region in a secret:

```sql
CREATE SECRET (
    TYPE s3,
    REGION '⟨my_region⟩'
);
SELECT *
FROM delta_scan('s3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩');
```

##### Reading from Azure Blob Storage {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::reading-from-azure-blob-storage}

To scan a Delta table in an [Azure Blob Storage container](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::azure-blob-storage), run:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM delta_scan('az://⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩');
```

To authenticate, create a [secret](#docs:2.0:configuration:secrets_manager):

```sql
CREATE SECRET (
    TYPE azure,
    PROVIDER credential_chain,
    ACCOUNT_NAME '⟨storage_account_name⟩'
);
SELECT *
FROM delta_scan('az://⟨my_container⟩/⟨path⟩');
```

##### Reading from Google Cloud Storage {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::reading-from-google-cloud-storage}

To scan a Delta table in a GCS bucket through its [S3 API compatibility](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:httpfs:s3api), use [HMAC keys](https://console.cloud.google.com/storage/settings;tab=interoperability) and create a secret:

```sql
CREATE SECRET (
    TYPE gcs,
    KEY_ID '⟨hmac_key_id⟩',
    SECRET '⟨hmac_secret⟩'
);
SELECT *
FROM delta_scan('gs://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩');
```

##### Creating Tables {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::creating-tables}

> New This feature was introduced in DuckDB 2.0.

To create a Delta table, attach the location for it and create a table named after the attached database:

```sql
ATTACH 's3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩' AS events (TYPE delta);
CREATE TABLE events.events (id BIGINT, region VARCHAR)
PARTITIONED BY (region);
INSERT INTO events VALUES (1, 'eu');
```

Only `CREATE TABLE` needs the full `events.events` name: without the database name, it creates the table in the default database.

The table can be read and written without attaching it again.

> **Warning.** `ATTACH` does not check that the path holds a Delta table. A mistyped path attaches as an empty database and only fails on the first read.

###### Table Properties {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::table-properties}

Options in a `WITH` clause are stored as Delta table properties, except `location`, which must match the attached path:

```sql
ATTACH 's3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨other_path⟩' AS audit (TYPE delta);
CREATE TABLE audit.audit (id BIGINT, name VARCHAR)
WITH ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = 'true', 'delta.appendOnly' = 'true');
```

Properties that enable a Delta feature, such as deletion vectors, also upgrade the table's protocol as needed. Values can be any constant expression except `NULL`. Some properties cannot be set at creation, such as `'delta.enableVariantShredding'`.

To create a table with [column mapping](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::column-mapping), set `'delta.columnMapping.mode'` to `'name'` or `'id'`.

##### Appending Data {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::appending-data}

To append rows to a Delta table, attach it and use `INSERT INTO`:

```sql
ATTACH 's3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩' AS my_table (TYPE delta);
INSERT INTO my_table SELECT * FROM other_table;
```

Since v1.5.6, if the table schema declares `CHAR(n)` or `VARCHAR(n)` (Spark writes these), a write with a value longer than `n` characters fails as a whole.

##### Time Travel {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::time-travel}

> New Time travel by timestamp was introduced in DuckDB 2.0.

To read a table as it was at an earlier version or point in time, use the `AT` clause, an `ATTACH` option or a `delta_scan` parameter:

```sql
-- Query an attached table
SELECT * FROM my_table AT (VERSION => 5);
SELECT * FROM my_table AT (TIMESTAMP => TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-09-01 12:00:00+00');

-- Attach the table at a version or point in time
ATTACH 's3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩' AS my_table_v5 (TYPE delta, VERSION 5);
ATTACH 's3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩' AS my_table_then (TYPE delta, TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-09-01 12:00:00+00');

-- Scan without attaching
SELECT * FROM delta_scan('s3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩', version => 5); -- since v1.5.4
SELECT * FROM delta_scan('s3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩', timestamp => TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-09-01 12:00:00+00');
```

* A table attached at a version or timestamp is read-only.
* A version or timestamp given to `ATTACH` is the default for queries on that table; an `AT` clause overrides it.
* A version and a timestamp cannot be given together.
* A timestamp reads the latest version committed at or before it. One later than `now()` or earlier than the table's first commit fails.
* A timestamp without a time zone uses the session's `TimeZone`.
* Within a transaction, a timestamp always reads the same version.

##### Checkpointing {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::checkpointing}

Since v1.5.1, [`CHECKPOINT`](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:checkpoint) compacts the Delta log of an attached table into a checkpoint file, which speeds up reads of tables with long logs:

```sql
ATTACH '⟨path⟩' AS my_table (TYPE delta);
CHECKPOINT my_table;
```

##### Idempotent Appends {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::idempotent-appends}

To retry a batch without writing it twice, tag the append with an application ID and a version. DuckDB commits the append only if the table's last recorded version for that ID is the one you expect. This uses Delta's per-application transaction versions.

Within a transaction, tag the append with `delta_set_transaction_version(⟨table⟩, ⟨app_id⟩, ⟨new_version⟩, ⟨expected_previous_version⟩)`{:.language-sql .highlight}:

```sql
ATTACH '⟨path⟩' AS my_table (TYPE delta);

BEGIN TRANSACTION;
CALL delta_set_transaction_version('my_table', 'my_app_id', 1::UBIGINT, NULL::UBIGINT);
INSERT INTO my_table VALUES (1);
COMMIT;
```

If another process committed a different version for `my_app_id` first, `COMMIT` fails. A rolled-back transaction leaves the version unchanged. Read the current version with `delta_get_transaction_version(⟨table⟩, ⟨app_id⟩)`{:.language-sql .highlight}, which returns `NULL` if no version has been recorded yet.

##### Attach Options {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::attach-options}

When attaching a Delta table you can pass the following options to `ATTACH`:

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `VERSION` | `UBIGINT` | latest | Attach the table at a specific [table version](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::time-travel). |
| `TIMESTAMP` | `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | latest | Attach the table at the version current at a [point in time](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::time-travel). |
| `PIN_SNAPSHOT` | `BOOLEAN` | `false` | Resolve the latest table snapshot once, on first use, and reuse it for every later query. Without it, each transaction reads the latest version; since v1.5.3, it loads only the log entries committed since the previous read. |
| `PUSHDOWN_PARTITION_INFO` | `BOOLEAN` | `true` | Push down partition information so that whole files can be skipped based on partition values. |
| `PUSHDOWN_FILTERS` | `VARCHAR` | `all` | Filter pushdown mode for file skipping. One of `none`, `all`, `constant_only`, `dynamic_only`. |

```sql
ATTACH 's3://⟨my_bucket⟩/⟨path⟩' AS my_table (
    TYPE delta,
    PIN_SNAPSHOT true,
    PUSHDOWN_FILTERS 'constant_only'
);
```

##### Inspecting Scanned Files {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::inspecting-scanned-files}

`delta_list_files` returns the data files a scan would read for a table, together with their cardinality, partition values, and whether they carry deletion vectors. This is useful for understanding the effect of [data skipping](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::features):

```sql
SELECT * FROM delta_list_files('file:///⟨path⟩');
```

| Column | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `data_file` | `VARCHAR` | Path to the Parquet data file. |
| `cardinality` | `UBIGINT` | Number of rows in the file. |
| `partitions` | `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` | Partition column values for the file. |
| `have_deletes` | `BOOLEAN` | Whether the file has an associated deletion vector. |

To list the files of an earlier table version, pass `version => ⟨version⟩`{:.language-sql .highlight}. To add a `delete_count` column with the number of rows each file's deletion vector removes, pass `delete_count => true`:

```sql
SELECT data_file, cardinality, delete_count
FROM delta_list_files('file:///⟨path⟩', version => 3, delete_count => true);
```

##### Reading Domain Metadata {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::reading-domain-metadata}

Since v1.5.1, `delta_domain_metadata` returns one row per [domain](https://github.com/delta-io/delta/blob/master/PROTOCOL.md#domain-metadata) of a table, with the `VARCHAR` columns `domain` and `configuration`. Pass `version => ⟨version⟩`{:.language-sql .highlight} for an earlier version:

```sql
SELECT domain, configuration
FROM delta_domain_metadata('file:///⟨path⟩');
```

For an attached table, `duckdb_tables()` shows the same pairs in its `tags` column.

##### Column Mapping {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::column-mapping}

Delta tables with [column mapping](https://github.com/delta-io/delta/blob/master/PROTOCOL.md#column-mapping) enabled are read as the Delta protocol specifies for each mode: in `id` mode, columns are matched by Parquet field ID; in `name` mode, by physical column name.

The protocol requires every data file of an `id`-mode table to carry Parquet field IDs, but some writers omit them, including DuckDB 1.5.5 and earlier. Since v1.5.6, the `delta_column_mapping_policy` setting decides how such files are read:

* `strict`: fail with an error that names the file.
* `lenient`: match the file's columns by physical name, or failing that by logical name, and log a warning under the `delta.ColumnMapping` log type. The names must cover every column in the file, otherwise the read fails.

> **Warning.** The default changed from `lenient` in DuckDB 1.5 to `strict` in v2.0. To read such files as v1.5 did, run `SET delta_column_mapping_policy = 'lenient';`{:.language-sql .highlight}.

##### VARIANT Columns {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::variant-columns}

Delta `variant` columns are read as DuckDB [`VARIANT`](#docs:2.0:sql:data_types:variant), whether their files are shredded or not, and top-level `VARIANT` columns can be appended to.

> New The following were introduced in DuckDB 2.0.

* A query that reads one field of a `VARIANT` or `STRUCT` column, such as `SELECT v.a`, reads only that field from the Parquet files, so on a shredded table it skips the columns of the other fields. This does not apply to a column with a `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` field at any depth: DuckDB reads all of it.
* `CREATE TABLE` accepts `VARIANT` columns.
* When writing, DuckDB shreds `VARIANT` values only if the table sets `'delta.enableVariantShredding'` to `'true'`, as the Delta protocol requires; otherwise it writes them unshredded. Because `CREATE TABLE` cannot set this property, a table created by DuckDB holds unshredded files.

##### Catalog-Managed Tables {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::catalog-managed-tables}

A Delta table with the `catalogManaged` feature, such as a Unity Catalog managed table, has commits that only its catalog tracks. Reading or writing such a table straight from storage, with `delta_scan` or `ATTACH ... (TYPE delta)`, fails with an error. Attach its catalog instead, for example with the [`unity_catalog` extension](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:unity_catalog), and query the table through it.

##### Credential Chains in Delta {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::credential-chains-in-delta}

For some network operations, the `delta` extension uses `delta-kernel-rs` and `object_store`, which try credential sources in a different order than DuckDB and include different ones by default. If more than one source is available, e.g., a service principal in the environment and the Azure CLI, credential loading may be inconsistent. Configure exactly one credential type in the chain of your secret.

Since v1.5.6, the `delta` extension supports [Azure workload identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/workload-id/workload-identities-overview) (for example on AKS): name `workload_identity` in the `CHAIN` of an [Azure `credential_chain` secret](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:azure::credential_chain-provider), and set the `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE`, `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` and `AZURE_TENANT_ID` environment variables.

#### Settings {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::settings}

The `delta` extension adds the following settings:

| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `delta_column_mapping_policy` | `VARCHAR` | `strict` | How to read an `id`-mode data file without Parquet field IDs: `strict` raises an error, `lenient` matches its columns by name. See [Column Mapping](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::column-mapping). |
| `delta_kernel_logging` | `BOOLEAN` | `false` | Forward the internal logging of the [Delta Kernel](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-kernel-rs) to the DuckDB logger. May impact performance even when DuckDB logging is disabled. |
| `delta_scan_explain_files_filtered` | `BOOLEAN` | `true` | Add the filtered files to the `EXPLAIN` output. May impact the performance of `delta_scan` during `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` queries. |

#### Features {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::features}

The `delta` extension supports:

* multithreaded scans and Parquet metadata reading
* data skipping/filter pushdown
    * skipping row groups in file (based on Parquet metadata)
    * skipping complete files (based on Delta partition information and file statistics)
* projection pushdown, down to single fields of struct and [`VARIANT`](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::variant-columns) columns
* scanning tables with deletion vectors
* [column mapping](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::column-mapping) in `name` and `id` mode
* [time travel](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::time-travel) by version or timestamp
* all primitive types except intervals
* nested types (structs, lists and maps)
* creating tables (` CREATE TABLE`)
* blind appends (` INSERT INTO`), with file statistics for data skipping
* [idempotent appends](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::idempotent-appends)
* [checkpoints](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::checkpointing) (` CHECKPOINT`)
* cloud storage (AWS S3, Azure, GCS) with secrets

#### Limitations {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::limitations}

* `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE` and `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` are not supported. Create the table, then `INSERT` into it.
* `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, [`MERGE INTO`](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:merge_into), `ALTER TABLE` and `DROP TABLE` are not supported, nor are `RETURNING` and `ON CONFLICT` clauses on `INSERT`.
* `CREATE TABLE` does not support:
    * constraints, including `NOT NULL`
    * `DEFAULT` values and generated columns
    * `SORTED BY`
    * column types without a Delta equivalent, such as `TIME` or unsigned integers
    * a table whose columns are all partition columns
* A table created with [column mapping](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::column-mapping) cannot have nested or partition columns, because DuckDB cannot write to such tables yet.
* Tables with an interval (` interval year to month` or `interval day to second`), `geometry` or `geography` column cannot be read.
* Writing to a table with the `allowColumnDefaults` writer feature fails, even if no column has a default yet: DuckDB cannot fill in Delta defaults and does not write `NULL` instead. Reading works.
* Writing to a table that declares a `CHAR(n)` or `VARCHAR(n)` width on a nested field, such as `ARRAY<VARCHAR(5)>`, is not supported.
* Writing to a table with a `VARIANT` inside a struct, list or map is not supported.

#### Supported Platforms {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::supported-platforms}

The `delta` extension currently only supports the following platforms:

* Linux (x86_64 and ARM64): `linux_amd64` and `linux_arm64`
* macOS Intel and Apple Silicon: `osx_amd64` and `osx_arm64`
* Windows AMD64: `windows_amd64`

Support for the [other DuckDB platforms](#docs:2.0:extensions:extension_distribution::platforms) is work-in-progress.

#### Using delta-rs with DuckDB {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta::using-delta-rs-with-duckdb}

This example writes a Delta table with the `delta-rs` Python package and reads it with DuckDB. It then reads the table's change data feed through the Arrow zero-copy integration. For larger data, use [Arrow Datasets](https://delta-io.github.io/delta-rs/latest/integrations/delta-lake-arrow/) to read it lazily.

The example needs `deltalake`, the Python package of `delta-rs`, with its `pyarrow` extra:

```batch
pip install duckdb "deltalake[pyarrow]"
```



<details markdown='1'>
<summary markdown='span'>
Full example
</summary>

```python
import deltalake as dl
import duckdb
import pyarrow as pa

# Create a delta table and read it with DuckDB Delta extension
dl.write_deltalake(
    "tmp/some_table",
    pa.table({
        "id": [1, 2, 3],
        "value": ["a", "b", "c"]
    })
)
with duckdb.connect() as conn:
    conn.sql("""
        SELECT * FROM delta_scan('tmp/some_table')
    """).show()

# Append some data and read the change data feed, an Arrow record batch reader
dl.write_deltalake(
    "tmp/some_table",
    pa.table({
        "id": [4, 5],
        "value": ["d", "e"]
    }),
    mode="append"
)
table = dl.DeltaTable("tmp/some_table").load_cdf(starting_version=1, ending_version=2)
with duckdb.connect() as conn:
    conn.register("t", table)
    conn.sql("SELECT * FROM t").show()
```

</details>


## DuckLake {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake}

> DuckLake 1.1 was released together with DuckDB 2.0.
> Read the [announcement blog post](https://ducklake.select/2026/10/21/ducklake-11/).

The `ducklake` extension adds support for attaching to databases stored in the [DuckLake format](http://ducklake.select/). 
The complete documentation of this extension is available at the [DuckLake website](https://ducklake.select/docs/stable/duckdb/introduction).

#### Installing and Loading {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::installing-and-loading}

To install `ducklake`, run:

```sql
INSTALL ducklake;
```

The `ducklake` extension will be transparently [autoloaded](#docs:2.0:extensions:overview::autoloading-extensions) on first use in an [`ATTACH`](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:attach) clause.
If you would like to load it manually, run:

```sql
LOAD ducklake;
```

#### Usage {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::usage}

```sql
ATTACH 'ducklake:metadata.ducklake' AS my_ducklake (DATA_PATH 'data_files');
USE my_ducklake;
```

#### Tables {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::tables}

In DuckDB, the `ducklake` extension stores the [catalog tables](http://ducklake.select/docs/stable/specification/tables/overview) for a DuckLake named
`my_ducklake`{:.language-sql .highlight} in the
`__ducklake_metadata_⟨my_ducklake⟩`{:.language-sql .highlight} catalog.

#### Functions {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::functions}

Note that DuckLake registers several functions.
These should be called with the catalog name as the first argument, e.g.:

```sql
FROM ducklake_snapshots('my_ducklake');
```

```text
┌─────────────┬────────────────────────────┬────────────────┬──────────────────────────┬─────────┬────────────────┬───────────────────┐
│ snapshot_id │       snapshot_time        │ schema_version │         changes          │ author  │ commit_message │ commit_extra_info │
│    int64    │  timestamp with time zone  │     int64      │ map(varchar, varchar[])  │ varchar │    varchar     │      varchar      │
├─────────────┼────────────────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────────────────────┼─────────┼────────────────┼───────────────────┤
│           0 │ 2026-10-20 23:56:36.256+02 │              0 │ {schemas_created=[main]} │ NULL    │ NULL           │ NULL              │
└─────────────┴────────────────────────────┴────────────────┴──────────────────────────┴─────────┴────────────────┴───────────────────┘
```

##### `ducklake_snapshots` {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::ducklake_snapshots}

Returns the snapshots stored in the DuckLake catalog name `catalog`.

| Parameter name | Parameter type | Named parameter | Description |
| -------------- | -------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `catalog`      | `VARCHAR`      | no              |             |

The information is encoded into a table with the following schema:

| Column name         | Column type                |
| ------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `snapshot_id`       | `BIGINT`                   |
| `snapshot_time`     | `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` |
| `schema_version`    | `BIGINT`                   |
| `changes`           | `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR[])`  |
| `author`            | `VARCHAR`                  |
| `commit_message`    | `VARCHAR`                  |
| `commit_extra_info` | `VARCHAR`                  |

##### `ducklake_table_info` {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::ducklake_table_info}

The `ducklake_table_info` function returns information on the tables stored in the DuckLake catalog named `catalog`.

| Parameter name | Parameter type | Named parameter | Description |
| -------------- | -------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `catalog`      | `VARCHAR`      | no              |             |

The information is encoded into a table with the following schema:

| Column name              | Column type |
| ------------------------ | ----------- |
| `table_name`             | `VARCHAR`   |
| `schema_id`              | `BIGINT`    |
| `table_id`               | `BIGINT`    |
| `table_uuid`             | `UUID`      |
| `file_count`             | `BIGINT`    |
| `file_size_bytes`        | `BIGINT`    |
| `delete_file_count`      | `BIGINT`    |
| `delete_file_size_bytes` | `BIGINT`    |

##### `ducklake_table_insertions` {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::ducklake_table_insertions}

The `ducklake_table_insertions` function returns the rows inserted in a given table between snapshots of given versions or timestamps.
The function has two variants, depending on whether `start_snapshot` and `end_snapshot` have types `BIGINT` or `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`.

| Parameter name   | Parameter type                        | Named parameter | Description |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `catalog`        | `VARCHAR`                             | no              |             |
| `schema_name`    | `VARCHAR`                             | no              |             |
| `table_name`     | `VARCHAR`                             | no              |             |
| `start_snapshot` | `BIGINT` / `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | no              |             |
| `end_snapshot`   | `BIGINT` / `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | no              |             |

The schema of the table returned by the function is equivalent to that of the table `table_name`.

##### `ducklake_table_deletions` {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::ducklake_table_deletions}

The `ducklake_table_deletions` function returns the rows deleted from a given table between snapshots of given versions or timestamps.
The function has two variants, depending on whether `start_snapshot` and `end_snapshot` have types `BIGINT` or `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`.

| Parameter name   | Parameter type                        | Named parameter | Description |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `catalog`        | `VARCHAR`                             | no              |             |
| `schema_name`    | `VARCHAR`                             | no              |             |
| `table_name`     | `VARCHAR`                             | no              |             |
| `start_snapshot` | `BIGINT` / `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | no              |             |
| `end_snapshot`   | `BIGINT` / `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | no              |             |

The schema of the table returned by the function is equivalent to that of the table `table_name`.

##### `ducklake_table_changes` {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::ducklake_table_changes}

The `ducklake_table_changes` function returns the rows changed in a given table between snapshots of given versions or timestamps.
The function has two variants, depending on whether `start_snapshot` and `end_snapshot` have types `BIGINT` or `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`.

| Parameter name   | Parameter type                        | Named parameter | Description |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `catalog`        | `VARCHAR`                             | no              |             |
| `schema_name`    | `VARCHAR`                             | no              |             |
| `table_name`     | `VARCHAR`                             | no              |             |
| `start_snapshot` | `BIGINT` / `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | no              |             |
| `end_snapshot`   | `BIGINT` / `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | no              |             |

The schema of the table returned by the function contains the following three columns plus the schema of the table `table_name`.

| Column name   | Column type | Description                              |
| ------------- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `snapshot_id` | `BIGINT`    |                                          |
| `rowid`       | `BIGINT`    |                                          |
| `change_type` | `VARCHAR`   | The type of change: `insert` or `delete` |

#### Commands {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::commands}

##### `ducklake_cleanup_old_files` {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::ducklake_cleanup_old_files}

The `ducklake_cleanup_old_files` function cleans up old files in the DuckLake denoted by `catalog`.
It returns a table with a single column (` path`) listing the files that were deleted (or, with `dry_run`, would be deleted).

| Parameter name | Parameter type             | Named parameter | Description |
| -------------- | -------------------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `catalog`      | `VARCHAR`                  | no              |             |
| `cleanup_all`  | `BOOLEAN`                  | yes             |             |
| `dry_run`      | `BOOLEAN`                  | yes             |             |
| `older_than`   | `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | yes             |             |

##### `ducklake_expire_snapshots` {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::ducklake_expire_snapshots}

The `ducklake_expire_snapshots` function expires snapshots with the versions specified by the `versions` parameter or the ones older than the `older_than` parameter.
It returns the expired snapshots, using the same columns as [`ducklake_snapshots`](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::ducklake_snapshots).

| Parameter name | Parameter type             | Named parameter | Description |
| -------------- | -------------------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `catalog`      | `VARCHAR`                  | no              |             |
| `versions`     | `BIGINT[]`                 | yes             |             |
| `older_than`   | `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` | yes             |             |

##### `ducklake_merge_adjacent_files` {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::ducklake_merge_adjacent_files}

The `ducklake_merge_adjacent_files` function merges adjacent files in the storage.
It returns one row per table with the columns `schema_name`, `table_name`, `files_processed` and `files_created`.

| Parameter name | Parameter type | Named parameter | Description |
| -------------- | -------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| `catalog`      | `VARCHAR`      | no              |             |

#### Compatibility Matrix {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ducklake::compatibility-matrix}

The DuckLake specification and the `ducklake` DuckDB extension are currently released together.
See the [Compatibility Matrix](https://ducklake.select/release_calendar#compatibility-matrix).

## Encodings Extension {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:encodings}

The `encodings` extension adds support for reading CSVs using more than 1,000 character encodings.

For a complete list of supported encodings, see [All Supported Encodings](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:encodings::all-supported-encodings). For detailed information on character encoding, see the [ICU data repository](https://github.com/unicode-org/icu-data/tree/main/charset/data/ucm).

#### Installing and Loading {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:encodings::installing-and-loading}

```sql
INSTALL AND LOAD encodings;
```

#### Usage {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:encodings::usage}

Refer to the `encoding` while reading from files.

To read a `.csv` file with `shift_jis` encoding:

```sql
FROM read_csv('my_shift_jis.csv', encoding = 'shift_jis');
```

To read a `.csv` file with `windows-1251-2000` encoding:

```sql
FROM read_csv('my_windows_1251_2000.csv', encoding = 'windows-1251-2000');
```

To read a `.csv` file with `windows-1252-2000` encoding:

```sql
FROM read_csv('my_windows_1252_2000.csv', encoding = 'windows-1252-2000');
```

To read a `.csv` file with `EUC_CN` encoding:
```sql
FROM read_csv('my_euc_cn.csv', encoding = 'EUC_CN');
```

## Excel Extension {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:excel}

The `excel` extension provides functions to format numbers per Excel's formatting rules by wrapping the [i18npool library](https://www.openoffice.org/l10n/i18n_framework/index.html) and to read/write Excel (` .xlsx`) files. However, please note that `.xls` files are not supported.

#### Installing and Loading {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:excel::installing-and-loading}

The `excel` extension will be transparently [autoloaded](#docs:2.0:extensions:overview::autoloading-extensions) on first use from the official extension repository.
If you would like to install and load it manually, run:

```sql
INSTALL AND LOAD excel;
```

#### Excel Scalar Functions {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:excel::excel-scalar-functions}

| Function                            | Description                                                          |
| :---------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `excel_text(number, format_string)` | Format the given `number` per the rules given in the `format_string` |
| `text(number, format_string)`       | Alias for `excel_text`                                               |

#### Examples {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:excel::examples}

```sql
SELECT excel_text(1_234_567.897, 'h:mm AM/PM') AS timestamp;
```

| timestamp |
| --------- |
| 9:31 PM   |

```sql
SELECT excel_text(1_234_567.897, 'h AM/PM') AS timestamp;
```

| timestamp |
| --------- |
| 9 PM      |

#### Reading XLSX Files {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:excel::reading-xlsx-files}

Reading a `.xlsx` file is as simple as just `SELECT`ing from it immediately, e.g.:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM 'test.xlsx';
```

|   a |   b |
| --: | --: |
| 1.0 | 2.0 |
| 3.0 | 4.0 |

However, if you want to set additional options to control the import process, you can use the `read_xlsx` function instead. The following named parameters are supported.

| Option             | Type      | Default                  | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------ | --------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `header`           | `BOOLEAN` | _automatically inferred_ | Whether to treat the first row as containing the names of the resulting columns.                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `sheet`            | `VARCHAR` | _automatically inferred_ | The name of the sheet in the xlsx file to read. Default is the first sheet.                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `all_varchar`      | `BOOLEAN` | `false`                  | Whether to read all cells as containing `VARCHAR`s.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `ignore_errors`    | `BOOLEAN` | `false`                  | Whether to ignore errors and silently replace cells that can't be cast to the corresponding inferred column type with `NULL`'s.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `range`            | `VARCHAR` | _automatically inferred_ | The range of cells to read, in spreadsheet notation. For example, `A1:B2` reads the cells from A1 to B2. If not specified the resulting range will be inferred as rectangular region of cells between the first row of consecutive non-empty cells and the first empty row spanning the same columns. |
| `stop_at_empty`    | `BOOLEAN` | _automatically inferred_ | Whether to stop reading the file when an empty row is encountered. If an explicit `range` option is provided, this is `false` by default, otherwise `true`.                                                                                                                                           |
| `empty_as_varchar` | `BOOLEAN` | `false`                  | Whether to treat empty cells as `VARCHAR` instead of `DOUBLE` when trying to automatically infer column types.                                                                                                                                                                                        |

```sql
SELECT *
FROM read_xlsx('test.xlsx', header = true);
```

|   a |   b |
| --: | --: |
| 1.0 | 2.0 |
| 3.0 | 4.0 |

Alternatively, the `COPY` statement with the `XLSX` format option can be used to import an Excel file into an existing table, in which case the types of the columns in the target table will be used to coerce the types of the cells in the Excel file.

```sql
CREATE TABLE test (a DOUBLE, b DOUBLE);
COPY test FROM 'test.xlsx' WITH (FORMAT xlsx, HEADER);
SELECT * FROM test;
```

##### Type and Range Inference {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:excel::type-and-range-inference}

Because Excel itself only really stores numbers or strings in cells, and does not enforce that all cells in a column are of the same type, the `excel` extension has to do some guesswork to "infer" and decide the types of the columns when importing an Excel sheet. While almost all columns are inferred as either `DOUBLE` or `VARCHAR`, there are some caveats:

* `TIMESTAMP`, `TIME`, `DATE` and `BOOLEAN` types are inferred when possible based on the _format_ applied to the cell.
* Text cells containing `TRUE` and `FALSE` are inferred as `BOOLEAN`.
* Empty cells are considered to be `DOUBLE` by default, unless the `empty_as_varchar` option is set to `true`, in which case they are typed as `VARCHAR`.

If the `all_varchar` option is set to `true`, none of the above applies and all cells are read as `VARCHAR`.

When no types are specified explicitly, (e.g., when using the `read_xlsx` function instead of `COPY TO ... FROM '⟨file⟩.xlsx'`{:.language-sql .highlight})
the types of the resulting columns are inferred based on the first "data" row in the sheet, that is:

* If no explicit range is given
  * The first row after the header if a header is found or forced by the `header` option
  * The first non-empty row in the sheet if no header is found or forced
* If an explicit range is given
  * The second row of the range if a header is found in the first row or forced by the `header` option
  * The first row of the range if no header is found or forced

This can sometimes lead to issues if the first "data row" is not representative of the rest of the sheet (e.g., it contains empty cells) in which case the `ignore_errors` or `empty_as_varchar` options can be used to work around this.

However, when the `COPY TO ... FROM '⟨file⟩.xlsx'`{:.language-sql .highlight} syntax is used, no type inference is done and the types of the resulting columns are determined by the types of the columns in the table being copied to. All cells will simply be converted by casting from `DOUBLE` or `VARCHAR` to the target column type.

#### Writing XLSX Files {#docs:2.0:core_extensions:excel::writing-xlsx-files}

Writing `.xlsx` files is supported using the `COPY` statement with `XLSX` given as the format. The following additional parameters are supported.

| Option            | Type      | Default   | Description                                                                          |
| ----------------- | --------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `header`          | `BOOLEAN` | `false`   | Whether to write the column names as the first row in the sheet                      |
| `sheet`           | `VARCHAR` | `Sheet1`  | The name of the sheet in the xlsx file to write.                                     |
