The storage version can also be set with the `storage_compatibility_version` configuration option or the `STORAGE_VERSION` option of the [`ATTACH` statement](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:attach).
For the full set of methods and the mapping between DuckDB versions and storage versions, see the [Storage Versions and Format page](#docs:2.0:internals:storage).

###### Converting Existing Databases {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::converting-existing-databases}

To move an existing database file to the v2.0.0 storage format, open it with the older DuckDB version and export it, then import it with v2.0.0:

```bash
/older/duckdb mydata.old.db -c "EXPORT DATABASE 'tmp'"
/newer/duckdb mydata.new.db -c "IMPORT DATABASE 'tmp'"
```

For details on this and other conversion methods, including `COPY FROM DATABASE`, see [How to Move between Storage Formats](#docs:2.0:internals:storage::how-to-move-between-storage-formats).

##### Lambda Syntax {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::lambda-syntax}

DuckDB 2.0.0 takes the next step in the lambda syntax transition that began in [v1.3](https://duckdb.org/2025/05/21/announcing-duckdb-130).
The old single arrow syntax (` x -> x + 1`) is now disabled by default in favor of the Python-style syntax (` lambda x : x + 1`).

```sql
-- disabled by default in v2.0.0
SELECT list_transform([1, 2, 3], x -> x + 1);
-- use the Python-style syntax instead
SELECT list_transform([1, 2, 3], lambda x : x + 1);
```

If you cannot update your queries yet, you can re-enable the old syntax for the session:

```sql
SET lambda_syntax = 'enable_single_arrow';
```

This flag is a temporary bridge: DuckDB 2.1 will remove it and the single arrow syntax entirely.
For details, see [Deprecated Syntax](#docs:2.0:sql:functions:lambda::deprecated-syntax).

##### SQL Parser {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::sql-parser}

DuckDB 2.0.0 replaced the PostgreSQL-derived parser with a new [PEG-based parser](#docs:2.0:sql:peg_parser).
It is designed to be compatible with the previous parser, so queries that parsed before should continue to parse, and error messages now include more precise source locations.
If a query that parsed on an earlier version fails on v2.0.0, please [file an issue](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues).
For details, see the [PEG parser page](#docs:2.0:sql:peg_parser).

A few expressions deliberately behave differently in v2.0.0, which can silently change query results:

* The `~` and `!~` operators now perform [partial regular expression matching](#docs:2.0:sql:functions:pattern_matching::regular-expressions), following PostgreSQL: `'abc' ~ 'b'` now returns `true` (previously `false`). The deprecated `regex_match_operator_semantics` setting restores full matching: `SET regex_match_operator_semantics = 'full';`{:.language-sql .highlight}
* The [factorial operator `!`](#docs:2.0:sql:functions:numeric::factorialx) binds more tightly: `2 * 3!` now returns `12` (previously `720`). Use parentheses to get the old behavior, e.g., `(2 * 3)!`.
* `X'…'` and `B'…'` literals now produce [`BLOB`](#docs:2.0:sql:data_types:blob) and [`BITSTRING`](#docs:2.0:sql:data_types:bitstring) values instead of the `VARCHAR` strings `'x…'` and `'b…'`.

If you would like to revert to the old parser, use the [`legacy_parser` extension](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:legacy_parser).
To install and activate it, run the following commands:

```sql
INSTALL AND LOAD legacy_parser;
SET enable_legacy_parser = true;
```

##### C API v2 {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::c-api-v2}

DuckDB 2.0.0 ships a revamped [C API](#docs:2.0:clients:c:overview::c-api-v2), which is considerably more powerful than its predecessor and exposes components such as file systems and table functions to extensions.
The C API v2 is not yet stable: its interface may change in upcoming releases.
For background on extension stability levels, see [Versioning of Extensions](#docs:2.0:extensions:versioning_of_extensions); for the C API reference, see the [C API page](#docs:2.0:clients:c:api).

##### ICU Removed from the Core Build {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::icu-removed-from-the-core-build}

DuckDB 2.0.0 removed the dependency on the [ICU library](https://github.com/unicode-org/icu).
Time zones, calendars and collations are now implemented natively by the [`icu` extension](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:icu), and will continue to behave as before.
No query changes are required, but if you ship a custom build, note that ICU is no longer bundled.
If you find that ICU's behavior changed, please [file an issue](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues).

##### Division by Zero {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::division-by-zero}

Integer division (` //`) and modulo (` %`) by zero, e.g., `1 // 0` and `1 % 0`, now throw an error instead of returning `NULL`:

```console
Invalid Input Error: Division by zero in expression (1 // 0). Use TRY(...) to return NULL for this expression, or SET error_on_division_by_zero=false to return NULL for all divisions by zero.
```

To get `NULL` for a single expression, wrap it in `TRY`, e.g., `TRY(1 // 0)`.
Regular division (` 1 / 0`) still returns `inf`.

##### `MERGE INTO` with Multiple Matching Source Rows {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::merge-into-with-multiple-matching-source-rows}

A [`MERGE INTO` statement](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:merge_into::multiple-matching-source-rows) that would update or delete the same target row more than once, because the row matches multiple source rows, now throws an error instead of silently using one of the source rows.
Deduplicate the source rows or make the `ON` condition unique.

##### Untyped `NULL` Columns {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::untyped-null-columns}

An untyped `NULL` now keeps the `NULL` type instead of defaulting to `INTEGER`.
For example, `CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT NULL AS x` creates a column of type `"NULL"`, which rejects subsequent inserts of non-`NULL` values.
Cast the `NULL` to the intended type, e.g., `NULL::VARCHAR AS x`, or restore the previous behavior with `SET legacy_disable_null_type = true;`{:.language-sql .highlight}.

##### Identifier Case Setting {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::identifier-case-setting}

The [`preserve_identifier_case` setting](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview) changed from a `BOOLEAN` to a `VARCHAR` with the values `'preserve_case'` (default), `'lowercase'` and `'uppercase'`.
The old values `true` and `false` are still accepted and map to `'preserve_case'` and `'lowercase'`, respectively.

##### S3 URL Parameters {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::s3-url-parameters}

Passing S3 settings as URL parameters (e.g., `s3://bucket/file.csv?s3_access_key_id=...`) is disabled by default: the `?` and the following text are now treated as part of the object key.
Use [secrets](#docs:2.0:configuration:secrets_manager) instead or, if you need the legacy behavior, opt in with `SET s3_enable_deprecated_url_parameters = true` (available after loading the `httpfs` extension).

##### Removed and Deprecated Settings {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::removed-and-deprecated-settings}

* The `custom_profiling_settings` setting was removed. Use `tracked_metrics` instead, see [Profiling](#docs:2.0:dev:profiling).
* The `enable_http_logging` and `http_logging_output` settings were removed. Use `CALL enable_logging('HTTP')` instead, see [Logging](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview).
* The `profiling_mode` setting is deprecated and its value has no effect: detailed profiling information is always collected. Use `PRAGMA enable_profiling` to enable profiling.

##### Log Storage in the CLI {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::log-storage-in-the-cli}

Since v1.5.0, the CLI uses the `shell_log_storage` log storage by default, which prints warnings to the console but cannot be queried.
To query logs via `duckdb_logs` in the CLI, enable logging with `CALL enable_logging(storage = 'memory')`. Clients other than the CLI still default to the `memory` log storage.

##### Client APIs {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::client-apis}

Some client APIs ship their own breaking changes with DuckDB 2.0.
In particular, the Python client requires Python 3.11 or newer and changes several APIs, see [Migrating Python Code to DuckDB 2.0](#docs:2.0:clients:python:migration).

#### What's New in v2.0 {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::whats-new-in-v20}

Beyond the breaking changes above, DuckDB 2.0.0 added a large set of new features.
Rather than repeat the feature documentation here, this section points to where each new feature is covered in full.
For the complete tour, see the [preview announcement](https://duckdb.org/2026/08/17/duckdb-20-highlights) and the [detailed release announcement](https://duckdb.org/2026/10/21/announcing-duckdb-200).
The [What's New in the Docs for 2.0 page](#docs:2.0:whats_new_in_the_docs) links every high-level new feature to its documentation, organized by theme:

* DuckDB as a server with the [`quack` extension](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:quack) and the [`CONNECT` statement](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:connect)
* The [`VARIANT` type](#docs:2.0:sql:data_types:variant) for semi-structured data
* [Triggers](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:create_trigger) that run actions automatically in response to table changes
* SQL dialect additions, including [data-modifying CTEs](#docs:2.0:sql:query_syntax:with::data-modifying-ctes) and [nested schemas](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:create_schema::nested-schemas)
* [Asynchronous I/O](#docs:2.0:data:io) for faster reads from object storage
* Optimizer and engine improvements that speed up existing queries, including on Windows
* Self-hostable [extension repositories](#docs:2.0:extensions:extension_repositories) for signing and distributing your own extensions

Several of the headline v2.0.0 changes are covered in [Breaking Changes](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::breaking-changes) above: the new default [storage format](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::storage-format), the [PEG-based SQL parser](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::sql-parser), the revamped [C API v2](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::c-api-v2) and the native timezone, calendar and collation support left after [ICU was removed from the core build](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::icu-removed-from-the-core-build).

#### See Also {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:migration::see-also}

* [Storage Versions and Format](#docs:2.0:internals:storage)
* [Operations Manual](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:overview)

## Backup Extension Repositories {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:backup_extension_repositories}

The core and community extension repositories have backup servers (see [duckdb-backup.org](https://www.duckdb-backup.org/)):

| Repository  | Primary server                           | Backup server                                   |
|:------------|:-----------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| `core`      | `http://extensions.duckdb.org`           | `http://extensions.duckdb-backup.org`           |
| `community` | `http://community-extensions.duckdb.org` | `http://community-extensions.duckdb-backup.org` |

The backup servers serve byte-identical binaries, so [signature checks](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:securing_extensions) are unaffected.

#### Automatic Fallback {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:backup_extension_repositories::automatic-fallback}

Fallback is automatic: if the primary server is unreachable or returns a 5xx error, `INSTALL` retries the download from the backup server. No configuration is needed.

* A 4xx error (e.g., a non-existent extension) is reported directly, without contacting the backup server.
* The fallback only applies to the built-in `core` and `community` repositories. Repositories set via `custom_extension_repository` or `INSTALL ... FROM '⟨url⟩'` are used as-is.
* The installed extension's origin is still recorded as `core` or `community`.

#### Using the Backup Server Manually {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:backup_extension_repositories::using-the-backup-server-manually}

To always install core extensions from the backup server, run:

```sql
SET custom_extension_repository = 'http://extensions.duckdb-backup.org';
```

## DuckDB's Footprint {#operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb}

### Files Created by DuckDB {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:files_created_by_duckdb}

DuckDB creates several files and directories on disk. This page lists both the global and the local ones.

#### Global Files and Directories {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:files_created_by_duckdb::global-files-and-directories}

DuckDB creates the following global files and directories in the user's home directory (denoted with `~`):

| Location | Description | Shared between versions | Shared between clients |
|-------|-------------------|--|--|
| `~/.duckdbrc` | The content of this file is executed when starting the [DuckDB CLI client](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:overview). The commands can be both [dot command](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:dot_commands) and SQL statements. The naming of this file follows the `~/.bashrc` and `~/.zshrc` “run commands” files. | Yes | Only used by CLI |
| `~/.duckdb_history` | History file, similar to `~/.bash_history` and `~/.zsh_history`. Used by the [DuckDB CLI client](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:overview). | Yes | Only used by CLI |
| `~/.duckdb/extensions` | Binaries of installed [extensions](#docs:2.0:extensions:overview). | No | Yes |
| `~/.duckdb/stored_secrets` | [Persistent secrets](#docs:2.0:configuration:secrets_manager::persistent-secrets) created by the [Secrets manager](#docs:2.0:configuration:secrets_manager). | Yes | Yes |
| `~/.duckdb/extension_repositories` | Definitions of custom [extension repositories](#docs:2.0:extensions:extension_repositories), including their pinned public keys, stored as one JSON file per repository. Created by `CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY`. | Yes (v2.0 and later) | Yes |

#### Local Files and Directories {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:files_created_by_duckdb::local-files-and-directories}

DuckDB creates the following files and directories in the working directory (for in-memory connections) or relative to the database file (for persistent connections):

| Name | Description | Example |
|-------|-------------------|---|
| `⟨database_filename⟩`{:.language-sql .highlight} | Database file. Only created in on-disk mode. The file can have any extension with typical extensions being `.duckdb`, `.db` and `.ddb`. | `weather.duckdb` |
| `.tmp/` | Temporary directory. Only created in in-memory mode. | `.tmp/` |
| `⟨database_filename⟩.tmp/`{:.language-sql .highlight} | Temporary directory. Only created in on-disk mode. | `weather.duckdb.tmp/` |
| `⟨database_filename⟩.wal`{:.language-sql .highlight} | [Write-ahead log](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Write-ahead_logging) file. If DuckDB exits normally, the WAL file is deleted upon exit. If DuckDB crashes, the WAL file is required to recover data. | `weather.duckdb.wal` |

If you are working in a Git repository and would like to disable tracking these files by Git,
see the instructions on using [`.gitignore` for DuckDB](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:gitignore_for_duckdb).

### Gitignore for DuckDB {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:gitignore_for_duckdb}

If you work in a Git repository, you may want to configure your [Gitignore](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore) to disable tracking [files created by DuckDB](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:files_created_by_duckdb).
These potentially include the DuckDB database, write-ahead log, and temporary files.

#### Sample Gitignore Files {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:gitignore_for_duckdb::sample-gitignore-files}

In the following, we present sample Gitignore configuration snippets for DuckDB.

##### Ignore Temporary Files but Keep Database {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:gitignore_for_duckdb::ignore-temporary-files-but-keep-database}

This configuration is useful if you would like to keep the database file in the version control system:

```text
*.wal
*.tmp/
```

##### Ignore Database and Temporary Files {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:gitignore_for_duckdb::ignore-database-and-temporary-files}

If you would like to ignore both the database and the temporary files, extend the Gitignore file to include the database file.
The exact Gitignore configuration to achieve this depends on the extension you use for your DuckDB databases (` .duckdb`, `.db`, `.ddb`, etc.).
For example, if your DuckDB files use the `.duckdb` extension, add the following lines to your `.gitignore` file:

```text
*.duckdb*
*.wal
*.tmp/
```

### Reclaiming Space {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:reclaiming_space}

DuckDB uses a single-file format, which has some inherent limitations w.r.t. reclaiming disk space.

#### `CHECKPOINT` {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:reclaiming_space::checkpoint}

To reclaim space after deleting rows, use the [`CHECKPOINT` statement](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:checkpoint).

#### `VACUUM` {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:reclaiming_space::vacuum}

The [`VACUUM` statement](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:vacuum) does _not_ trigger vacuuming deletes and hence does not reclaim space.

#### Compacting a Database by Copying {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:footprint_of_duckdb:reclaiming_space::compacting-a-database-by-copying}

To compact the database, you can create a fresh copy of the database using the [`COPY FROM DATABASE` statement](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:copy::copy-from-database--to). In the following example, we first connect to the original database `db1`, then the new (empty) database `db2`. Then, we copy the content of `db1` to `db2`.

```sql
ATTACH 'db1.db' AS db1;
ATTACH 'db2.db' AS db2;
COPY FROM DATABASE db1 TO db2;
```

## Installing DuckDB {#operations_manual:installing_duckdb}

### Install Script {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:installing_duckdb:install_script}

You can install the [DuckDB CLI client](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:overview) using an install script.

#### Linux and macOS {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:installing_duckdb:install_script::linux-and-macos}

To use the [DuckDB install script](https://install.duckdb.org) on Linux and macOS, run:

```bash
curl https://install.duckdb.org | bash
```



<details markdown='1'>
<summary markdown='span'>
Click to see the output of the install script.
</summary>
```text
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
100 13209  100 13209    0     0   126k      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:--  127k

*** DuckDB Linux/MacOS installation script, version 2.0.0 ***


         .;odxdl,
       .xXXXXXXXXKc
       0XXXXXXXXXXXd  cooo:
      ,XXXXXXXXXXXXK  OXXXXd
       0XXXXXXXXXXXo  cooo:
       .xXXXXXXXXKc
         .;odxdl,


########################################################################## 100.0% {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:installing_duckdb:install_script::1000}

Successfully installed DuckDB 2.0.0 to /Users/your_user/.duckdb/cli/2.0.0/duckdb
Updated symlink from /Users/your_user/.duckdb/cli/latest/duckdb to
                     /Users/your_user/.duckdb/cli/2.0.0/duckdb

Hint: Append the following line to your shell profile:
export PATH="/Users/your_user/.duckdb/cli/latest":$PATH

To launch DuckDB 2.0.0 now, type
/Users/your_user/.duckdb/cli/latest/duckdb
```
</details>



By default, this installs the latest stable version of DuckDB to `~/.duckdb/cli/latest/duckdb`.
To add the DuckDB binary to your path, append the following line to your shell profile or RC file (e.g., `~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`):

```bash
export PATH="~/.duckdb/cli/latest":$PATH
```

You can install [past DuckDB releases](https://duckdb.org/release_calendar#past-releases) (all the way back to v1.0.0) using the `DUCKDB_VERSION` variable. For example, to install v1.2.2, run:

```bash
curl https://install.duckdb.org | DUCKDB_VERSION=1.2.2 bash
```

##### Installing the C/C++ Libraries {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:installing_duckdb:install_script::installing-the-cc-libraries}

Starting with DuckDB 2.0, the install script can also install the DuckDB C/C++ headers and libraries using the `DUCKDB_INSTALL` variable. It takes a comma-separated list of components: `cli` (default), `static` and `shared`. For example, to install the static library and the CLI, run:

```bash
curl https://install.duckdb.org | DUCKDB_INSTALL=static,cli bash
```

The libraries and headers are installed to `~/.duckdb/lib/⟨version⟩/release_⟨platform⟩`, e.g., `~/.duckdb/lib/2.0.0/release_osx_arm64`. For more details, see [Linking Extensions](#docs:2.0:dev:building:linking_extensions).

#### Windows {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:installing_duckdb:install_script::windows}

On Windows, we provide a beta install script. To use it, run the following command from the Run menu (Win+R) or the Command Prompt:

```bash
powershell -NoExit -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "irm https://install.duckdb.org/install.ps1 | iex"
```

### Requirements {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:installing_duckdb:requirements}

DuckDB is designed to be [portable](https://duckdb.org/why_duckdb#portable) and has very few runtime dependencies. Still, there are a few requirements to be aware of before installing or running DuckDB.

#### Supported Platforms {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:installing_duckdb:requirements::supported-platforms}

DuckDB officially supports Linux, macOS and Windows on both x86_64 (AMD64) and AArch64 (ARM64) CPU architectures. Official binaries are distributed for these platforms for both the latest stable version and the preview version (nightly build).

| Platform name   | Operating system | Architecture    | CPU types                      | Support level |
| --------------- | ---------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------- |
| `linux_amd64`   | Linux            | x86_64 (AMD64)  | Intel, AMD, etc.               | Full          |
| `linux_arm64`   | Linux            | AArch64 (ARM64) | AWS Graviton, Snapdragon, etc. | Full          |
| `osx_amd64`     | macOS 12+        | x86_64 (AMD64)  | Intel                          | Partial       |
| `osx_arm64`     | macOS 12+        | AArch64 (ARM64) | Apple Silicon M1, M2, etc.     | Full          |
| `windows_amd64` | Windows 10+      | x86_64 (AMD64)  | Intel, AMD, etc.               | Full          |
| `windows_arm64` | Windows 10+      | AArch64 (ARM64) | Copilot+ PC with Qualcomm CPU  | Full          |

> **Warning.** macOS on Intel CPUs (` osx_amd64`) is only partially supported. DuckDB binaries and [core extensions](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:overview) are still distributed for this platform but, starting with DuckDB 2.0.0, [community extensions](#docs:2.0:extensions:community_extensions) are no longer built for it. DuckDB 2.1 will stop supporting `osx_amd64`.

DuckDB can also run on other platforms, such as Linux distributions using musl libc (e.g., Alpine Linux), Android and WebAssembly, with varying levels of support. For details, see the [list of platforms on the “Building DuckDB” page](#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::platforms). For the platforms extensions are distributed for, see the [“Extension Distribution” page](#docs:2.0:extensions:extension_distribution::platforms).

#### Linux {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:installing_duckdb:requirements::linux}

DuckDB's official Linux binaries require [glibc](https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/) 2.28 or newer. Since DuckDB 1.3.0, the official Linux binaries are [built using the `manylinux_2_28` image](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/16956), which combines an older glibc with a newer compiler. As a result, extensions are no longer distributed for the `linux_amd64_gcc4` platform.

Most mainstream Linux distributions ship with [glibc 2.28](https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/info-gnu/2018-08/msg00000.html) or newer, so no action is needed on these systems. If you need to run DuckDB on a system with an older glibc, you can [build DuckDB from source](#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview) against that version.

## Logging {#operations_manual:logging}

### Logging {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview}

DuckDB implements a logging mechanism that provides users with detailed information about events such as query execution,
performance metrics and system events.

> **Warning.** Logs may contain sensitive information, including secrets and credentials. Enable logging with care and consider where logs are stored and who can access them. Review their contents before sharing them.

#### Basics {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::basics}

The DuckDB logging mechanism can be enabled or disabled using a special function, `enable_logging`. Logs are stored in a special view
named `duckdb_logs`, which can be queried like any standard table.

Example:

```sql
CALL enable_logging(storage = 'memory');
-- Run some queries...
SELECT * FROM duckdb_logs;
```

> In the [CLI client](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:overview), the default log storage is `shell_log_storage`, which prints log messages to the console but does not support querying. Therefore, the example above passes `storage = 'memory'`. In other clients, the default log storage is `memory`, so `CALL enable_logging();` suffices. See [Log Storages](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::log-storages) for details.

To disable logging, run

```sql
CALL disable_logging();
```

To clear the current log, run

```sql
CALL truncate_duckdb_logs();
```

#### Log Level {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::log-level}

DuckDB supports different logging levels that control the verbosity of the logs:

* `FATAL`: Only logs fatal errors
* `ERROR`: Logs error messages
* `WARNING`: Logs warnings and errors
* `INFO`: Logs general information, warnings and errors (default)
* `DEBUG`: Logs detailed debugging information
* `TRACE`: Logs very detailed tracing information

The log level can be set using:

```sql
CALL enable_logging(level = 'debug');
```

#### Warnings {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::warnings}

DuckDB emits warnings, for example when you use deprecated syntax or a deprecated setting, through the logging system at the `WARNING` level. In the CLI, warnings are printed by default. To capture them from any client, or to inspect them after the fact, enable logging and query the `duckdb_logs` view, filtering on the log level:

```sql
CALL enable_logging(level = 'warning', storage = 'memory');
-- Run some queries that may emit warnings...
SELECT timestamp, message
FROM duckdb_logs
WHERE log_level = 'WARNING';
```

The default log level is `INFO`, which already includes warnings, so calling `enable_logging()` without a `level` also captures warnings. Setting `level = 'warning'` excludes lower-severity `INFO` messages.

> **Note.** Switching the CLI to a log storage other than `shell_log_storage` means that warnings are no longer printed to the console. To restore the default behavior, run `CALL enable_logging(storage = 'shell_log_storage')`.

#### Log Types {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::log-types}

In DuckDB, log messages can have an associated log type. Log types allow two main things:

* Fine-grained control over log message generation
* Support for structured logging

##### Logging-Specific Types {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::logging-specific-types}

To log only messages of a specific type:

```sql
CALL enable_logging('HTTP');
```

The above function will automatically set the correct log level and will add the `HTTP` type to the `enabled_log_types` settings. This ensures
only log messages of the `HTTP` type will be written to the log.

> New As of DuckDB 2.0, the dedicated `enable_http_logging` and `http_logging_output` settings have been removed. Use the unified logging framework shown here (` CALL enable_logging('HTTP')` together with `duckdb_logs_parsed('HTTP')`) instead. The `redact_http_logs` setting (default `true`) controls whether HTTP header values are redacted in the logs.

To enable multiple log types, simply pass:

```sql
CALL enable_logging(['HTTP', 'QueryLog']);
```

##### Structured Logging {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::structured-logging}

Some log types like `HTTP` will have an associated message schema. To make DuckDB automatically parse the message, use the `duckdb_logs_parsed()` macro. For example:

```sql
SELECT request.headers FROM duckdb_logs_parsed('HTTP');
```

To view the schema of each structure log type simply run:

```sql
DESCRIBE FROM duckdb_logs_parsed('HTTP');
```

##### List of Available Log Types {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::list-of-available-log-types}

This is a (non-exhaustive) list of the available log types in DuckDB.

| Log Type           | Description                                              | Structured |
|--------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|------------|
| `QueryLog`         | Logs which queries are executed in DuckDB                | No         |
| `FileSystem`       | Logs all FileSystem interaction with DuckDB's Filesystem | Yes        |
| `HTTP`             | Logs all HTTP traffic from DuckDB's internal HTTP client | Yes        |
| `PhysicalOperator` | Logs events emitted by physical operators during query execution | Yes |
| `Metrics`          | Logs profiling metrics collected during query execution  | Yes        |

The structured log types expose the following schemas, which you can inspect at any time with
`DESCRIBE FROM duckdb_logs_parsed(⟨log_type⟩)`{:.language-sql .highlight}:



| Log Type           | Schema |
|--------------------|--------|
| `FileSystem`       | `fs VARCHAR`, `path VARCHAR`, `op VARCHAR`, `bytes BIGINT`, `pos BIGINT` |
| `HTTP`             | `request STRUCT(type, url, start_time, duration_ms, headers MAP)`, `response STRUCT(status, reason, headers MAP)` |
| `PhysicalOperator` | `operator_type VARCHAR`, `parameters MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`, `class VARCHAR`, `event VARCHAR`, `info MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` |
| `Metrics`          | `metric VARCHAR`, `value VARCHAR` |

#### Log Storages {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::log-storages}

By default, DuckDB logs to an in-memory log storage (` memory`), except in the CLI client, which uses `shell_log_storage`. DuckDB supports different types of log storage. Currently,
the following log storage types are implemented in core DuckDB.

| Log storage         | Description                                                               |
|---------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `memory`            | Log to an in-memory buffer (default in clients other than the CLI)        |
| `stdout`            | Log to the stdout of the current process (in CSV format)                  |
| `file`              | Log to (a) csv file(s)                                                    |
| `shell_log_storage` | Print log messages to the console (default in the CLI)                    |

The `shell_log_storage` cannot be queried: `duckdb_logs`, `duckdb_logs_parsed()` and `truncate_duckdb_logs()` all return an error. It also does not accept configuration options such as `storage_config` or `storage_buffer_size`. To query logs in the CLI, switch to a queryable storage such as `memory` or `file`:

```sql
CALL enable_logging(storage = 'memory');
```


Note that the `duckdb_logs` view is automatically updated to target the currently active log storage. This means that switching
the log storage may influence what is returned by the `duckdb_logs` function.

##### Logging to stdout {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::logging-to-stdout}

```sql
CALL enable_logging(storage = 'stdout');
```

##### Logging to File  {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::logging-to-file-}

```sql
CALL enable_logging(storage = 'file', storage_config = {'path': 'path/to/store/logs'});
```

or using the equivalent shorthand:

```sql
CALL enable_logging(storage_path = 'path/to/store/logs');
```

#### Advanced Usage {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::advanced-usage}

##### Normalized vs. Denormalized Logging {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::normalized-vs-denormalized-logging}

DuckDB's log storages can log in two ways: normalized vs. denormalized.

In denormalized logging, the log context information is appended directly to each log entry, while in normalized logging
the log entries are stored separately with `context_id`s referencing the context information.

| Log storage | Normalized   |
|-------------|--------------|
| `memory`    | yes          |
| `file`      | configurable |
| `stdout`    | no           |

For file storage, you can switch between normalized and denormalized by providing a path to a directory (for normalized)
or a path ending in `.csv` (for denormalized). For file logging, denormalized is generally recommended since this increases performance 
and reduces the total size of the logs. To configure normalization of `file` log storage:

```sql
-- normalized: creates `/tmp/duckdb_log_contexts.csv` and `/tmp/duckdb_log_entries.csv`
CALL enable_logging(storage_path = '/tmp');
-- denormalized: creates `/tmp/logs.csv`
CALL enable_logging(storage_path = '/tmp/logs.csv');
```

Note that the difference between normalized and denormalized is typically hidden from users through the `duckdb_logs` function,
which automatically joins normalized tables into a single unified result. To illustrate, both configurations above will be
queryable using `FROM duckdb_logs;` and will produce identical results.

##### Buffer Size {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::buffer-size}

The log storage in DuckDB implements a buffering mechanism to optimize logging performance. This implementation
introduces a potential delay between message logging and storage writing. This delay can obscure the actual message writing time,
which is particularly problematic when debugging crashes, as messages generated immediately before a crash might not be
written. To address this, the buffer size can be configured as follows:

```sql
CALL enable_logging(storage = 'memory', storage_config = {'buffer_size': 0});
```

or using the equivalent shorthand:

```sql
CALL enable_logging(storage = 'memory', storage_buffer_size = 0);
```

Note that the default buffer size is different for different log storages:

| Log storage | Default buffer size           |
|-------------|-------------------------------|
| `memory`    | `STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE` (2048) |
| `file`      | `STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE` (2048) |
| `stdout`    | Disabled (0)                  |

So for example, if you want to increase your `stdout` logging performance, simply enable buffering to greatly (>10x) speed up 
your logging:

```sql
CALL enable_logging(storage = 'stdout', storage_buffer_size = 2048);
```

Or imagine you are debugging a crash in DuckDB and you want to use the `file` logger to understand what's going on.
Simply disable the buffering using:

```sql
CALL enable_logging(storage_path = '/tmp/mylogs', storage_buffer_size = 0);
```

##### Syntactic Sugar {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:logging:overview::syntactic-sugar}

DuckDB contains some syntactic sugar to make common paths easier. For example, the following statements are all equal:

```sql
-- regular invocation 
CALL enable_logging(storage = 'file', storage_config = {'path': 'path/to/store/logs'});
-- using shorthand for common path storage config param 
CALL enable_logging(storage = 'file', storage_path = 'path/to/store/logs');
-- omitting `storage = 'file'` -> is implied from presence of `storage_config`
CALL enable_logging(storage_config = {'path': 'path/to/store/logs'});
```

## HTTP User-Agent {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:user_agents}

#### HTTP User-Agent {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:user_agents::http-user-agent}

Core DuckDB sets the default user-agent as follows:

```text
duckdb/v2.0.0(osx_arm64) cli
```

which indicates the DuckDB version, the platform and the client API (the value of the `duckdb_api` setting, e.g., `cli`, `capi` or `cpp`). If the `custom_user_agent` setting is set, its value is appended to the user-agent string. Note that `custom_user_agent` can only be set when starting DuckDB (e.g., via the connection configuration), not while the database is running, see [Configuration](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview). The currently generated user-agent string can be seen via `PRAGMA user_agent;`, see [Configuration/Pragmas](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::user-agent).

In addition, some extensions set their own user agents; notable examples here include the following.

#### Extensions {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:user_agents::extensions}

##### Azure {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:user_agents::azure}

Azure uses the Azure SDK which sets its own user agents. For identity and storage calls you may see respectively strings like these:

- via Azure Identity: `azsdk-cpp-identity/1.11.0 (Darwin 25.2.0 arm64 Darwin Kernel Version 25.2.0: Tue Nov 18 21:07:05 PST 2025; root:xnu-12377.61.12~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T6020 Cpp/201402)`
- via Azure Blob/ADLSv2: `azsdk-cpp-storage-blobs/12.15.0 (Darwin 25.2.0 arm64 Darwin Kernel Version 25.2.0: Tue Nov 18 21:07:05 PST 2025; root:xnu-12377.61.12~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T6020 Cpp/201402)`

##### Delta (and Unity Catalog) {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:user_agents::delta-and-unity-catalog}

The Delta extension employs calls from DuckDB core, tagged as the DuckDB default above, and also has calls originating from the Delta Kernel, which may look like:

- `object_store/0.12.5`

Unity Catalog calls also use a mix of DuckDB default user-agents, and the Delta style agent above.

##### HTTPFS - HTTPS/S3 {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:user_agents::httpfs---httpss3}

Calls via HTTPFS the extension use the DuckDB default strings noted above.

## Securing DuckDB {#operations_manual:securing_duckdb}

### Securing DuckDB {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview}

DuckDB is a powerful analytical database engine. It can read and write files, access the network, load extensions, 
and use system resources. Like any powerful tool, these capabilities require appropriate configuration when 
working with sensitive data or in shared environments.

This page documents DuckDB's security model and security-related settings. The right configuration depends on your use case, environment, and threat model.
If you plan to embed DuckDB in your application, also consult the ["Embedding DuckDB"](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:embedding_duckdb) page.

#### Untrusted Input {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::untrusted-input}

##### Untrusted SQL Input {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::untrusted-sql-input}

> **Warning.** Treat SQL in DuckDB like code in Bash or Python. Do not execute SQL from untrusted sources without proper sandboxing.

DuckDB executes SQL with the full privileges of the user running it, much like a shell or scripting interpreter (such as bash or Python).
Just as you wouldn't run an untrusted shell script or Python program without sandboxing, apply the same caution to SQL in DuckDB.

If your application must execute SQL from untrusted sources, use additional safeguards when running untrusted code such as:

* Use [duckdb-wasm](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-wasm) for sandboxing
* Run DuckDB in an isolated container (e.g., Docker with restricted capabilities)
* Use a virtual machine or separate process with minimal privileges
* Apply operating system-level sandboxing
* Use network isolation to prevent data exfiltration
* Implement strict query timeouts at the application level

The settings described on this page provide **defense-in-depth** and can limit certain capabilities, but they are not a substitute for proper sandboxing. Also keep in mind that
sandboxing should not just be considered for security purposes, but also for preventing denial of service (DoS) attacks: malicious inputs can easily cause DuckDB to consume excessive resources such 
as memory, disk, CPU, or network.

##### Untrusted Non-SQL Input {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::untrusted-non-sql-input}

> **Warning.** Even non-SQL input into DuckDB can easily have unintended consequences. When building security-sensitive applications with DuckDB, always make sure you properly understand the impact of feeding untrusted input into DuckDB.

Besides SQL, DuckDB also has several non-SQL APIs that can be used to interact with the database. For example, there is a [relational API](#docs:2.0:clients:python:relational_api) in Python that allows building queries programmatically.

These APIs accept user input such as file paths, table names, column names, and filter expressions. While they don't execute raw SQL strings, they still trigger DuckDB operations that can read files, access the network, and use system resources.

**Example considerations for non-SQL APIs:**

* **File paths:** Functions like `duckdb.read_csv(path)` or `duckdb.read_parquet(path)` accept file paths. An attacker-controlled path could read sensitive files (e.g., `/etc/passwd`) or access remote URLs.
* **Table and column names:** While these are typically identifiers rather than executable code, unsanitized input could lead to unexpected behavior or information disclosure.
* **Filter expressions:** Some APIs accept filter expressions that are compiled into DuckDB expressions, which often support subqueries containing arbitrary SQL. Treat these with the same caution as SQL.

**Recommendations:**

* Validate and sanitize all user-provided inputs before passing them to DuckDB APIs.
* Apply the same sandboxing principles as for untrusted SQL when accepting input from untrusted sources.
* Properly read the documentation of all used functions to ensure you understand whether a function is safe to use with untrusted input under your specific use case.

#### Extensions {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::extensions}

DuckDB has a flexible [extension mechanism](#docs:2.0:extensions:overview) that adds functionality such as new file formats, functions, and remote file system access. Extensions run with the same privileges as the DuckDB process itself, so they warrant careful consideration in security-sensitive environments.

##### Autoloading {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::autoloading}

DuckDB can automatically load [core extensions](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:overview) when certain SQL statements require them. To maintain full control over which extensions are loaded, you can disable autoloading:

```sql
SET autoload_known_extensions = false;
SET autoinstall_known_extensions = false;
```

##### Core vs. Community Extensions {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::core-vs-community-extensions}

DuckDB extensions fall into two categories:

* **Core extensions:** Maintained by the DuckDB team with full support. These include extensions like `parquet`, `json`, and `httpfs`.
* **[Community extensions](https://duckdb.org/community_extensions/):** Contributed by third parties and installed via `INSTALL extension_name FROM community`. These are not maintained by the DuckDB team, so only install community extensions from sources you trust.

To disable community extensions entirely:

```sql
SET allow_community_extensions = false;
```

#### Serving DuckDB over the Network {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::serving-duckdb-over-the-network}

With the [`quack` extension](#docs:2.0:quack:overview), a DuckDB process can act as a server (` CALL quack_serve(...)` or `duckdb -serve`). A Quack server exposes the full SQL surface of the instance, including read and write access to every table its session can see, to any client holding the token. The server binds to `localhost` by default; for remote access, put it behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy instead of using `allow_other_hostname`. Note that `duckdb -serve` stores its token in a persistent (unencrypted) `quack` secret. For authentication and authorization hooks, see the [Quack security page](#docs:2.0:quack:security).

#### Reporting Vulnerabilities {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::reporting-vulnerabilities}

If you discover a potential vulnerability, please [report it confidentially via GitHub](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/security/advisories/new).

#### Settings to Limit DuckDB's Capabilities {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::settings-to-limit-duckdbs-capabilities}

The settings documented in this section provide additional hardening for DuckDB deployments. However, they should not be
relied upon as comprehensive security mechanisms in all configurations. These settings are designed as defense-in-depth
measures to limit the impact of potential security issues, but they cannot provide complete protection against all
attack vectors, especially when executing untrusted SQL. For robust security when dealing with untrusted input, combine
these settings with proper sandboxing at the operating system or container level, as described in
the ["Untrusted SQL Input"](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::untrusted-sql-input) section.

##### Safe Mode (CLI) {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::safe-mode-cli}

DuckDB's CLI client supports [“safe mode”](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:safe_mode), which prevents DuckDB from accessing external files other than the database file.
This can be activated via a command line argument or a [dot command](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:dot_commands):

```batch
duckdb -safe ...
```

```plsql
.safe_mode
```


##### Restricting File Access {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::restricting-file-access}

DuckDB can list directories and read arbitrary files via its CSV parser’s [`read_csv` function](#docs:2.0:data:csv:overview) or read text via the [`read_text` function](#docs:2.0:sql:functions:text::read_textsource).
This makes it possible to read from the local file system, for example:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM read_csv('/etc/passwd', sep = ':');
```

###### Disabling File Access {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::disabling-file-access}

File access can be disabled in two ways. First, you can disable individual file systems. For example:

```sql
SET disabled_filesystems = 'LocalFileSystem';
```

Second, you can also completely disable external access by setting the [`enable_external_access` option](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview::configuration-reference) option to `false`.

```sql
SET enable_external_access = false;
```

This setting implies that:

* [`ATTACH`](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:attach) cannot attach to a database in a file.
* [`COPY`](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:copy) cannot read from or write to files.
* Functions such as `read_csv`, `read_parquet`, `read_json`, etc. cannot read from an external source.

###### The `allowed_directories` and `allowed_paths` Options {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::the-allowed_directories-and-allowed_paths-options}

You can restrict DuckDB's access to certain directories or files using the `allowed_directories` and `allowed_paths` options (respectively).
These options allow fine-grained access control for the file system.
For example, you can set DuckDB to only use the `/tmp` directory.

```sql
SET allowed_directories = ['/tmp'];
SET enable_external_access = false;
FROM read_csv('test.csv');
```

With the setting applied, DuckDB will refuse to read files in the current working directory:

```console
Permission Error:
Cannot access file "test.csv" - file system operations are disabled by configuration
```

##### Locking Configurations {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::locking-configurations}

Security-related configuration settings generally lock themselves for safety reasons. For example, while we can disable [community extensions](https://duckdb.org/community_extensions/) using the `SET allow_community_extensions = false`{:.language-sql .highlight}, we cannot re-enable them again after the fact without restarting the database. Trying to do so will result in an error:

```console
Invalid Input Error:
Cannot change allow_community_extensions setting while database is running
```

This prevents re-enabling settings that were explicitly disabled.

Nevertheless, many configuration settings do not disable themselves, such as the resource constraints. If you allow users to run SQL statements unrestricted on your own hardware, you might want to consider locking the configuration after your own configuration has finished using the following command:

```sql
SET lock_configuration = true;
```

This prevents any configuration settings from being modified from that point onwards.

To allow specific settings to remain configurable even when `lock_configuration` is enabled, use the `allowed_configs` option:

```sql
SET allowed_configs = ['memory_limit', 'threads'];
SET lock_configuration = true;
```

With this configuration, `memory_limit` and `threads` can still be changed, while all other settings are locked.

#### Secrets {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::secrets}

[Secrets](#docs:2.0:configuration:secrets_manager) are used to manage credentials to log into third party services like AWS or Azure. DuckDB can show a list of secrets using the `duckdb_secrets()` table function. This will redact any sensitive information such as security keys by default. The `allow_unredacted_secrets` option can be set to show all information contained within a security key. It is recommended not to turn on this option if you are running untrusted SQL input.

> The `allow_unredacted_secrets` option can only be set when the database is instantiated. It cannot be changed at runtime. Setting it with `SET` after the database is running fails with `Cannot change allow_unredacted_secrets setting while database is running`. Provide it as a startup configuration option instead, for example via the `config` argument when connecting from a client.

Queries can access the secrets defined in the Secrets Manager. For example, if there is a secret defined to authenticate with a user, who has write privileges to a given AWS S3 bucket, queries may write to that bucket. This is applicable for both persistent and temporary secrets.

[Persistent secrets](#docs:2.0:configuration:secrets_manager::persistent-secrets) are stored in unencrypted binary format on the disk. These have the same permissions as SSH keys, `600`, i.e., only the user who is running the DuckDB (parent) process can read and write them.

#### Prepared Statements to Prevent SQL Injection {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::prepared-statements-to-prevent-sql-injection}

Similarly to other SQL databases, it's recommended to use [prepared statements](#docs:2.0:sql:query_syntax:prepared_statements) in DuckDB to prevent [SQL injection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL_injection).

> Important Prepared statements protect against SQL injection when **you control the query structure** but accept **untrusted data values** (e.g., user-provided search terms or IDs). If users can supply the SQL query itself, this is equivalent to allowing them to run arbitrary code – see ["Untrusted SQL Input"](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::untrusted-sql-input).

**Therefore, avoid concatenating strings for queries:**

```python
import duckdb
duckdb.execute("SELECT * FROM (VALUES (32, 'a'), (42, 'b')) t(x) WHERE x = " + str(42)).fetchall()
```

**Instead, use prepared statements:**

```python
import duckdb
duckdb.execute("SELECT * FROM (VALUES (32, 'a'), (42, 'b')) t(x) WHERE x = ?", [42]).fetchall()
```

#### Constrain Resource Usage {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::constrain-resource-usage}

DuckDB can use quite a lot of CPU, RAM, and disk space. These resources can be limited to control the usage of the DuckDB instance.

The number of CPU threads that DuckDB can use can be set using, for example:

```sql
SET threads = 4;
```

Where 4 is the number of allowed threads.

The maximum amount of memory (RAM) can also be limited, for example:

```sql
SET memory_limit = '4GB';
```

The size of the temporary file directory can be limited with:

```sql
SET max_temp_directory_size = '4GB';
```

#### Privileges {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::privileges}

Avoid running DuckDB as a root user (e.g., using `sudo`).
There is no good reason to run DuckDB as root.

### Embedding DuckDB {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:embedding_duckdb}

#### CLI Client {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:embedding_duckdb::cli-client}

The [Command Line Interface (CLI) client](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:overview) is intended for interactive use cases and not for embedding.
As a result, it has more features that could be abused by a malicious actor.
For example, the CLI client has the `.sh` feature that allows executing arbitrary shell commands.
This feature is only present in the CLI client and not in any other DuckDB clients.

```sql
.sh ls
```

> **Tip.** Calling DuckDB's CLI client via shell commands is **not recommended** for embedding DuckDB. It is recommended to use one of the client libraries, e.g., [Python](#docs:2.0:clients:python:overview), [R](#docs:2.0:clients:r), [Java](#docs:2.0:clients:java:overview), etc.

### Securing Extensions {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:securing_extensions}

DuckDB has a powerful extension mechanism, which has the same privileges as the user running DuckDB's (parent) process.
This introduces security considerations. Therefore, we recommend reviewing the configuration options listed on this page and setting them according to your attack models.

#### DuckDB Signature Checks {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:securing_extensions::duckdb-signature-checks}

DuckDB extensions are checked on every load using the signature of the binaries.
There are currently three categories of extensions:

* Signed with a `core` key. Only extensions vetted by the core DuckDB team are signed with these keys.
* Signed with a `community` key. These are open-source extensions distributed via the [DuckDB Community Extensions repository](https://duckdb.org/community_extensions/).
* Unsigned.

#### Overview of Security Levels for Extensions {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:securing_extensions::overview-of-security-levels-for-extensions}

DuckDB offers the following security levels for extensions.

| Usable extensions | Description | Configuration |
|-----|---|---|
| `core` | Extensions can only be loaded if signed from a `core` key. | `SET allow_community_extensions = false`{:.language-sql .highlight} |
| `core` and `community` | Extensions can only be loaded if signed from a `core` or `community` key. | This is the default security level. |
| Any extension including unsigned | Any extensions can be loaded. | Set `allow_unsigned_extensions = true` at startup (e.g., `duckdb -unsigned` in the CLI). It cannot be changed while the database is running. |

Security-related configuration settings [lock themselves](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::locking-configurations), i.e., it is only possible to restrict capabilities in the current process.

For example, attempting the following configuration changes will result in an error:

```sql
SET allow_community_extensions = false;
SET allow_community_extensions = true;
```

```console
Invalid Input Error:
Cannot change allow_community_extensions setting while database is running
```

#### Custom Extension Repositories {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:securing_extensions::custom-extension-repositories}

DuckDB 2.0 introduced trusted [custom extension repositories](#docs:2.0:extensions:extension_repositories), which can serve extensions signed with user-provided keys. Two settings control them:

* `allow_extension_repositories`: whether custom trusted extension repositories are `'allowed'`, `'forbidden'` (which also distrusts existing repositories) or `'undecided'` (the default: blocks adding new repositories, but keeps trusting existing ones). While the database is running, the setting can only move from `'undecided'` to `'allowed'` or `'forbidden'`, or from `'allowed'` to `'forbidden'`.
* `extension_repository_directory`: the directory in which trusted extension repositories are stored. This is the trust anchor for user-provided repositories, so while signature checking is enabled (` allow_unsigned_extensions = false`), it can only be set at startup, not while the database is running.

If you run DuckDB in an environment where only extensions signed by the DuckDB team should be loaded, disable custom repositories:

```sql
SET allow_extension_repositories = 'forbidden';
```

#### Community Extensions {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:securing_extensions::community-extensions}

DuckDB has a [Community Extensions repository](https://duckdb.org/community_extensions/), which allows convenient installation of third-party extensions.
Community extension repositories like pip or npm are essentially enabling remote code execution by design. This is less dramatic than it sounds. For better or worse, we are quite used to piping random scripts from the web into our shells, and routinely install a staggering amount of transitive dependencies without thinking twice. Some repositories like CRAN enforce a human inspection at some point, but that’s no guarantee for anything either.

We’ve studied several different approaches to community extension repositories and have picked what we think is a sensible approach: we do not attempt to review the submissions, but require that the *source code of extensions is available*. We do take over the complete build, sign and distribution process. Note that this is a step up from pip and npm that allow uploading arbitrary binaries but a step down from reviewing everything manually. We allow users to [report malicious extensions](https://github.com/duckdb/community-extensions/security/advisories/new) and show adoption statistics like GitHub stars and download count. Because we manage the repository, we can remove problematic extensions from distribution quickly.

Despite this, installing and loading DuckDB extensions from the community extension repository will execute code written by third party developers, and therefore *can* be dangerous. A malicious developer could create and register a harmless-looking DuckDB extension that steals your crypto coins.
If you’re running a web service that executes untrusted SQL from users with DuckDB, we recommend disabling community extensions. To do so, run:

```sql
SET allow_community_extensions = false;
```

#### Disabling Autoinstalling and Autoloading Known Extensions {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:securing_extensions::disabling-autoinstalling-and-autoloading-known-extensions}

By default, DuckDB automatically installs and loads known extensions. To disable autoinstalling known extensions, run:

```sql
SET autoinstall_known_extensions = false;
```

To disable autoloading known extensions, run:

```sql
SET autoload_known_extensions = false;
```

To lock this configuration, use the [`lock_configuration` option](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:overview::locking-configurations):

```sql
SET lock_configuration = true;
```

#### Always Require Signed Extensions {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:securing_duckdb:securing_extensions::always-require-signed-extensions}

By default, DuckDB requires extensions to be either signed as core extensions (created by the DuckDB developers) or community extensions (created by third-party developers but distributed by the DuckDB developers).
The [`allow_unsigned_extensions` setting](#docs:2.0:extensions:extension_distribution::unsigned-extensions) can be enabled on start-up to allow loading unsigned extensions.
While this setting is useful for extension development, enabling it will allow DuckDB to load _any extensions,_ which means more care must be taken to ensure malicious extensions are not loaded.

## Non-Deterministic Behavior {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:non-deterministic_behavior}

Several operators in DuckDB exhibit non-deterministic behavior.
Most notably, SQL uses set semantics, which allows results to be returned in a different order.
DuckDB exploits this to improve performance, particularly when performing multi-threaded query execution.
Other factors, such as using different compilers, operating systems and hardware architectures, can also cause changes in ordering.
This page documents the cases where non-determinism is an _expected behavior_.
If you would like to make your queries deterministic, see the [“Working Around Non-Determinism” section](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:non-deterministic_behavior::working-around-non-determinism).

#### Set Semantics {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:non-deterministic_behavior::set-semantics}

One of the most common sources of non-determinism is the set semantics used by SQL.
E.g., if you run the following query repeatedly, you may get two different results:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT 'A' AS x
    UNION
    SELECT 'B' AS x
);
```

Both results `A`, `B` and `B`, `A` are correct.

#### Different Results on Different Platforms: `array_distinct` {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:non-deterministic_behavior::different-results-on-different-platforms-array_distinct}

The `array_distinct` function may return results [in a different order on different platforms](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/13746):

```sql
SELECT array_distinct(['A', 'A', 'B', NULL, NULL]) AS arr;
```

For this query, both `[A, B]` and `[B, A]` are valid results.

#### Floating-Point Aggregate Operations with Multi-Threading {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:non-deterministic_behavior::floating-point-aggregate-operations-with-multi-threading}

Floating-point inaccuracies may produce different results when run in multi-threaded configurations:
For example, [`stddev` and `corr` may produce non-deterministic results](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/13763):

```sql
CREATE TABLE tbl AS
    SELECT 'ABCDEFG'[floor(random() * 7 + 1)::INT] AS s, 3.7 AS x, i AS y
    FROM range(1, 1_000_000) r(i);

SELECT s, stddev(x) AS standard_deviation, corr(x, y) AS correlation
FROM tbl
GROUP BY s
ORDER BY s;
```

The expected standard deviations and correlations from this query are 0 for all values of `s`.
However, when executed on multiple threads, the query may return small numbers (` 0 <= z < 10e-16`) due to floating-point inaccuracies.

#### Working Around Non-Determinism {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:non-deterministic_behavior::working-around-non-determinism}

For the majority of use cases, non-determinism is not causing any issues.
However, there are some cases where deterministic results are desirable.
In these cases, try the following workarounds:

1. Limit the number of threads to prevent non-determinism introduced by multi-threading.

   ```sql
   SET threads = 1;
   ```

2. Enforce ordering. For example, you can use the [`ORDER BY ALL` clause](#docs:2.0:sql:query_syntax:orderby::order-by-all):

   ```sql
   SELECT *
   FROM (
       SELECT 'A' AS x
       UNION
       SELECT 'B' AS x
   )
   ORDER BY ALL;
   ```

   You can also sort lists using [`list_sort`](#docs:2.0:sql:functions:list::list_sortlist):

   ```sql
   SELECT list_sort(array_distinct(['A', 'A', 'B', NULL, NULL])) AS i
   ORDER BY i;
   ```

   It's also possible to introduce a [deterministic shuffling](https://duckdb.org/2024/08/19/duckdb-tricks-part-1#shuffling-data).

## Limits {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:limits}

This page contains DuckDB's built-in limit values.
To check the value of a setting on your system, use the `current_setting` function.

#### Limit Values {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:limits::limit-values}

| Limit | Default value | Configuration option | Comment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Array size | 100000 | - | |
| BLOB size | 4 GB | - | |
| Expression depth | 1000 | [`max_expression_depth`](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview) | |
| Memory allocation for a vector | 128 GB | - | |
| Memory use | 80% of RAM | [`memory_limit`](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::memory-limit) | Note: This limit only applies to the buffer manager. |
| String size | 4 GB | - | |
| Temporary directory size | 90% of available disk space | [`max_temp_directory_size`](#docs:2.0:configuration:overview) | |

#### Size of Database Files {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:limits::size-of-database-files}

DuckDB doesn't have a practical limit for the size of a single DuckDB database file.
We have database files using 15 TB+ of disk space and they work fine.
However, connecting to such a huge database may take a few seconds and [checkpointing](#docs:2.0:sql:statements:checkpoint) can be slower.

## DuckDB Docker Container {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:duckdb_docker}

DuckDB has an [official Docker image](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-docker), which supports both the ARM64 (AArch64) and x86_64 (AMD64) architectures.

#### Usage {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:duckdb_docker::usage}

To use the DuckDB Docker image, run:

```batch
docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" -w /workspace duckdb/duckdb
```

#### Using the DuckDB UI with Docker {#docs:2.0:operations_manual:duckdb_docker::using-the-duckdb-ui-with-docker}

To use the [DuckDB UI](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:ui) with Docker, enable host networking.

> This setting forwards all ports from the container, so exercise caution and avoid it in secure environments.

```batch
docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" -w /workspace --net host duckdb/duckdb
```

Then, launch the UI as follows:

```plsql
CALL start_ui();
```

To enable host networking in Docker Desktop, follow the instructions on the [Host network driver](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/host/#docker-desktop) page.

The pages in this section are intended for developers who contribute to DuckDB or build extensions for it. If you would like to contribute, please also read the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).

#### Project Structure and Processes {#docs:2.0:dev:overview::project-structure-and-processes}

* [DuckDB Repositories](#docs:2.0:dev:repositories) lists the repositories that host DuckDB's components, such as clients and extensions.
* [Release Cycle](#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle) describes the release process of DuckDB and its core extensions.

* [Build Configuration](#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration) lists the build types and options.

* [sqllogictest Introduction](#docs:2.0:dev:sqllogictest:intro) introduces the sqllogictest format used for most of DuckDB's tests.
* [Writing Tests](#docs:2.0:dev:sqllogictest:writing_tests) describes how to write new tests.

#### Performance {#docs:2.0:dev:overview::performance}
