## Release Cycle {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle}

This document outlines the DuckDB and core extension release cycle framework. It is intended for developers working on
DuckDB extensions to better understand the underlying processes.

#### Overview {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::overview}

- DuckDB follows [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/) (` v<MAJOR>.<MINOR>.<PATCH>`)
- Feature releases (new minor or major versions) are released approximately every 6 months, e.g., v1.4.0 in September 2025, v1.5.0 in March 2026 and v2.0.0 in October 2026
- Patch releases are issued as needed for all supported versions:
    - The latest stable version
    - Long Term Support (LTS) versions within their support period
    - Versions with extended support (e.g., v1.5, which is supported until March 2027)
- All releases and their end-of-life dates are listed in the [Release Calendar](https://duckdb.org/release_calendar)

##### Terminology {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::terminology}

In the release docs we use some basic terminology to describe versions and branches. We briefly go over them here.

- **`vx.y.z`**: The latest stable release
- **`vx.y-codename`**: The name of the branch that will produce `vx.y.<n>` releases
- **`vx.<y+1>-codename`**: The branch name that is used for the branch that will produce the next minor release
- **`Main release cycle`**: The branches, commits, and PRs related to producing `vx.<y+1>.0` and `vx.y.<z+1>` releases
- **`Active branch`**: A branch that is part of the main release cycle. Either main or vx.<y+n>-codename where n >= 0
- **`Single branch extension`**: Extension with 1 active branch. Since main is always an active branch this is always
  main. This means all other branches of format `vx.y-codename` must be `vx.<y-n>-codename` where `n >= 1`
- **`Multi branch extension`**: Extension with more than 1 active branch
- **`Two branch extension`**: Extension with two active branches: main and `vx.y-codename`
- **`Three branch extension`**: Extension with three active branches: main, `vx.y-codename`, and `vx.<y+1>-codename`
- **`LTS release`**: Long term support release. These releases will receive support (patch releases) beyond their
  lifetime in the active release cycle. Currently LTS releases will receive 1 year of support
- **`Unstable API extension`**: An extension targeting the *unstable* extension API. This can be both the C++ API or the
  unstable C API. These extensions are not binary-compatible across multiple DuckDB versions
- **`Stable API extension`**: An extension targeting the *stable* C API of DuckDB. These extensions are
  binary-compatible across multiple DuckDB versions
- **`In-tree extensions`**: Extensions that live inside the `duckdb/duckdb` source tree

##### Main Branches and Tags {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::main-branches-and-tags}

In git-based version control, branches are used to allow multiple versions of the same codebase to co-exist. At DuckDB,
there are two core branches that play the main role in the DuckDB (and extensions) release cycle. We will start off by
listing the format these core branches come in.

- **`main`** branch: the main branch can mean various things, but can generally be considered the catch-all branch
- **`vx.y-codename`** branch: the branch used to produce all `vx.y.z` releases
- **`vx.y.z`** tag: a stable release of DuckDB. These tags are write-only and will always be tied to the same commit

#### The Main DuckDB Release Cycle {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::the-main-duckdb-release-cycle}

> LTS (Long-Term Support) releases follow a separate maintenance cycle to provide extended support and stability.

The main DuckDB release cycle consists of 3 main phases: *Mid-cycle*, *Pre-release* and *Feature freeze*. These phases are clearly defined and communicated to ensure the
whole team is synchronized and working together towards the next release.

##### Phase 1: Mid-Cycle {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::phase-1-mid-cycle}

###### Active DuckDB Branches {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::active-duckdb-branches}

- `main`
- `vx.y-codename`

###### Description {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::description}

The *mid-cycle* phase is the most common phase of the release cycle, with about 75% of the time being spent in this
phase. It can be seen as *business-as-usual*, where the upcoming release is still far away and the team is working hard
on merging a variety of features and bug-fixes. During this phase, patch releases (` vx.y.<z+n>`) may be created from the
`vx.y-codename` branch. The patches are merged into the `vx.y-codename` branch, and the `vx.y-codename` branch is
frequently merged into main to keep the two in sync.

###### PRs into DuckDB {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::prs-into-duckdb}

- Bug-fixes for `vx.y.<z+n>` patch releases are merged into `vx.y-codename`
- Features and bug-fixes for `vx.<y+1>.0` are merged into `main`

##### Phase 2: Pre-Release {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::phase-2-pre-release}

###### Active Branches {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::active-branches}

- `main`
- `vx.y-codename`
- `vx.<y+1>-codename`

###### Description {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::description}

The pre-release phase is intended to prepare for the upcoming `vx.<y+1>.0` minor release. At the start of this phase,
the `vx.<y+1>-codename` branch is created. This branch will be used to produce the upcoming minor release and is the
branch from which all subsequent `vx.<y+1>.<n>` patch releases are released.

###### PRs into DuckDB {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::prs-into-duckdb}

- Bug-fixes for `vx.y.<z+1>` patch releases are merged into `vx.y-codename`
- Features and bug-fixes for `vx.<y+1>.0` are merged into `vx.<y+1>-codename`
- Features for `vx.<y+2>.0` are merged into `main`

##### Phase 3: Feature Freeze {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::phase-3-feature-freeze}

###### Active Branches {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::active-branches}

- `main`
- `vx.y-codename`
- `vx.<y+1>-codename`

###### Description {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::description}

The feature freeze phase is the phase closest to release. During this phase features are no longer allowed to be merged
into `vx.<y+1>-codename` and only bug fixes are merged. This phase is intended to ensure the quality of the upcoming
release. During this phase additional testing and benchmarking is performed while reducing the risk of introducing
last-minute bugs by disallowing feature merges.

###### PRs into DuckDB {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::prs-into-duckdb}

- Bug-fixes for `vx.y.<z+1>` are no longer allowed, should target `vx.<y+1>.0` instead
- Bug-fixes for `vx.<y+1>.0` are merged into `vx.<y+1>-codename`
- Features for `vx.<y+1>.0` are no longer allowed, should target `vx.<y+2>.0` instead
- Features for `vx.<y+2>.0` are merged into `main`

#### Main Extension Release Cycle {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::main-extension-release-cycle}

Most DuckDB extensions are completely separate from the main `duckdb/duckdb` repository and are free to follow their own
release cycle. In this section we categorize different types of DuckDB extensions and go over their release cycles.

To describe the release cycle of extensions, we need to first categorize extensions in three different groups, as
extensions share the same release cycle based on which of these three categories they belong to.

- In-tree extensions
- Unstable API extensions
- Stable API extensions

We will now go over the release cycles of the three different categories, in order of increasing complexity.

##### In-Tree Extensions {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::in-tree-extensions}

For *in-tree extensions*, the release cycle is very simple. Since their code lives in the `duckdb/duckdb` repository,
they move in complete lock-step with DuckDB. This means they share the same versioning and branching. In this sense they
are not really extensions, but more lazy-loadable parts of the `duckdb/duckdb` codebase.

##### Stable API Extensions {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::stable-api-extensions}

Stable API extensions in DuckDB are a relatively new concept, but are planned to form the majority of extensions in the
future. Stable API extensions are built on the stable C extension API, making them binary compatible with multiple
versions of DuckDB. This means that their release cycle can/should also be completely separate from the DuckDB release
cycle.

While the release cycle for stable API extensions is still work in progress, the basic idea is that the release cycle of
stable API extensions consists of a similar but separate cycle to that of `duckdb/duckdb`, where every version will
target 1 or more versions of DuckDB.

##### Unstable API Extensions {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::unstable-api-extensions}

Unstable API extensions currently make up the majority of DuckDB extensions. These extensions either target the C++
extension API, or the unstable C extension API. They are, from a release cycle point of view, the most complex. Every
version of an unstable API extension only targets a single DuckDB version. This 1:1 tie means that the release cycle of
these extensions tends to form a sometimes intricate dance around the main DuckDB release cycle. While the goal is to
move as many extensions over to stable APIs, we expect unstable API extensions to be around for quite some time so there
remains a need to clearly define their lifecycle. Therefore we will use the remainder of this section to describe it.

###### Categorizing by Branching {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::categorizing-by-branching}

To start, we will divide the unstable API extensions into different subcategories. Just like DuckDB itself, these
extensions follow the same branching scheme as DuckDB where a combination of `main` and `vx.y-codename` play the main
role. We will now define the three types of unstable extensions by looking at their **number of active branches**.

- **Single branch extensions** have only the `main` *active* branch
- **Two branch extensions** have two *active* branches: `main` and `vx.y-codename`
- **Three branch extensions** have three *active* branches: `main`, `vx.y-codename`, and `vx.<y+1>-codename`

###### DuckDB Targets {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::duckdb-targets}

Every unstable API extension should target a single version of DuckDB. This target version is defined by a combination
of **the `duckdb` submodule** and the target version in the [`MainDistributionPipeline`](https://github.com/duckdb/extension-template/blob/main/.github/workflows/MainDistributionPipeline.yml) workflow.
Which version an extension targets depends on the release cycle phase and the branch. We will now go over all
combinations

- Phase: **Mid-cycle**
    - Type: **Single branch**
        - Extension **`main`** `->` DuckDB **`vx.y.z`** or **`main`**
    - Type: **Two branch**
        - Extension **`main`** `->` DuckDB **`vx.y.z`** or **`main`**
        - Extension **`vx.y-codename`** `->` DuckDB **`vx.y.z`** or **`vx.y-codename`**
    - Type: **Three branch**: should not exist
- Phase: **Pre-release** / **Patch**
    - Type: **Single branch**
        - Extension **`main`** `->` DuckDB **`vx.y.z`** or **`vx.<y+1>-codename`**
    - Type: **Two branch**
        - Extension **`main`** `->` DuckDB **`vx.y.z`** or **`vx.<y+1>-codename`**
        - Extension **`vx.y-codename`** `->` DuckDB **`vx.y.z`** or **`vx.y-codename`**
    - Type: **Three branch**
        - Extension **`main`** `->` DuckDB **`main`**
        - Extension **`vx.y-codename`** `->` DuckDB **`vx.y.z`** or **`vx.y-codename`**
        - Extension **`vx.<y+1>-codename`** `->` DuckDB **`vx.<y+1>-codename`**

###### Where to Merge PRs {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::where-to-merge-prs}

To know where to merge a PR into an unstable API extension depends on two things: the
current release phase and the type of extensions. We will now go over all combinations.

- Phase: **Mid-cycle**
    - Type: **Single branch**
        - if DuckDB target: `vx.y.z`:
            - PR for **`vx.y.<z+1>`** into **`main`**[^1]
            - PR for **`vx.<y+1>.0`** merges into **`main`**
        - if DuckDB target: `main`:
            - PR for **`vx.y.<z+1>`** are **impossible**
            - PR for **`vx.<y+1>.0`** merges into **`main`**
    - Type: **Two branch**
        - PR for **`vx.y.<z+1>`** merges into **`vx.y-codename`**
        - PR for **`vx.<y+1>.0`** merges into **`main`**
    - Type: **Three branch**
        - PR for **`vx.y.<z+1>`** merges into **`vx.y-codename`**
        - PR for **`vx.<y+1>.0`** merges into **`vx.<y+1>-codename`**
        - PR for **`vx.<y+2>.0`** merges into **`main`**
- Phase: **Pre-release** / **Patch**
    - Type: **Single branch**
        - if DuckDB target: `vx.y.z`:
            - PR for **`vx.y.<z+1>`** into **`main`**[^1] [^2]
            - PR for **`vx.<y+1>.0`** merges into **`main`**
        - if DuckDB target: `main`:
            - PR for **`vx.y.<z+1>`** are **impossible**
            - PR for **`vx.<y+1>.0`** merges into **`main`**
    - Type: **Two branch**
        - PR for **`vx.y.<z+1>`** merges into **`vx.y-codename`** [^2]
        - PR for **`vx.<y+1>.0`** merges into **`main`**
    - Type: **Three branch**
        - PR for **`vx.y.<z+1>`** merges into **`vx.y-codename`**[^2]
        - PR for **`vx.<y+1>.0`** merges into **`vx.<y+1>-codename`**
        - PR for **`vx.<y+2>.0`** merges into **`main`**

[^1]: Single branch extensions require manual version updates to ensure changes are included in the targeted release.
[^2]: Patch releases during pre-release or feature-freeze phases are uncommon. Consider targeting changes for the next
minor release instead.

###### What Extension Version Will Be Released? {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::what-extension-version-will-be-released}

Every DuckDB release, a complete set of all core extensions should be available. For unstable API extensions, this means
a rebuild of the binaries. For the core extensions, this build generally happens through the `duckdb/duckdb` CI. This
means that the list of extensions that will be available on release is documented in
the [extension config files](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/tree/main/.github/config/extensions). However, this config
file may not always be up to date. To decide which version of an extension should be part of the upcoming release, we
define the following sources-of-truth for latest extension version based on the release type (major/minor) and extension
type (single/multi branch):

- Release type: **Patch**
    - Extension type: **Single branch**
        - Latest version: **commit
          in [config files](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/tree/main/.github/config/extensions)**
    - Extension type: **Multi branch**
        - Latest version: Extension **`vx.y-codename`** branch
- Release type: **Minor**
    - Extension type: **Single branch**
        - Latest version: Extension **`main`** branch
    - Extension type: **Two branch**
        - Latest version: Extension **`main`** branch
    - Extension type: **Three branch**
        - Latest version: Extension **`vx.<y+1>-codename`** branch

###### Switching between Single Branch, Two Branch and Three Branch {#docs:2.0:dev:release_cycle::switching-between-single-branch-two-branch-and-three-branch}

Switching between the different branch types for extensions is a fairly straightforward process and should be done as follows:

- Switch: **Single branch** `->` **Two branch**
    - When: during **any** phase
    - Reasons:
        - When desire arises to merge features not eligible for `vx.y.<z+1>` while also maintaining ability to do releases for `vx.y.<z+n>`
        - To be able to test with latest DuckDB main while maintaining ability to do releases for `vx.y.<z+n>` (including `vx.y.z` itself)
    - Actions:
        - Create branch `vx.y-codename` from a commit on main between HEAD of `main` and the commit in the DuckDB `vx.y.z` config file.
- Switch: **Two branch** `->` **Three branch**
    - When: during **Pre-release** or **Feature-freeze** phase
    - Reasons:
        - Whenever a feature needs to be merged that is not eligible for merging into `vx.<y+1>.0`.
    - Actions:
        - Create `vx.<y+1>-codename` branch from main
- Switch **Three branch** `->` **Two branch** or **Two branch** `->` **Single branch**
    - When: part of transition from **Feature Freeze** `->` **Mid-cycle**
    - Action: happens automatically (` vx.y-codename` becomes *inactive* by definition)

## Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics}

DuckDB provides a set of metrics that can be used to monitor the performance and health of the database.
Metrics are named `⟨group⟩.⟨metric⟩`, e.g., `query.total_time` or `operator.timing`.

The set of collected metrics is controlled with the [`tracked_metrics` setting](#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::pragmas), which takes a list of glob patterns, e.g., `['query.*', 'operator.timing']`.
By default, all metrics are collected (` ['*']`).
The available metrics, along with their types and units, can be listed with the `duckdb_available_metrics()` table function:

```sql
SELECT metric_name, metric_type, unit
FROM duckdb_available_metrics();
```



#### All Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::all-metrics}

The metrics are organized into the following groups:

* [`query`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::query-metrics)
* [`system`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::system-metrics)
* [`io`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::io-metrics)
* [`storage`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::storage-metrics)
* [`operator`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::operator-metrics)
* [`optimizer`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::optimizer-metrics)
* [`parser`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::parser-metrics)
* [`planner`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::planner-metrics)
* [`physical_planner`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::physical_planner-metrics)

##### `query` Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::query-metrics}

Metrics measured over the entire query.

| Name                                  | Type     | Unit       | Description                                                                |
|---------------------------------------|----------|------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `query.cpu_time`                      | `double` | seconds    | CPU time spent on the query                                                |
| `query.sql`                           | `string` |            | The SQL string of the query                                                |
| `query.total_intermediate_rows`       | `uint64` | rows       | Cumulative number of intermediate rows produced by the query               |
| `query.total_intermediate_size_bytes` | `uint64` | bytes      | Cumulative size in bytes of all intermediate results produced by the query |
| `query.total_row_groups_scanned`      | `uint64` | row_groups | Cumulative number of row groups scanned by the query                       |
| `query.total_row_groups_to_scan`      | `uint64` | row_groups | Cumulative total number of row groups available to scan                    |
| `query.total_rows_scanned`            | `uint64` | rows       | Cumulative number of rows scanned by the query                             |
| `query.total_time`                    | `double` | seconds    | Time spent executing the entire query                                      |

##### `system` Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::system-metrics}

Metrics on system resources, such as memory and threads, used while running the query.

| Name                                | Type     | Unit    | Description                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------------------|----------|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `system.blocked_thread_time`        | `double` | seconds | Time spent waiting for a thread to become available                                                                                                              |
| `system.peak_buffer_memory`         | `uint64` | bytes   | Peak memory usage of the buffer manager                                                                                                                          |
| `system.peak_streaming_buffer_size` | `uint64` | bytes   | Peak number of bytes a streaming query result held: queued bytes plus the units blocked workers hold, both exact. Units still under construction are not counted |
| `system.peak_temp_dir_size`         | `uint64` | bytes   | Peak size of the temporary directory                                                                                                                             |
| `system.total_memory_allocated`     | `uint64` | bytes   | The total memory allocated by the buffer manager                                                                                                                 |

##### `io` Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::io-metrics}

Metrics on the data read from and written to storage.

| Name                     | Type     | Unit   | Description                                  |
|--------------------------|----------|--------|----------------------------------------------|
| `io.total_bytes_read`    | `uint64` | bytes  | The total amount of bytes read from storage  |
| `io.total_bytes_written` | `uint64` | bytes  | The total amount of bytes written to storage |

##### `storage` Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::storage-metrics}

Metrics on storage operations, such as attaching databases, writing to the WAL and checkpointing.

| Name                                   | Type     | Unit    | Description                                                |
|----------------------------------------|----------|---------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| `storage.attach_load_storage_latency`  | `double` | seconds | Time spent loading from storage                            |
| `storage.attach_replay_wal_latency`    | `double` | seconds | Time spent replaying the WAL file                          |
| `storage.checkpoint_latency`           | `double` | seconds | Time spent running checkpoints                             |
| `storage.commit_local_storage_latency` | `double` | seconds | Time spent committing the transaction-local storage        |
| `storage.total_vacuum_time`            | `double` | seconds | Total time spent running vacuum tasks during checkpointing |
| `storage.waiting_to_attach_latency`    | `double` | seconds | Time spent waiting to ATTACH a file                        |
| `storage.wal_replay_entry_count`       | `uint64` | rows    | The total number of entries to replay in the WAL           |
| `storage.write_to_wal_latency`         | `double` | seconds | Time spent writing to the WAL                              |

##### `operator` Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::operator-metrics}

Metrics collected for each individual operator in the query plan. These are reported in the `operator` tree of the profiling output.

| Name                                | Type     | Unit       | Description                                                   |
|-------------------------------------|----------|------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| `operator.cpu_time`                 | `double` | seconds    | CPU time spent in the operator                                |
| `operator.extra_info`               | `map`    |            | Unique operator metrics                                       |
| `operator.intermediate_rows`        | `uint64` | rows       | Number of intermediate rows produced by the operator          |
| `operator.intermediate_size_bytes`  | `uint64` | bytes      | Intermediate size in bytes produced by the operator           |
| `operator.row_groups_scanned`       | `uint64` | row_groups | Number of row groups scanned by the operator                  |
| `operator.rows_scanned`             | `uint64` | rows       | Number of rows scanned by the operator                        |
| `operator.timing`                   | `double` | seconds    | Time spent in the operator                                    |
| `operator.total_row_groups_to_scan` | `uint64` | row_groups | Total number of row groups available for the operator to scan |
| `operator.type`                     | `string` |            | Type of the operator                                          |

##### `optimizer` Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::optimizer-metrics}

Metrics measuring the time spent in the [optimizers](#docs:2.0:internals:overview::optimizer).

| Name                   | Type     | Unit    | Description                           |
|------------------------|----------|---------|---------------------------------------|
| `optimizer.total_time` | `double` | seconds | Time spent in all optimizers combined |

Additionally, each optimizer has a corresponding metric that follows the template `optimizer.⟨optimizer_name⟩` and measures the time (in seconds) spent in that optimizer. These metrics are only collected when the specific optimizer is enabled. The available optimizers can be queried using the [`duckdb_optimizers()`{:.language-sql .highlight} table function](#docs:2.0:sql:meta:duckdb_table_functions::duckdb_optimizers):

`optimizer.expression_rewriter`, `optimizer.filter_pullup`, `optimizer.filter_pushdown`, `optimizer.empty_result_pullup`, `optimizer.cte_filter_pusher`, `optimizer.regex_range`, `optimizer.in_clause`, `optimizer.join_order`, `optimizer.deliminator`, `optimizer.unnest_rewriter`, `optimizer.unused_columns`, `optimizer.statistics_propagation`, `optimizer.common_subexpressions`, `optimizer.common_aggregate`, `optimizer.column_lifetime`, `optimizer.build_side_probe_side`, `optimizer.limit_pushdown`, `optimizer.top_n`, `optimizer.compressed_materialization`, `optimizer.duplicate_groups`, `optimizer.reorder_filter`, `optimizer.sampling_pushdown`, `optimizer.join_filter_pushdown`, `optimizer.extension`, `optimizer.materialized_cte`, `optimizer.aggregate_function_rewriter`, `optimizer.late_materialization`, `optimizer.cte_inlining`, `optimizer.row_group_pruner`, `optimizer.top_n_window_elimination`, `optimizer.common_subplan`, `optimizer.join_elimination`, `optimizer.window_self_join`, `optimizer.projection_pullup`, `optimizer.outer_join_simplification`, `optimizer.row_number_rewriter`, `optimizer.partitioned_execution`, `optimizer.partial_aggregate_pushdown`.

##### `parser` Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::parser-metrics}

Metrics on parsing the SQL query.

| Name                | Type     | Unit    | Description                      |
|---------------------|----------|---------|----------------------------------|
| `parser.total_time` | `double` | seconds | Time spent parsing the SQL query |

##### `planner` Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::planner-metrics}

Metrics on generating the logical plan.

| Name                   | Type     | Unit    | Description                            |
|------------------------|----------|---------|----------------------------------------|
| `planner.binding_time` | `double` | seconds | Time spent binding the logical plan    |
| `planner.total_time`   | `double` | seconds | Time spent generating the logical plan |

##### `physical_planner` Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::physical_planner-metrics}

Metrics on generating the physical plan.

| Name                              | Type     | Unit    | Description                                                            |
|-----------------------------------|----------|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `physical_planner.column_binding` | `double` | seconds | Time spent binding the columns in the logical plan to physical columns |
| `physical_planner.create_plan`    | `double` | seconds | Time spent creating the physical plan                                  |
| `physical_planner.resolve_types`  | `double` | seconds | Time spent resolving the types in the logical plan to physical types   |
| `physical_planner.total_time`     | `double` | seconds | Time spent generating the physical plan                                |

#### Examples {#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::examples}

The following example enables profiling, sets the output to a file and only collects the total query time along with the operator metrics.

```sql
CREATE TABLE students (name VARCHAR, sid INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE exams (eid INTEGER, subject VARCHAR, sid INTEGER);
INSERT INTO students VALUES ('Mark', 1), ('Joe', 2), ('Matthew', 3);
INSERT INTO exams VALUES (10, 'Physics', 1), (20, 'Chemistry', 2), (30, 'Literature', 3);

SET enable_profiling = 'json';
SET profiling_output = '/path/to/file.json';
SET tracked_metrics = ['query.total_time', 'operator.*'];

SELECT name
FROM students
JOIN exams USING (sid)
WHERE name LIKE 'Ma%';
```

The file's content after executing the query:

```json
{
    "operator": [
        {
            "extra_info": {},
            "intermediate_rows": 0,
            "intermediate_size_bytes": 0,
            "timing": 5.458e-06,
            "type": "RESULT_COLLECTOR",
            "children": [
                {
                    "extra_info": {
                        "Projections": "name",
                        "Estimated Cardinality": "1"
                    },
                    "intermediate_rows": 2,
                    "intermediate_size_bytes": 40,
                    "timing": 8.3e-08,
                    "type": "PROJECTION",
                    "children": [
                        {
                            "extra_info": {
                                "Join Type": "INNER",
                                "Conditions": "sid = sid",
                                "Estimated Cardinality": "1"
                            },
                            "intermediate_rows": 2,
                            "intermediate_size_bytes": 48,
                            "timing": 4.4209e-05,
                            "type": "HASH_JOIN",
                            "children": [
...
    "query": {
        "total_time": 0.001491167
    }
}
```

The second example collects all `query` and `planner` metrics, as well as the total time spent in the optimizers.

```sql
SET tracked_metrics = ['query.*', 'planner.*', 'optimizer.total_time'];

SELECT name
FROM students
JOIN exams USING (sid)
WHERE name LIKE 'Ma%';
```

The contents of the output file:

```json
{
    "optimizer": {
        "total_time": 0.000179833
    },
    "planner": {
        "binding_time": 5e-05,
        "total_time": 6.8959e-05
    },
    "query": {
        "cpu_time": 5.8541999999999996e-05,
        "sql": "SELECT name FROM students JOIN exams USING (sid) WHERE name LIKE 'Ma%';\n",
        "total_intermediate_rows": 8,
        "total_intermediate_size_bytes": 136,
        "total_row_groups_scanned": 2,
        "total_row_groups_to_scan": 2,
        "total_rows_scanned": 6,
        "total_time": 0.001529
    }
}
```

## Profiling {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling}

Profiling is essential to help understand why certain queries exhibit specific performance characteristics.
DuckDB contains several built-in features to enable query profiling, which this page covers.
For a high-level example of using `EXPLAIN`, see the [“Inspect Query Plans” page](#docs:2.0:guides:meta:explain).

#### Statements {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::statements}

##### The `EXPLAIN` Statement {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::the-explain-statement}

The first step to profiling a query can include examining the query plan.
The [`EXPLAIN`](#docs:2.0:guides:meta:explain) statement shows the query plan and describes what is going on under the hood.

##### The `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` Statement {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::the-explain-analyze-statement}

The query plan helps developers understand the performance characteristics of the query.
However, it is often also necessary to examine the performance numbers of individual operators and the cardinalities that pass through them.
The [`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`](#docs:2.0:guides:meta:explain_analyze) statement enables obtaining these, as it pretty-prints the query plan and also executes the query.
Thus, it provides the actual run-time performance numbers.

##### The `FORMAT` Option {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::the-format-option}

The `EXPLAIN [ANALYZE]` statement allows exporting to several formats:

* `text` – default ASCII-art style output
* `graphviz` – produces a DOT output, which can be rendered with [Graphviz](https://graphviz.org/)
* `html` – produces an HTML output, which can be rendered with [treeflex](https://dumptyd.github.io/treeflex/)
* `json` – produces a JSON output
* `mermaid` – produces a [Mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org/) flowchart
* `web` – opens the query graph in a web browser (command line client only)

To specify a format, use the `FORMAT` tag:

```sql
EXPLAIN (FORMAT html) SELECT 42 AS x;
```

> New As of DuckDB 2.0, the `web` format is available in the [command line client](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:overview). `EXPLAIN ANALYZE (FORMAT WEB)` renders the query graph and opens it in a web browser, and the [`.web`](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:dot_commands) dot command does the same for the previous query. Both are disabled in [safe mode](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:safe_mode).

#### Pragmas {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::pragmas}

DuckDB supports several pragmas for turning profiling on and off and controlling the level of detail in the profiling output.

The following pragmas are available and can be set using either `PRAGMA` or `SET`.
They can also be reset using `RESET`, followed by the setting name.
For more information, see the [“Profiling”](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::profiling) section of the pragmas page.

| Setting                                                                                                                                                                            | Description                                     | Default                                                  | Options                                                                                                                                                            |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`enable_profiling`](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::enable-profiling), [`enable_profile`](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::enable-profiling)     | Turn on profiling                               | `query_tree`                                             | `query_tree`, `json`, `query_tree_optimizer`, `no_output`                                                                                                          |
| [`profiling_coverage`](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::profiling-coverage)                                                                                        | Set the operators to profile                    | `SELECT`                                                 | `SELECT`, `ALL`                                                                                                                                                    |
| [`profiling_output`](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::profiling-output)                                                                                            | Set a profiling output file                     | Console                                                  | A filepath                                                                                                                                                         |
| [`profiling_mode`](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::profiling-mode)                                                                                                | Deprecated, has no effect                       | `standard`                                               | `standard`, `detailed`, `all`                                                                                                                                       |
| [`tracked_metrics`](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::custom-metrics)                                                                                               | Select which metrics to collect                 | `['*']` (all metrics)                                    | A list of metric glob patterns, e.g. `['query.*', 'optimizer.*']`. ([List of all available metrics](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::all-metrics)) |
| [`disable_profiling`](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::disable-profiling), [`disable_profile`](#docs:2.0:configuration:pragmas::disable-profiling) | Turn off profiling                              |                                                          |                                                                                                                                                                    |

#### Table Functions {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::table-functions}

> These table functions were introduced in DuckDB 1.5.0.

DuckDB provides table functions to enable and disable profiling, consolidating multiple settings into a single call.

##### `enable_profiling()` {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::enable_profiling}

The `enable_profiling()` function configures profiling with the specified options.

```sql
CALL enable_profiling(
    format := 'json',
    save_location := '/path/to/output.json',
    coverage := 'select',
    metrics := ['query.sql', 'query.total_time', 'operator.timing']
);
```

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `metrics` | `LIST`, `STRUCT`, or JSON | Specifies which metrics to enable |
| `mode` | `VARCHAR` | Deprecated, has no effect (detailed profiling information is always collected) |
| `save_location` | `VARCHAR` | File path for profiling output |
| `coverage` | `VARCHAR` | Query coverage: `'select'` or `'all'` |
| `format` | `VARCHAR` | Output format: `'query_tree'`, `'json'`, `'query_tree_optimizer'`, `'no_output'` |

All parameters are optional and named. You can also pass metrics as an unnamed parameter:

```sql
CALL enable_profiling(['query.total_time', 'query.total_intermediate_size_bytes']);
```

##### `disable_profiling()` {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::disable_profiling}

The `disable_profiling()` function turns off profiling.

```sql
CALL disable_profiling();
```

#### Metrics {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::metrics}

DuckDB supports a wide range of metrics that can be enabled or disabled independently. To learn more and to see the full list of available metrics, refer to the [metrics documentation](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::all-metrics).

> New In DuckDB 2.0, the set of collected metrics is controlled with the `tracked_metrics` setting, which takes a list of metric glob patterns such as `['query.*', 'optimizer.*']`. This replaces the `custom_profiling_settings` `PRAGMA` used in earlier versions. The available metric names, types, and units can be listed with the `duckdb_available_metrics()` table function:
>
> ```sql
> SELECT metric_name, metric_type, unit
> FROM duckdb_available_metrics();
> ```

#### Detailed Profiling {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::detailed-profiling}

> **Deprecated.** In DuckDB 2.0, the `profiling_mode` setting is deprecated and has no effect: detailed profiling information, such as the [`planner`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::planner-metrics) and [`optimizer`](#docs:2.0:dev:metrics::optimizer-metrics) metrics, is always collected.
> To restrict the collected metrics, use the `tracked_metrics` setting.

#### Query Graphs {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::query-graphs}

It is also possible to render the profiling output as a query graph.
The query graph visually represents the query plan, showing the operators and their relationships.
The query plan must be output in the `json` format and stored in a file.
After writing a profiling output to its designated file, the Python script can render it as a query graph.
The script requires the `duckdb` Python module to be installed.
It generates an HTML file and opens it in your web browser.

```batch
python -m duckdb.query_graph /path/to/file.json
```

#### Notation in Query Plans {#docs:2.0:dev:profiling::notation-in-query-plans}

In query plans, the [hash join](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_join) operators adhere to the following convention:
the _probe side_ of the join is the left operand, while the _build side_ is the right operand.

Join operators in the query plan show the join type used:

* Inner joins are denoted as `INNER`.
* Left outer joins and right outer joins are denoted as `LEFT` and `RIGHT`, respectively.
* Full outer joins are denoted as `FULL`.

> **Tip.** To visualize query plans, consider using the [DuckDB execution plan visualizer](https://db.cs.uni-tuebingen.de/explain/) developed by the [Database Systems Research Group at the University of Tübingen](https://github.com/DBatUTuebingen).

## Building DuckDB {#dev:building}

### Building DuckDB from Source {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview}

#### When Should You Build DuckDB? {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::when-should-you-build-duckdb}

DuckDB binaries are available for _stable_ and _preview_ builds on the [installation page](https://duckdb.org/install).
In most cases, it's recommended to use these binaries.
When you are running on an experimental platform (e.g., [Raspberry Pi](#docs:2.0:dev:building:raspberry_pi)) or you would like to build the project for an unmerged pull request,
you can build DuckDB from source based on the [`duckdb/duckdb` repository hosted on GitHub](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/).
This page explains the steps for building DuckDB.

#### Build Instructions {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::build-instructions}

##### Prerequisites {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::prerequisites}

> New DuckDB 2.0 requires a C++17 compiler, while earlier versions required a C++11 compiler.

DuckDB needs CMake and a C++17-compliant compiler (e.g., GCC, Clang, Apple-Clang, MSVC).
Additionally, we recommend using the [Ninja build system](https://ninja-build.org/), which automatically parallelizes the build process.

##### Building with the Makefile {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::building-with-the-makefile}

A `Makefile` wraps the build process.
See [Build Configuration](#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration) for targets and configuration flags.

```bash
make
make release # same as plain make
make relassert
make debug
GEN=ninja make # for use with Ninja
BUILD_BENCHMARK=1 make # build with benchmarks
```

> `debug` builds use a lot of disk space – make sure you have at least 25 GB available.

##### Speeding up Subsequent Builds {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::speeding-up-subsequent-builds}

You can speed up subsequent builds using [ccache](https://ccache.dev/).
On macOS, you can install and configure it as follows:

```bash
brew install ccache
ccache -M 50G
```

#### Platforms {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::platforms}

##### Platforms with Full Support {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::platforms-with-full-support}

DuckDB fully supports Linux, macOS and Windows. Both x86_64 (amd64) and AArch64 (ARM64) builds are available for these platforms (except for macOS on x86_64, which only has partial support, see below), and almost all extensions are distributed for these platforms.

| Platform name      | Description                                                            | Comment |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------|
| `linux_amd64`      | Linux x86_64 (AMD64) with [glibc](https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/)  | |
| `linux_arm64`      | Linux AArch64 (ARM64) with [glibc](https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/) | |
| `osx_arm64`        | macOS 12+ ARM64 (Apple Silicon CPUs)                                   | |
| `windows_amd64`    | Windows 10+ x86_64 (AMD64)                                             | |
| `windows_arm64`    | Windows 10+ AArch64 (ARM64)                                            | |

For these platforms, builds are available for both the latest stable version and the preview version (nightly build).
In some circumstances, you may still want to build DuckDB from source, e.g., to test an unmerged [pull request](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pulls).
For build instructions on these platforms, see:

* [Linux](#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux)
* [macOS](#docs:2.0:dev:building:macos)
* [Windows](#docs:2.0:dev:building:windows)

##### Platforms with Partial Support {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::platforms-with-partial-support}

There are several partially supported platforms.
For some platforms, DuckDB binaries and extensions (or a [subset of extensions](#docs:2.0:extensions:extension_distribution::platforms)) are distributed.
For others, building from source is possible.

| Platform name          | Description                                                                                          |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `osx_amd64`            | macOS 12+ x86_64 (AMD64) (Intel CPUs). DuckDB binaries and [core extensions](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:overview) are distributed, but [community extensions](#docs:2.0:extensions:community_extensions) are no longer built for this platform. DuckDB 2.1 will stop supporting `osx_amd64`. |
| `linux_amd64_musl`     | Linux x86_64 (AMD64) with [musl libc](https://musl.libc.org/), e.g., Alpine Linux                    |
| `linux_arm64_musl`     | Linux AArch64 (ARM64) with [musl libc](https://musl.libc.org/), e.g., Alpine Linux                   |
| `linux_arm64_android`  | Android AArch64 (ARM64)                                                                              |
| `wasm_eh`              | WebAssembly Exception Handling                                                                       |

Below, we provide detailed build instructions for some platforms:

* [Android](#docs:2.0:dev:building:android)
* [Raspberry Pi](#docs:2.0:dev:building:raspberry_pi)

##### Platforms with Best Effort Support {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::platforms-with-best-effort-support}

| Platform name          | Description                                                                                          |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `freebsd_amd64`        | FreeBSD x86_64 (AMD64)                                                                               |
| `freebsd_arm64`        | FreeBSD AArch64 (ARM64)                                                                              |
| `openharmony_arm64`    | OpenHarmony AArch64 (ARM64)                                                                          |
| `wasm_mvp`             | WebAssembly Minimum Viable Product                                                                   |
| `windows_amd64_mingw`  | Windows 10+ x86_64 (AMD64) with MinGW                                                                |
| `windows_arm64_mingw`  | Windows 10+ AArch64 (ARM64) with MinGW                                                               |

> These platforms are not covered by DuckDB's community support. For details on commercial support, see the [support policy page](https://ducklabs.com/community_support_policy#platforms).

See the [OpenHarmony page](#docs:2.0:dev:building:openharmony) for build instructions.

See also the [“Unofficial and Unsupported Platforms” page](#docs:2.0:dev:building:unofficial_and_unsupported_platforms) for details.

##### Outdated Platforms {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::outdated-platforms}

Some platforms were supported in older DuckDB versions but are no longer supported.

| Platform name          | Description                                                                                          |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `linux_amd64_gcc4`     | Linux x86_64 (AMD64) with GCC 4, e.g., CentOS 7                                                      |
| `linux_arm64_gcc4`     | Linux AArch64 (ARM64) with GCC 4, e.g., CentOS 7                                                     |
| `windows_amd64_rtools` | Windows 10+ x86_64 (AMD64) for [RTools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/)              |

DuckDB can also be built for end-of-life platforms such as [macOS 11](https://endoflife.date/macos) and [CentOS 7/8](https://endoflife.date/centos) using the instructions provided for macOS and Linux.

#### Troubleshooting Guides {#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::troubleshooting-guides}

We provide troubleshooting guides for building DuckDB:

* [Generic issues](#docs:2.0:dev:building:troubleshooting)
* [Python](#docs:2.0:dev:building:python)
* [R](#docs:2.0:dev:building:r)

### Building Configuration {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration}

#### Build Types {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::build-types}

DuckDB can be built in many different settings, most of these correspond directly to CMake but not all of them.

##### `release` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::release}

This build has been stripped of all the assertions and debug symbols and code, optimized for performance.

##### `debug` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::debug}

This build runs with all the debug information, including symbols, assertions and `#ifdef DEBUG` blocks.
Due to these, binaries of this build are expected to be slow.
Note: the special debug defines are not automatically set for this build.

##### `relassert` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::relassert}

This build does not trigger the `#ifdef DEBUG` code blocks but it still has debug symbols that make it possible to step through the execution with line number information and `D_ASSERT` lines are still checked in this build.
Binaries of this build mode are significantly faster than those of the `debug` mode.

##### `reldebug` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::reldebug}

This build is similar to `relassert` in many ways, only assertions are also stripped in this build.

##### `benchmark` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::benchmark}

This build is a shorthand for `release` with `BUILD_BENCHMARK=1` set.

##### `tidy-check` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::tidy-check}

This creates a build and then runs [Clang-Tidy](https://clang.llvm.org/extra/clang-tidy/) to check for issues or style violations through static analysis.
The CI will also run this check, causing it to fail if this check fails.

##### `format-fix` | `format-changes` | `format-main` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::format-fix--format-changes--format-main}

This doesn't actually create a build, but uses the following format checkers to check for style issues:

* [clang-format](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ClangFormat.html) to fix format issues in the code.
* [cmake-format](https://cmake-format.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) to fix format issues in the `CMakeLists.txt` files.

The CI will also run this check, causing it to fail if this check fails.

#### Extension Selection {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::extension-selection}

[Core DuckDB extensions](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:overview) are the ones maintained by the DuckDB team. These are hosted in the `duckdb` GitHub organization and are served by the `core` extension repository.

Additional extensions can be built as part of DuckDB via the `BUILD_EXTENSIONS` flag, then listing the names of the extensions that are to be built.

```batch
BUILD_EXTENSIONS='tpch;httpfs;fts;json;parquet' make
```

More on this topic at [building DuckDB extensions](#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions).

#### Package Flags {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::package-flags}

The Makefile has flags to control which components are built.
These can be enabled by either setting them in the current `env`, through set up files like `bashrc` or `zshrc`, or by setting them before the call to `make`, for example:

```batch
BUILD_BENCHMARK=1 make debug
```

> The Python, Java (JDBC) and ODBC clients are maintained in separate repositories and are no longer built from the main DuckDB repository. See the [Python](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-python), [Java](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-java) and [ODBC](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-odbc) repositories for their build instructions.

##### `BUILD_BENCHMARK` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::build_benchmark}

When this flag is set, DuckDB's in-house benchmark suite is built.
More information about this can be found [in the README](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/main/benchmark/README.md).

##### `DISABLE_SHELL` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::disable_shell}

The [CLI](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:overview) is built by default. When this flag is set, the CLI is not built.

#### Miscellaneous Flags {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::miscellaneous-flags}

##### `DISABLE_UNITY` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::disable_unity}

To improve compilation time, we use [Unity Build](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/prop_tgt/UNITY_BUILD.html) to combine translation units.
This can however hide include bugs, this flag disables using the unity build so these errors can be detected.

##### `DISABLE_SANITIZER` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::disable_sanitizer}

In some situations, running an executable that has been built with sanitizers enabled is not supported / can cause problems. Julia is an example of this.
With this flag enabled, the sanitizers are disabled for the build.

#### Overriding Git Hash and Version {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::overriding-git-hash-and-version}

It is possible to override the Git hash and version when building from source using the `OVERRIDE_GIT_DESCRIBE` environment variable.
This is useful when building from sources that are not part of a complete Git repository (e.g., an archive file with no information on commit hashes and tags).
For example:

```batch
OVERRIDE_GIT_DESCRIBE=v0.10.0-843-g09ea97d0a9 GEN=ninja make
```

Will result in the following output when running `./build/release/duckdb`:

```text
v0.10.1-dev843 09ea97d0a9
...
```

##### Building without Git {#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration::building-without-git}

Git and Python are optional dependencies for building DuckDB from source.
DuckDB normally derives its version and commit hash from Git, so `OVERRIDE_GIT_DESCRIBE` is primarily useful when building from sources that are not a complete Git checkout.
The version and commit hash are resolved as follows:

* If `OVERRIDE_GIT_DESCRIBE` is set to a full `git describe --tags --long` string (for example, `v1.0.0-843-g09ea97d0a9`), the version, the development iteration, and the commit hash are all extracted from it.
* If `OVERRIDE_GIT_DESCRIBE` is set to a version only (for example, `v1.0.0`), the remaining details are filled in from the current Git commit when Git is available.
* If `OVERRIDE_GIT_DESCRIBE` is not set and Git is available, DuckDB runs `git describe --tags --long` to determine the version and commit hash.
* If `OVERRIDE_GIT_DESCRIBE` is not set and Git is not available, DuckDB falls back to a placeholder version and commit hash, and logs a message during the CMake configuration step. The build still succeeds.

### Building Extensions {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions}

[Extensions](#docs:2.0:extensions:overview) can be built from source and installed from the resulting local binary.

#### Building Extensions {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::building-extensions}

To build using extension flags, set the `BUILD_EXTENSIONS` flag to the list of extensions that you want to be built. For example:

```bash
BUILD_EXTENSIONS='autocomplete;httpfs;icu;json;tpch' GEN=ninja make
```

This option also accepts out-of-tree extensions such as [`delta`](#docs:2.0:core_extensions:delta):

```bash
BUILD_EXTENSIONS='autocomplete;httpfs;icu;json;tpch;delta' GEN=ninja make
```

Since DuckDB 2.0, extensions listed in `BUILD_EXTENSIONS` are built but not statically linked into the DuckDB executable by default: they are installed from the build's own extension repository and loaded on first use. To link them into the executable, set `LINK_CORE_EXTENSIONS=1` or list them in `STATICALLY_LINK_EXTENSIONS` (see [Linking Extensions](#docs:2.0:dev:building:linking_extensions)).

#### Special Extension Flags {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::special-extension-flags}

##### `BUILD_JEMALLOC` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::build_jemalloc}

This flag controls whether the [`jemalloc`](#docs:2.0:internals:jemalloc) memory allocator is linked into DuckDB. Unlike TPC-H and TPC-DS, `jemalloc` is not an extension. It is only supported on 64-bit Linux, where it is enabled by default. To disable it, set `BUILD_JEMALLOC=0`.

##### `BUILD_TPCE` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::build_tpce}

When this flag is set, the [TPCE](https://www.tpc.org/tpce/) library is built. Unlike TPC-H and TPC-DS this is not a proper extension and it's not distributed as such. Enabling this allows TPC-E enabled queries through our test suite.

#### Debug Flags {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::debug-flags}

##### `CRASH_ON_ASSERT` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::crash_on_assert}

`D_ASSERT(condition)` is used all throughout the code, these will throw an InternalException in debug builds.
With this flag enabled, when the assertion triggers it will instead directly cause a crash.

##### `DISABLE_STRING_INLINE` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::disable_string_inline}

In our execution format `string_t` has the feature to “inline” strings that are under a certain length (12 bytes), this means they don't require a separate allocation.
When this flag is set, we disable this and don't inline small strings.

##### `DISABLE_MEMORY_SAFETY` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::disable_memory_safety}

Our data structures that are used extensively throughout the non-performance-critical code have extra checks to ensure memory safety, these checks include:

* Making sure `nullptr` is never dereferenced.
* Making sure index out of bounds accesses don't trigger a crash.

With this flag enabled we remove these checks, this is mostly done to check that the performance hit of these checks is negligible.

##### `DESTROY_UNPINNED_BLOCKS` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::destroy_unpinned_blocks}

When previously pinned blocks in the BufferManager are unpinned, with this flag enabled we destroy them instantly to make sure that there aren't situations where this memory is still being used, despite not being pinned.

##### `DEBUG_STACKTRACE` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::debug_stacktrace}

When a crash or assertion hit occurs in a test, print a stack trace.
This is useful when debugging a crash that is hard to pinpoint with a debugger attached.

#### Using a CMake Configuration File {#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions::using-a-cmake-configuration-file}

To build using a CMake configuration file, create an extension configuration file named `extension_config.cmake` with e.g., the following content:

```cmake
duckdb_extension_load(autocomplete)
duckdb_extension_load(tpch)
duckdb_extension_load(tpcds)
duckdb_extension_load(icu)
duckdb_extension_load(json)
duckdb_extension_load(parquet)
```

Build DuckDB as follows:

```bash
GEN=ninja EXTENSION_CONFIGS="extension_config.cmake" make
```

Then, to install the extensions in one go, run:

```bash
# for release builds
cd build/release/extension/
# for debug builds
cd build/debug/extension/
# install extensions
for EXTENSION in *; do
    ../duckdb -c "INSTALL '${EXTENSION}/${EXTENSION}.duckdb_extension';"
done
```

### Statically Linking Extensions {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linking_extensions}

This page is for client and binding authors, and for anyone who embeds `libduckdb` in their own application.
It describes how statically linking extensions changed in DuckDB 2.0 and what builders on top of DuckDB need to do.

> This change is independent of the new C API. It applies even if you continue to build against the existing (v1) C API: the difference is in how extension archives are linked and registered, not in which API your bindings call.

#### What Changed in DuckDB 2.0 {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linking_extensions::what-changed-in-duckdb-20}

> New Link-time static linking of extensions was introduced in DuckDB 2.0.

Before v2.0, the set of statically linked extensions was a _compile-time_ decision.
The sources were compiled with knowledge of which extensions were included, so a build with `CORE_EXTENSIONS='json;parquet;icu'` could not reuse the object files of a build with `CORE_EXTENSIONS='json;parquet;icu;tpch'`, even though one is a subset of the other.

DuckDB 2.0 modularized this into a _link-time_ decision ([`duckdb#25814`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/25814)).
Each extension is compiled once into its own static archive, for example:

```text
libduckdb_static.a
libcore_functions_extension.a
libparquet_extension.a
libjson_extension.a
libicu_extension.a
```

The list of extensions to link in is now chosen when linking, not when compiling.
As a follow-up, the extension loader and the built-in `httplib` also became opt-in at link time ([`duckdb#26188`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/26188)).

Two aspects that earlier builds relied on are gone:

* The `bundle-library` Makefile target that merged everything into a single `libduckdb_bundle.a`. Extensions, `httplib`, and loadable extensions are now separate archives.
* The generated loader that `libduckdb_static.a` used to register extensions automatically. `libduckdb_static.a` no longer registers extensions on its own.

#### Registering Statically Linked Extensions {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linking_extensions::registering-statically-linked-extensions}

Because extension selection moved to link time, a client that statically links extensions must now _register_ them with the engine before any database is opened.
Each extension archive carries a generated describe function, `duckdb_extension_⟨name⟩_describe`, that fills a `duckdb_extension_descriptor` declared in the new public header `duckdb_static_extension.h`.
The descriptor carries a layout version, so the engine refuses an archive whose descriptor layout it does not support, with a clear message instead of misbehaving.

The engine exposes a C API call, `duckdb_register_static_extension(describe)`, which validates the descriptor and registers the extension for every database opened afterwards.
A generated loader (` static_extension_loader.c`) defines `duckdb_register_static_extensions()`, which passes every linked extension's describe function to `duckdb_register_static_extension` in turn.
Call it once at startup, before any database is opened, from any language that can call C:

```cpp
// Register the statically linked extensions before any database can be opened
if (duckdb_register_static_extensions() != 0) {
    throw std::runtime_error("Failed to register the statically linked DuckDB extensions");
}
```

If registration is skipped, the linked extensions (such as `core_functions`, `icu`, `json`, and `parquet`) are not loaded.
Queries that depend on them then fail at runtime. For example, `SELECT to_minutes(5)` reports that the function exists in the `core_functions` extension, even though that extension was linked in.

A program can also skip the generated loader and call `duckdb_register_static_extension` directly on the describe functions it declares itself.
An archive whose describe function is never registered contributes nothing, and a registered extension whose archive is missing fails the link.

##### Calling the Loader Before `main` {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linking_extensions::calling-the-loader-before-main}

A C++ program that wants registration to happen automatically before `main` compiles `extension/loader/static_extension_autoregister.cpp` alongside the loader.
Compile it into the program itself, not into an archive, or the linker drops it.

If you do package the loader and the auto-register object into an archive, keep the registration symbol from being discarded by forcing it onto the link line:

```bash
-Wl,-u,duckdb_register_static_extensions
```

#### Build Options {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linking_extensions::build-options}

When building DuckDB or `libduckdb`, select the extensions to compile with `BUILD_EXTENSIONS` (or `CORE_EXTENSIONS`):

```bash
BUILD_EXTENSIONS='core_functions;json;parquet;icu' GEN=ninja make
```

Which of the built extensions are statically linked is a separate decision.
By default the DuckDB targets link the extensions that the build configs mark for static linking, plus the ones named in `BUILD_EXTENSIONS` when you build with `LINK_CORE_EXTENSIONS=1`.
To link an explicit set instead, set `STATICALLY_LINK_EXTENSIONS` (the older name for this flag is `LINK_EXTENSIONS`):

```bash
STATICALLY_LINK_EXTENSIONS='core_functions;parquet;json;icu;tpch' make
```

Changing the linked set only re-generates the loader, compiles it, and re-links; it does not recompile the extensions themselves.
An extension that is built but not statically linked is still available: it is installed from the build's own extension repository and loaded the first time a query needs it.

##### Linking the Archives by Hand {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linking_extensions::linking-the-archives-by-hand}

Outside CMake, link one archive per extension, compile the generated loader, and put the engine archive last:

```bash
LINK_EXTENSIONS='parquet;json' make static_extension_loader
cc -I src/include main.c build/release/static_extension_loader.c libparquet_extension.a libjson_extension.a libduckdb_static.a -lstdc++
```

The order matters: each extension archive must come before `libduckdb_static.a` on the link line.

See [Build Configuration](#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration) and [Building Extensions](#docs:2.0:dev:building:building_extensions) for the full set of flags.

#### Obtaining Prebuilt Archives {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linking_extensions::obtaining-prebuilt-archives}

Rather than building `libduckdb` yourself, you can download the static and shared archives for DuckDB 2.0 and later using the [`duckdb-install-scripts`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-install-scripts) tooling ([`duckdb-install-scripts#5`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-install-scripts/pull/5)).
Setting `DUCKDB_INSTALL=static` installs the archives and headers under `~/.duckdb/lib/⟨version⟩/⟨build_type⟩_⟨platform⟩` (e.g., `~/.duckdb/lib/2.0.0/release_osx_arm64`):

```bash
curl https://install.duckdb.org | DUCKDB_INSTALL=static bash
```

Use `DUCKDB_INSTALL=shared` for the shared library, or combine components, e.g., `DUCKDB_INSTALL=static,shared,cli`. See the [install script page](#docs:2.0:operations_manual:installing_duckdb:install_script) for details.

This installs, for example:

```text
duckdb.h                      duckdb_v2.h
duckdb_extension.h            duckdb_extension_v2.h
duckdb_static_extension.h
libduckdb_static.a            libcore_functions_extension.a
libparquet_extension.a        libjson_extension.a
libicu_extension.a            libautocomplete_extension.a
libtpch_extension.a           libtpcds_extension.a
```

A specific release can be installed by setting `DUCKDB_VERSION` (e.g., `DUCKDB_VERSION=2.0.0`). Static and shared libraries are only available for DuckDB 2.0 and later.

> For DuckDB 2.0 and later, most artifacts are distributed as `.tar.gz` files instead of `.zip` files ([`duckdb#24773`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/24773)).

#### Reference Implementations for Clients {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linking_extensions::reference-implementations-for-clients}

The following pull requests adapt the official clients to the v2.0 linking model.
They provide a path forward for anyone maintaining a binding or an application that links `libduckdb`.



| Client | Status | Reference pull requests |
|---|---|---|
| Python | Migrated | [`duckdb-python#634`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-python/pull/634) |
| Rust | Migrated | [`duckdb-rs#834`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-rs/pull/834), [`duckdb-rs#839`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-rs/pull/839), [`duckdb-rs#883`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-rs/pull/883), [`duckdb-rs#835`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-rs/pull/835) |
| Node.js | In progress | [`duckdb-node-neo#476`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-node-neo/pull/476), [`duckdb-node-neo#508`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-node-neo/pull/508), [`duckdb-node-neo#512`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-node-neo/pull/512) |
| Go | In progress | [`duckdb-go-bindings#112`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-go-bindings/issues/112), [`duckdb-go-bindings#116`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-go-bindings/pull/116) |
| Wasm | In progress | [`duckdb-wasm#2281`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-wasm/pull/2281) |

> The Python pull request is the clearest end-to-end example: it restores static linking of the default `BUILD_EXTENSIONS` set by calling `duckdb_register_static_extensions()` and shows how to override the linked set.

### Android {#docs:2.0:dev:building:android}

DuckDB has experimental support for Android. Please use the latest `main` branch of DuckDB instead of the stable versions.

#### Building the DuckDB Library Using the Android NDK {#docs:2.0:dev:building:android::building-the-duckdb-library-using-the-android-ndk}

We provide build instructions for setups using macOS and Android Studio. For other setups, please adjust the steps accordingly.

1. Open [Android Studio](https://developer.android.com/studio).
   Select the **Tools** menu and pick **SDK Manager**.
   Select the SDK Tools tab and tick the **NDK (Side by side)** option.
   Click **OK** to install.

1. Set the Android NDK's location. For example:

   ```bash
   ANDROID_NDK=~/Library/Android/sdk/ndk/28.0.12433566/
   ```

1. Set the [Android ABI](https://developer.android.com/ndk/guides/abis). For example:

   ```bash
   ANDROID_ABI=arm64-v8a
   ```

   Or:

   ```bash
   ANDROID_ABI=x86_64
   ```

1. If you would like to use the [Ninja build system](#docs:2.0:dev:building:overview::prerequisites), make sure it is installed and available on the `PATH`.

1. Set the list of DuckDB extensions to build. These will be statically linked in the binary. For example:

   ```bash
   DUCKDB_EXTENSIONS="icu;json;parquet"
   ```

1. Navigate to DuckDB's directory and run the build as follows:

   ```bash
   PLATFORM_NAME="android_${ANDROID_ABI}"
   BUILDDIR=./build/${PLATFORM_NAME}
   mkdir -p ${BUILDDIR}
   cd ${BUILDDIR}
   cmake \
       -G "Ninja" \
       -DEXTENSION_STATIC_BUILD=1 \
       -DDUCKDB_EXTRA_LINK_FLAGS="-llog" \
       -DBUILD_EXTENSIONS=${DUCKDB_EXTENSIONS} \
       -DENABLE_EXTENSION_AUTOLOADING=1 \
       -DENABLE_EXTENSION_AUTOINSTALL=1 \
       -DCMAKE_VERBOSE_MAKEFILE=on \
       -DANDROID_PLATFORM=${ANDROID_PLATFORM} \
       -DLOCAL_EXTENSION_REPO="" \
       -DOVERRIDE_GIT_DESCRIBE="" \
       -DDUCKDB_EXPLICIT_PLATFORM=${PLATFORM_NAME} \
       -DBUILD_UNITTESTS=0 \
       -DBUILD_SHELL=1 \
       -DANDROID_ABI=${ANDROID_ABI} \
       -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=${ANDROID_NDK}/build/cmake/android.toolchain.cmake \
       -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release ../..
   cmake \
       --build . \
       --config Release
   ```

1. For the `arm64-v8a` ABI, the build will produce the `build/android_arm64-v8a/duckdb` and `build/android_arm64-v8a/src/libduckdb.so` binaries.

#### Building the CLI in Termux {#docs:2.0:dev:building:android::building-the-cli-in-termux}

1. To build the [command line client](#docs:2.0:clients:cli:overview) in the [Termux application](https://termux.dev/), install the following packages:

   ```bash
   pkg install -y git ninja clang cmake python3
   ```

1. Set the list of DuckDB extensions to build. These will be statically linked in the binary. For example:

   ```bash
   DUCKDB_EXTENSIONS="icu;json"
   ```

1. Build DuckDB as follows:

   ```bash
   mkdir build
   cd build
   export LDFLAGS="-llog"
   cmake \
      -G "Ninja" \
      -DBUILD_EXTENSIONS="${DUCKDB_EXTENSIONS}" \
      -DDUCKDB_EXPLICIT_PLATFORM=linux_arm64_android \
      -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      ..
   cmake --build . --config Release
   ```

Note that you can also use the Python client on Termux:

```bash
pip install --pre --upgrade duckdb
```

#### Troubleshooting {#docs:2.0:dev:building:android::troubleshooting}

##### Log Library Is Missing {#docs:2.0:dev:building:android::log-library-is-missing}

**Problem:**
The build throws the following error:

```console
ld.lld: error: undefined symbol: __android_log_write
```

**Solution:**
Make sure the log library is linked:

```bash
export LDFLAGS="-llog"
```

### OpenHarmony {#docs:2.0:dev:building:openharmony}

DuckDB supports building for OpenHarmony (OHOS) AArch64 (ARM64) on a best-effort basis.
On this platform, DuckDB reports the platform name `openharmony_arm64`.
Prebuilt binaries and extensions are not distributed for this platform.

#### Prerequisites {#docs:2.0:dev:building:openharmony::prerequisites}

DuckDB needs CMake, Ninja, and a C++17 compiler on the build host, plus the OpenHarmony SDK.
The Linux x64 SDK from the OpenHarmony release page can be used for cross-compilation.
The repository ships a toolchain file that handles both the Linux x64 SDK layout and the
on-device SDK layout.

Set `OHOS_SDK` to the `native` directory of the SDK:

```bash
export OHOS_SDK=/path/to/ohos-sdk/linux/native
```

#### Cross-Compiling {#docs:2.0:dev:building:openharmony::cross-compiling}

Configure with the OpenHarmony toolchain file:

```bash
cmake -G Ninja -B build/openharmony \
    -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE="$PWD/scripts/ohos-toolchain.cmake" \
    -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
    -DDUCKDB_EXPLICIT_PLATFORM=openharmony_arm64

cmake --build build/openharmony --parallel
```

`DUCKDB_EXPLICIT_PLATFORM` is required when cross-compiling because the platform probe
binary cannot run on the build host.
The resulting `build/openharmony/duckdb` is an AArch64 musl binary.

#### Building on an OpenHarmony Device {#docs:2.0:dev:building:openharmony::building-on-an-openharmony-device}

On a device, CMake detects the OpenHarmony toolchain and the platform probe runs natively,
so `DUCKDB_EXPLICIT_PLATFORM` is not required:

```bash
cmake -G Ninja -B build/openharmony \
    -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE="$PWD/scripts/ohos-toolchain.cmake" \
    -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

cmake --build build/openharmony --parallel
./build/openharmony/duckdb -c "PRAGMA platform;"
```

#### Notes {#docs:2.0:dev:building:openharmony::notes}

- The shell must not be stripped on OpenHarmony: the OS verifies the ELF `.codesign`
  section on exec.
- No prebuilt extensions are distributed for `openharmony_arm64`; build the extensions you
  need from source. `INSTALL <extension>` reports that no extension is available for this
  platform.
- Loadable extensions built with the CMake build are re-signed after DuckDB appends
  its metadata footer, so they can be `dlopen`ed on OpenHarmony.
- The unittest binary is linked against the static DuckDB library on OpenHarmony because
  the shared library does not export the internal symbols used by the test helpers.

### Linux {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux}

#### Prerequisites {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::prerequisites}

On Linux, install the required packages with the package manager of your distribution.

##### Ubuntu and Debian {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::ubuntu-and-debian}

###### CLI Client {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::cli-client}

On Ubuntu and Debian (and also MX Linux, Linux Mint, etc.), the requirements for building the DuckDB CLI client are the following:

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y git g++ cmake ninja-build libssl-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev
git clone https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb
cd duckdb
GEN=ninja make
```

##### Fedora, CentOS and Red Hat {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::fedora-centos-and-red-hat}

###### CLI Client {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::cli-client}

The requirements for building the DuckDB CLI client on Fedora, CentOS, Red Hat, AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux, etc. are the following:

```bash
sudo yum install -y git g++ cmake ninja-build openssl-devel
git clone https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb
cd duckdb
GEN=ninja make
```

Note that on older Red Hat-based distributions, you may have to change the package name for `g++` to `gcc-c++`,
skip Ninja and manually configure the number of Make jobs:

```bash
sudo yum install -y git gcc-c++ cmake openssl-devel
git clone https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb
cd duckdb
mkdir build
cd build
cmake ..
make -j`nproc`
```

##### Arch Linux {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::arch-linux}

The following instructions are intended for Arch Linux and Arch-based distributions (e.g., Manjaro, Omarchy).

###### CLI Client {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::cli-client}

DuckDB is [available in Arch's Extra package repository](https://archlinux.org/packages/extra/x86_64/duckdb/).
To install it, run:

```bash
sudo pacman -S duckdb
```

The requirements for building the DuckDB CLI client on Arch, Manjaro, etc. are the following:

```bash
sudo pacman -S git gcc cmake ninja openssl
git clone https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb
cd duckdb
GEN=ninja make
```

##### Alpine Linux {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::alpine-linux}

###### CLI Client {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::cli-client}

The requirements for building the DuckDB CLI client on Alpine Linux are the following:

```bash
apk add g++ git make cmake ninja
git clone https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb
cd duckdb
GEN=ninja make
```

###### Performance with musl libc {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::performance-with-musl-libc}

Note that Alpine Linux uses [musl libc](https://musl.libc.org/) as its C standard library.
DuckDB binaries built with musl libc have lower performance compared to the glibc variants: for some workloads, the slowdown can be more than 5×.
Therefore, it's recommended to use glibc for performance-oriented workloads.

###### Distribution for the `linux_*_musl` Platforms {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::distribution-for-the-linux__musl-platforms}

Starting with DuckDB 1.2.0, [_DuckDB extensions_ are distributed for the `linux_amd64_musl` platform](https://duckdb.org/2025/02/05/announcing-duckdb-120#musl-extensions), and starting with DuckDB 1.5.0 also for the `linux_arm64_musl` platform.
Since DuckDB 1.5.0, official CLI binaries and libraries are also distributed for both musl platforms (e.g., `duckdb-cli-linux-amd64-musl.tar.gz` on the [GitHub release page](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/releases)). You can also build DuckDB with musl libc manually following the instructions on this page.

###### Python Client on Alpine Linux {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::python-client-on-alpine-linux}

Currently, installing the DuckDB Python on Alpine Linux requires compilation from source.
To do so, install the required packages before running `pip`:

```bash
apk add g++ py3-pip python3-dev
pip install duckdb
```

#### Using the DuckDB CLI Client on Linux {#docs:2.0:dev:building:linux::using-the-duckdb-cli-client-on-linux}

Once the build finishes successfully, you can find the `duckdb` binary in the `build` directory:

```bash
build/release/duckdb
```

For different build configurations (` debug`, `relassert`, etc.), please consult the [“Build Configurations” page](#docs:2.0:dev:building:build_configuration).
